Mr. Thomas Keay Tapling,Conservative M.P.,' who died on Saturday, was head of the firm of Tapling and Co., carpetmen, Gresham-st. He was about 35, , and had represented the Harborough Division since 188 G after being beaten for the same division in 1885. It may fairly be said that his geniality not only won him the seat, but retained for him the cordial respect of his political opponents. He was called to the Bar, but never practised, and never bad occasion to do so, as his father left him a large fortune and a flourishing business. He was not a good politician—did not take to the study of poli- tics as he did. to stamp collecting, which was his hobby. His collection includes over a hundred thousand specimens, and is said to be worth over .£5,000. He was probably the best cricketer iu the present House of Commons, his name having fre- quently figured in the Leicestershire County Eleven.

div.head: "CAPITAL CHAT."
div.p: "CAPITAL CHAT."
Mr. Seale-Hayne, MJP., will entertain Mr. Glad- 'stone at dinner next Wednesday, to meet the other members of Parliament who were educated at Eton. Of these there are eleven.

It has been ananged in conference between the leading counsel in the baccarat case that it shall not be taken before to-day (Saturday.) The Prince of Wales has not been subpcenaed as a witness, but we understand that he will throughout the trial be in attendance in the neighbourhood of the Court.

The Government will shortly have occasion to appoint another Royal Commission. The task al- lotted to it mill be to assist British merchants in making arrangements for exhibiting their products at the World's Fa k to be held at Chicago next year in commemoration of the centenary of the United States Republic. The British Government has re- ceived a formal invitation to take part in the Fair, and ithas been accepted by Lord Salisbury.

Mr. George Rignold, brother of Lionel, and lessee of her Majesty's Theatre, Sydney, stopped an inci- pient panic recently in a very plain-spoken fashion. Appearing before the curtain, he said :—" Ladies and gentlemen, sit still and don't make fools of your- selves. You smell fire, and so do I, but there's no danger. We've simply lit a fire for stage purposes." Then the people who were making for the doors returned, looking rather sheepish, and resumed their seats.

With reference to a quotation which appeared the other day to the effect that Lady Henry Somerset, president of the English Women's Temperance Society, owns several public-houses, we learn that she cannot help herself. The houses were let on lease by her father, and she is not able to deal with them until the leases expire. Up to now she has shut up every public-house over which she has had con- trol as the leases fell in, and has refused to grant any extension of leases.

By the sudden death of Mr..lieeley Halswelle,just reported from Paris though it occurred on Saturday last, our picture galleries lose one of their most popular and diligent contributors of landscape paintings.. He was strong in the river scenery, as became a native of Richmond and a frequent dwel- ler in a house-boat on the Thames. This style of painting, however, was not his first fancy. His early pictures, the result of studies in Rome, were mainly figure subjects.

Two million oysters are being laid down at Whit- stable with a view to re-stocking the bedsafter the very serious loss sustained through the recent frosts. The damage has now beer definitely ascer- tained to amount to about .£30,000. The natives which lie deep in the water, have escaped with but little injury, but the" seconds 'S quality are alrPady almost out of supply. Oysters of this class are im- portedioung, and have to be kept for two winters at least in the English beds before they are ready for sale.

Mr.THenry !lucks Gibbs, the new City M.P. (that is to be), is qualified, like his predecessor, Mr. Bar- ing, by 'little else than great wealth and great re- spectability. Mr. Gibbs is a tall, well-built man, rather pompous and sententions in his manner. He is a High Churchman and a High Tory,and is chiefly distinguished for spending fabulous amounts on the restoration of St. Albans Abbey. He is 71, but bears • his years manfully. He is a director of the Bank of England, and he lives at Aldenham-park, Herts, when he is at home.

The curfew-bell at the old town of Sandwich, Kent, which has tolled for many centuries, is now in some danger of suppression. owing to the strained relations between the vicar and the sexton of St. Peter's. The latter is paid £8 a year by the Corpor- ation for ringing the bell ; but the churchwardens have claimet the fund from which his salary as sex- ton has hitherto been paid.,, The rector declines to pay it, and it seems as though the dispute may result in the cessation of the bell that has sounded in the quiet little town at eight o'clock for so many hundred years.

Nothingis sacred to French editors. They are now actually hinting that the Duke of Edinburgh is not a good performer on the fiddle! And they do this in a mean, sneaking fashion by inventing and circulating the story that, when the Duke of Cam- bridge was at Malta he was invited to attend a con- cert at the 'Albert B.all on his return to London, on which he replied by telegraph, "Yes, provided that the Duke of'Edinburgh does not play the fiddle." Sad indeed, is it to observe the moral deteriora- tion which accompanies a Republican form of government.

Here is a story of the possibilities of red-tape which I venture to think unique. An Indian Civil servant was summoned home by telegraph owing to the serious illness of a near relative. The same cause protracted his stay until it became necessary to apply for an extension of leave. He was informed in reply that this would be granted, but only on the condition that he returned to India for one night. I ask in all seriousness. Can this be true? With the high authority from whom I have it, I should like to have the facts vertified, if only for the satisfac- tion of future generations.

Mr. Benson, the candidate for Mid-Oxfordshire, whose absence in Spain has placed his friends at so serious a disadvantage in the approaching cmtest, is a member of a distinguished family. Mr. Benson is in himself a distinguished graduate of Balliol,and was for some years on the teaching staff of that *famous college. He was disqualified for a fellow- ship—his income being above the limit compatible swith the holding of such a post. Mr. Benson has ,seen some service in the Irish campaign. He assisted Messrs. Conybeare and Harrison to break the law by giving food to Mr. Olphert's starving tenants in Donegal.

Lieutenant Grant, the young officer who led his small detachment of native troops to victory in Manipur, is the eldest son of Lieutenant-General D. G.S.ffit. J. Grant, of the Indian Staff Corps. This gentleman very naturally corrects in this morning's Times" the false impression created by a recent speech of Mr. Stanhope, who represented Lieuten- ant Grant as being quite another person. The proud father adds that the eighty men commanded by his son are chiefly Sikhs drawn from the regular Ben- gal regiments for service in niiiitary police regi- ments in Burmah, and were organised by their .young officer and others of the Madras staff last year. It was not too much to expect that our War •Ministerleight have seen that the +laurels of victory 'were placed on the right head.

In a spacious white house in the remote village of Funtington, near Chichester, Admiral of the Fleet, Sir Provo William Parry Wallis, G.C.8., on Sunday attained his century. Born at Halifax. Nova Scotia, on 12th April 1791, be entered the Navy at the early age of thirteen, was engaged in active service a year before the memorable battle cf. Trafalgar, fought as second lieutenant on board the Shannon in her duel with the Chesapeake, and after passing through all grades of promotion, attained his pre- sent rank in 1875. div.head: WAY WE LOOK AT IT.
div.p: THE WAY WE LOOK AT IT.
No. IV. BY E. WICITRAIL,

I think it quite necessary that, in discussing the labour question, an attentive respect should be paid to those who venture to speak on behalf of the labourers. We are quite used to being told that "the interests of labour and capital are alike," and if I venture to say that in theory this may be so, but in practice it is not so, 1 hope the sticklers for an old and effete political economy will just try to look at my, or shall I say,

OUR SIDE OF THE SHIELD. I have unfortunately •mislaid my copy of the "Examiner" in which was published the report of Mr. Monks's paper on hiswisit to America and a letter from Mr. C. M. Percy, who is, I suppose' the miners' candidate for Parliamentary honours. Well, I must try to get on without these two, to me, very neces- sary helps to what I wish to say on the labour question. It is an undoubted truth that there are two burning subjects standing out intiold relief, both of which are heclged,all around,with traditionand privi- lege.to such an extent•as to prevent anything like an early settlement.; I refer to theological Christianity and the relation of labour to capital. Some years ago I fancied I was something of a Socialist; I think now that I should rank in the mean between Individualism and Socialismoand I state this right here so that no one may jump to conclusions. How do we workmen look at the question ?—we who lay no claim to being either leaders of men, or to being endowed with any extraordinary amount of intellec- tual vigour? Just here allow me to say. I have read the Bible with considerable attention, and know pretty well all that is in it touching at least two questions which have something to do with labour, these being general principles in connection with usury and the trials and difficulties of the rich man in his journey from this world to the next. There is also in the old book quite a number of texts to be found enjoining upon us a greater love for each other. Theselexts must have been lost sight of for quite a number of years, or, until recently found by Professor Drummond. I say this without levity, simply putting into words what I, and millions more of workmen, are thinking of. Since this year came in, the "Manchester Examiner" gave the names of twenty-two Manchester millionaires whose aggregate wealth was £15,083,956. I have before me a pamphlet containing the names of English millionaires who have died, and run the risk of getting into heaven,during the past twenty years; I cannot quote—the thing is too stale. Again, turning to "In Darkest England," look at the appalling figures given, "3,000,000 people poorer off than a London tab horse, 100,000 prostitutes, and about 100,000 more poor women who secretly increase their earnings with their shame." Like Cassandra, I am only pointing out

div.head: ROCKS_ AHEAD,
div.p: ROCKS_ AHEAD,

for I know, unless care is taken, the vessel will be on them before very long. "3.000 sweaters' dens employing 5,000 children, 522,000 next door to starvation," and so on ad infinaum. The above is one phase of the labour question, and, dear reader, it is not confined to England. Come out to this New World, and you will find the same thing making mighty great strides, as I will show before I finish. Go to Australia and you will find the Rev. Dr. Rose- by, of Sydney, sermonising as follows :—" All such schemes as General Booth's are at best mere pallia- tives, and the only true remedy lies in the re- moval of the causes which produce alike the unem- ployed poor and the idle rich. He reminded his hearers that the same causes which produced the pauperism of the poor in London was at work here.; that in this new land enormous estates were steadily growing in value with every increase of population, and that. with material progress, imust come the increase of want, which characterises all civilised communities. He declared that our hope lay in such practical legislation as should give to every child born into this community an equal in- terest in the land, with all its natural resources, and the substitution of a beneficial system of mutual 'o-operation for our present destructive and waste- ful competition." So much for the special privileges we enjoy under 19th century civilisation. Oh, I don't think we are going back; not at all. Evolu- tion has to work out its given work ; its ends will be reached, and those ends will be "Peace on earth and good will towards all men." Well, I would ask Mr. Percy what is the trend of the above? Does it lead towards an eight hours day? Possibly he thinks not. I remember in the letter to the "Examiner," he said something about an Eight Hours Bill being unfair to British manufactUrers in their competing race to the manufacturers of other nations. Ah I heard this said hundreds of times before I left home. I hear it here, in this "Garden of the Lord," but we make an attempt at Chinese wall building, just by way of protecting ourselves, with the result of further imperilling men's souls by enabling a few of them to become rich to the extent of from one million up to three hundred mil- lion of dollars. Mr. Percy thinks that the profits are too small now, and an

EIGHT HOURS DAY would make them smaller by increasing the cost. NV ell, thert may be something in the argument,only i we don't see t. I have his pamphlet on Mining Royalties by me. Before it was published, I had already, in the "Examiner" written pretty con- siderably on the same subject. Now we know, and your readers know, that if several 'millions of pounds are annually paid to ground landlords for rent, over and above the total sum paid in wages to miners., ways and means may be. found to put an eight hours day into effect. It is not many years since capital made its headlong rush, from agricul- ture to manufacture. It dates from the passing of the Limited Liability Act, and the two were co-eval with the rise of the corn-importing trade, and the extended use of steam power. But what a .result Depopulation of the country, and the swelling out to dangerous proportions of the cities. 'ls this the highest result to be attained by the increased intel- ligence of the community? Certainly not. The most important point, nay, the fulcrum upon which the whole argument rests has not been touched. What is the whole world watching with amaze- ment, and with bated breath at this moment? The re-building of iron-clads, the struggle between steel plates, and guns which will, or will not send balls to pierce such plates. Of course this is all science and as such we lift our hats in respect. Manufacturing is in the same strait. McoSmith has machinery of the most modern kind, and 'Mr. Jones must go to the expense of having the same or better. I give here a list of

div.head: WHAT INkVENTION HAS DONE
div.p: WHAT INkVENTION HAS DONE

in the way of improvement for us : "in the manufacture of boots and shoes the work ef 500 operatives is now done by 100. In leather mann- factute modern methods have reduced the necessary number of workers from '5O to 5 per cent. A carpet measuring and brushing machine with one operator will do the work of 15 men by the old methods. In the manufacture of flour modern improvements save 75 per cent, of the manual labour that once was necessary. In making tin cans one man and a boy with modern appli- ances can do the work of ten workers by the old process. By the use of coal-mining machines 160 miners in a month can mine as much coal in the same time as 500 miners by the old methods. The horse power of steam used in the United States on railways, steamers, and in factories and mines was in 1888 12,100,000 againit 1,610,000 in 1850. In the manufacture of brick improved devices save one-tenth of the labour, and in the manu- facture of Bre brick 40 percent. of the manual labour is displaced. In the manufacture of carriages it used to take one man 35 days to make a carriage. It is now made, by the aid of machinery, with the work of one man, in twelve days. In the cotton mills in the United States, the manual labour has been reduced about 50 per , cent. Now one weaver manages from two to ten looms, where one loom was formerly tended by one worker." If this is not enough to eonvince Mr. Percy that the time for eight hours, yes, of a universal eight hours day, if he likes, has come, why I don't know what will convince. div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 18, 1891. A WARRINGTON ATHLETE.

which the whole question turns: we have improred machinery but we have made no workman's labour easier; in quite a number of trades it is considerably heavier. We have each and every employer at his wit's end trying to reduce expenses, doing with as few hands as possible. He knows full well that at his mill gates every morning scores are gazing wist- fully for a chance to earn thei i r living. It s just the same out here; I see it every morning, ah, and noon also. But machinery is doing more than all this, and it is as important as the rest. Machinery now has the brains; the fforkman doesn't need any. I heard a watch-maker state, the other day, that very few in his trade could now make a watch. The labour is all divided, every part having its number; so in an increasing number is it in other trades; work is ceasing to be interesting and it is fast be- •coming monotonous and deadly in its results. Boys leaving school with a good education look out for something that is genteel, or with their better education they are fitted to fill responsible positions in business houses.
"A LANCASHIRE LAD."

Under the above heading the following interesting account of Fair Turner, of Warrington, was given on Saturday, in the football edition of the "Liver- pool Echo :"—" The name of Fair Turner, is a house- hold word in Warrington, where he reigns as the beau ideal of an all-round athlete. He is the pride of the rising generation—aye, and of the well- advanced generation, too—and is an honour to Lan- cashire and all England. This is not puff got up specially for the occasion, for Turner is a real, genuine article, with very few equals, and fewer sit:. periors. His talent does not lie in one direction only, for all the various forms and requirements of the gymnasium, football, bicycling, running, jumping, and swimming find him at his ease. ''iNo athletic diary would be complete without a sketch of Fairfield Turner.

St. Valentine had just taken his departure from War- rington in 1860 when Fairfield Turner made his entrance into it. He was born in the small hours of the morning of the 15th of February, 1860, and just missed being christened "Valentine." He is the second son in a family of nine, his father being Mr. Frank Turner, the superin- tendent of the Warrington Fire Brigade. Fair comes of a very powerful race, and no one could uphold the family name with greater credit than he does. His school days were passed at Heatliside School, which he left at a very early age, afterwards applying himself to improve the limited education he had received.

Of his many accomplishments, Turner is best pleased with his swimming prowess. At ten years of age he took to the water like a duck. His first stroke was a fast one, and he has been a fast swimmer ever since. War- rington baths are not much to the credit of the Corpora- tion. They would be readier to keep swimmers away than to entice them in. It is all the more to Mr. Turner's credit that it was in these baths that he developed into the powerful swimmer we find him to-day. The fir t red-letter day in his career in this respect was when, in 1879, he for the first time entered the race for the cham- pionship of the Warrington Swimming Club. He had in the interval made such a name for himself that when it was known he had entered for the honour only one com- petitor (H. Toft) came up to the scratch. Turner won the race, and the gold medal and title of champion of the club he retains to this day. Encouraged by his success, and urged on by his enthusiastic and increasingadmirers, 'turner went in 'for bigger things. In 1834- we find him at Douglas Bay Regatta, where he came in first in the Amateur Swimming 100 Yards Race (open to all ama- teurs) and he beat Joey Nuttall (the present professional champion swimmer of England) by four yards, a feat of which he may justly be proud. The following year he entered the competition for the Amateur Swimming Championship of the North of England, held at Roch- dale. He was at the time under a great disadvan- tage, having been thoroughly "done up" through hard work; in fact he had to be roused from sleep when the race was announced. He made a gallant fight for the honour all the same, Nuttall on that oc- casion managing to get before him by six inches at the finish, and thereby winning the Championship of the North. In 1889, Turner first introduced himself as the notice of the Liverpool Gymnasium, and that in a very forcible way, by defeating their favourite Lenton. Just before the race. Turner, when he saw Lenton, said to Barker, "I shall 'lick' that man," and he did lick him, although the cheers which greated Lenton when he made his appearance might have unnerved any common mortal. But it is for love of the thing that turner revels so much in aquatic feats. He uses the overhand stroke, but is an adept at any style, and master of numberless tactics in the water. His longest swim, performed merely for a lark six , years ago, was from Eastham Ferry to New Ferry. The lark went too far, perhaps, when after the swim was over the owner of the steam yacht which accompamied Turner, said, "Look here, Fair; I'll pull you alone.." Both agreeing, a rope was fastened around Fair, and steam put on, and Fair was pulled at a great rate behind the boat for a great distance. He laughs at the recollection of the latter part of the joke, but admits that there was too much of the picture of a harpooned whale in it. Another of his many aquatic feats will bear to be re-told. A well-known swimmer in Warrington told his companions that there was no one in Warrington who could swim across the Mersey or the canal with his feet tied together and his hands tied together. This came to Turner's ears, and he resolved to attempt the taGk. So Turner was tied according to sample, entered the water unaccompanied, and easily performed the task, earning the applause of the spectators. Besides the places mentioned, Mr. Turner has won prizes for swimming at Manchester, Stockport. Salford, Pendleton, and North- wich. He has ten medals for swimming, an honour which few amateurs can lay claim to. The Warrington Gymnasium is still in its infancy— only three years old—but it has already won for itself an honourable name. For this Mr. Thomas Morris, one of its most ardent patrons, and Mr. Fair Turner, its most competent member, are largely responsible. Turner , was one of the team which did so well last season, beat- ing Exeter Hall, and only succumbing in the final round for the 200 guinea shield of the National Physical Recrea- tion Society. His crowning honour in the gymnastic line was when he won the shield presented by the Recreation Society in the physique competition at the tournament , at Hengler's Circus, Liverpool, on Saturday, 29th March, 1890. The conditions of the competition were to jump 17ft. without weights, lift lcwt. above the head at arm's ' length, to be over 6ft. in height, and to be more than 40in. round the chest, and to say that Fair Turner ful- filled all these conditions with the greatest of ease speaks volumes for what he could do if he were put to the test. ' The news of 1 urner's victory on that occasion raised quite a jubilation in Warrington, all, from the Mayor to the errand boy, being infected with the enthusiasm that prevailed. An injured knee prevents Turner taking his place in this season's gymnastic team. At a performance in the Warrington Circus last October by Samson and Cyclops, Fair Turner performed all the feats of the latter with the exception of lifting the 2001bs. with one hand. He lifted the 150Ibs.

Bicycling and running are Fair's second fiddle strings. He does not take such an interest or active part in either of these departments, but there is no doubt he could if he would. He holds two medals for prizes won at local foot races. It would be sanding coals to Newcastle to dwell on Fair Turner's skill as a Rugby footballer. He captained the Warrington club in 1384 and 1890, and in 1885 played in the county matches against Dur- ham and Somerset. If there was more "fair field" shown to Fairfield Turner and the Warrington team generally by the Football Committee ef the county, he and others of his team would be oftener seen in the county fixtures. He plays forward, and in this position has an able seconder in his younger brother Frank. Fair Turner is every inch of him a typical athlete, and as he has a height ot 6fl. 2in., and a chest measurement of 42Mn., lie has quantity as well as quality. He weighs ; is by no means corpulent, but rather the reverse, bone, muscle, and grit being his principal ingre- dients. These qualities, together with his open coun- tenance, his wondrous length and strength of 'arm, his square shoulders, and well-knit frame, at once point him eut as a real Lancashire lad. Were Fair's occupation as a wiredrawer to fail, he could very easily become a professional athlete ; but he is: an amateur, and an amateur he intends to remain."

div.head: WHAT OF THE EDUCATED MAN?
div.p: WHAT OF THE EDUCATED MAN?

Is he to be content to -;-v-e-a;-y—iii-m-s-e-li—with ten, twelve, or more hours in a stifling factory, or in a coal pit, or on a "loco," knowing no change but bed and work? Not so : with a taste for reading, and the thousand and one pleasures of life, he intends to take right hold of ,them, and if necessary will restrict not only his "Tmasters" but his shopmate.s. Greed is not confined to the capitalist. It seems to be the boast of American employers, and the talk of visitors to this country that American workmen work harder than those of other countries. There is something in this. "Bossing" is well understood here, but it fits all round. All the office people, from the head of the firm to the lowest office boy, all turn up at the same time; same with all the managers; no coming at nine o'clock. But I hear , it said amongst the workmen I meet occasionally, I they are getting tired of being patted oil the back for being hard workers : there is nothing in it. And this feeling is having some results. In some trades the eight hours day has been adopted. The car- penters have had it some time, and no reduction in wages. The President of the American Federated Trades is now in this city urging it, and he is going to stump the whole country urging it. If competi- tion stands in the way close your ports. Workmen are going to have a change though the heavens should fall. I must give an instance of what is going on here in the struggle for existence. MY DAtITER HARRIE has learned type-wri g and shorthand; she is seventeen years of age but looks much younger.. When she finished learning these, she was fortunate in getting a good position in a lawyer's office, but being a girl and young, she didn't suit, as they wanted one who could work every night until ten or eleven; also Sundays. She got a first-class re- commend and came home. She has been out five or six weeks watching the papers every morning. An advertisement at last met her eye; a good steno- grapher was wanted in a business house in the city. Off she went at once and to her surprise found from fifty to sixty girls and women waiting to be tested. An old stenographer had been engaged to test all the applicants. This being done, and all the weeding out over, about eight remained ; amongst whom was Harrie. Each was then asked privately what wages she wanted. Harrie asked 50 dollars a month. She was told she stood no chance at that figure; so they did the Dutch auction business, until the lowest possible figure was reached. Now this went on the same with the other girls, the employer never stat- ing what he would give,but making the girls under- bid each other. Now, all these girls are well edu- cated, much above the average of the same class of girls in England, mine, for instance, having her school and the city medal for scholarship, and still she can get no work. What if she hadn't a good home? I give this to your readers as a result of civilization and education! And still this is the best of all possible worlds, and competition is the god we worship. lam improving very much in health, but until two weeks ago have had a dreadful time since November.
March 14, 1891, 810, Bay-st., San Francisco.

div.head: NEW BOOKS, &c.
div.p: NEW BOOKS, &c.

"The Light that Failed" is the title of an extra- ordinary one-volume novel by Mr. itudyard Kipling, the new writer who has so suddenly sprung into the front rank. The characters in the story are not numerous, but they are all interesting, and their individualities are displayed by conversation, action, and incident, rather than by description. "Dick Heldar," who may be said to be the hero of the tale, is a clever young artist of an out-and-out Bohemian type, who has a hard struggle under the most varied conditions, and goes blind just when money and fame have reached him. This may be said to be part of the "light that failed," and the other part is the failure to secure the love which he pined for, but which was never his. The writing is throughout vigorous and picturesque, and the language is, for the most part, simple, natural, and direct. Mr. Kipling undoubtedly possesses genius as a story-teller, and never fails to interest, but there are, here and there, evidences of sketchiness and scrappiness which are hardly consistent with sus- tained effect. This is to say, that, well as he has begun, he is likely to do better in the future. The novel is published by Messrs. Macmillan & Co., price 6s. "The Light of the World, and other Sermons" is a work by the Rev. Phillips Brooks, rector of Trinity Church, Boston, U.S. The sermons are dedicated to the memory of his brother, who died in the American Civil War. There is much in this issue which will be exceed- ingly satisfactory to the reader of religious literature. There is nothing sensational in the style. On the con- trary, whilst fervid and elevated, it is yet chaste and simple. •Referring to the young of both sexes who are puzzled and perplexed, he says of religion :—" What does this truth mean for you? Does it not mean everything for you, if truth and courage, and unselfishness and goodness, are indeed natural to man, and all evil is un- natural and foreign ?" This may be said to be the key- note. and the theme is throughout well sustained. The price of the volume, which is one of 372 pages, is 3s. ed., and the publishers are Messrs. Macmillan & Co. Messrs. Frederick Warne k Co. have issued a third edi- tion of "John Ruskin: his life and teaching." It is from the pen of the Rev. J. Marshall Mather, of Rawtenstall, who shows himself well qualified to deal with his subject. He has made a careful and sympathetic study of the works of Rusk;n and presents his summary and explana- tion in a lucid and attractive style. The volume gives an account of the parentage and manhood of the great writer, as well as of his views on social science, educa- tion, art, and political economy, while there are chapters devoted to his moral influence, and his future rank as a teacher. The price of. the book is 2s. ed.

Scribner's 'Magazine," for April opens with an in- structive and profusely illustrated paper on "Ocean passenger travel." "A kangaroo hunt," also illustrated, contains an amount of interesting information about the kangaroo, which needs some hunting now-a-days, as compared with half a century ago. The subjects of other illustrated articles are :—" What is righhanded- ness ? " "Where the ice never melts," and "The relief of Capt. Nelson," by Mr. A. J. Mounteny Jephson, who was a member of Stanley's African expedition. "The Newberg House Magazine "for April is a more than usually strong number. In a paper on" Prayers for the dead "it is declared, that" praying for the dead was John Wesley's own practice." "Queen Elizabeth's church policy" brings to light certain despatches of an ambassador from Mantua which were addressed to his court during the period that Queen Elizabeth came to the throne. They are especially interesting as showing how Romish and Protestant practices were intermingled in her days It is suggestive that the writer complains of some revels performed before the Queen at which were repre- sented crows in the habits of cardinals, asses habited as bishops, and wolves representing abbots." There is a racy paper on "Humorous Divines," and amongst other subjects dealt with are the census, the old church- yard of St. Paul's, sundials, &c., while there is the usual supply of fiction. Messrs. Cassell and Co. have just issued the first part of what is called the " Universal Atlas," a new general atlas of the world. There will be no fewer than 117 pages of maps 91 by 141 inches, while there will be an index of 'll2 pages, containing over 100,000 names of places. This atlas is really an English version, with a number of English maps added, of Dr. Ardree's famous hand-atlas which has had suck an extraordinary run in Germany, It will be complete in 28 one shilling parts, and, judging from the first part to hand, it is likely to be in great demand in this country. "The Ladies" Treasury " opens with an illustrated article on "The house of Shakespeare," and another illustrated paper is on bric-a-brac. The contents include coloured fashion plates, notes on millinery, the fashions, gardening cookery, household management, Parisian gossip, , &C. There are besides, several interesting stories.

div.head: LIBERAL LEADER OF THE _VEERS.
div.p: THE LIBERAL LEADER OF THE _VEERS.

The Press Association is authorised to state that it is not intended to appoint at present a successor to Lord Granville as leader of the Liberal party in the House of Lords. On the occasion of Lord Granville's absence from his place, Lord Kimberley has habitually conducted any communications with the Government which are required by the course of business, and he will continue to discharge his duty with a view to the general con- vemience. _ _ _

A meeting of Liberal peers was held in London on Tuesday, at the house of Lord Oxenbridge. It is under- stood that the object was to provide for the leadership of the House of Lords, rendered vacant by the death of Earl Granville. Although the greatest reticence was observed as to the restilt,it is understood that the leader- ship will rest for the present with Lord Kimberley.

div.head: FRENCH VILLAGERS AND THEIR SUSPENDED PRIEST.
div.p: FRENCH VILLAGERS AND THEIR SUSPENDED PRIEST.

At Monteynard, a village near La Mure, a district town of the Department of Isere, the parish priest, who lived openly with a family of his own, including several child- ren, was recently suspended by the Bishop of Grenoble, a measure which aroused great discontent in the village. The newly appointed priest on attempting to take poss- ession of the church was received with a volley of stones, and half the village, more or loss, to show their dis- pleasure, have embraced Protestantism. The converts have petitioned the Prefect to allow them to hold services of the Reformed Church in the schoolroom until they have a church of their own. Their request, says a Paris Correspondent, will probably be granted, as Protestant and Catholic churches are in France on a footing of abso- lute equality, both in fact being supported by the State. The unfrocked priest of Monteynard was exceedingly popular in the country; and as he had been a medical student, he was often able to heal those among the poor who were sick. Some twenty yeaes ago a village in the Creuse turned Protestant, the tyranny of a parish priest being the immediate cause,/ One or two similar cases have probably occurred within this period.

div.head: PERCIVAL GORDON;
div.p: PERCIVAL GORDON;
OR, THE CHILD OF THE REGIMENT. ET SYLVANUS COBB.
CHAPTER VII. THE CAPTORS MADE CAPTIVE.

As St. Vincent's squadron approached the scene of Maxwell's capture, Percival rode on in advance to guard against discovery by any of the brigands who might, perchance, be on the road; but he found the way clear, and at the spot where was the concealed entrance to the mountain path he waited for the troop to come up. There were two hundred men, all told; and they were the best and strongest men of the command, not braver than their fellows, nor bettcer soldiers, but they were healthy, and rugged, and used to sharp, critical work. .

The curiously contrived curtain at the entrance to the brigands' path commanded the admiration of those who were privileged to see it before it was torn aside, but no stop was made. They had pulled up to rest their horses not far from the charcoal. burner's hut, and had there waited for the most favourable hour, as it was St. Vincent's desire not to reach the cavern before midnight.

Having reached the point where the ascent of the mountain commenced, the commander, with two picked men and the boy, went on ahead, the latter going on foot, and taking the lead of all. The night, as Maxwell had thought, was clear and bright, so far as the undimmed stars could make it; yet, without a moon, the way was dark, and the horses picked their way slowly and carefully. Arrived near the post of the first sentinel, the three men stopped and dismounted, while Percival erept on ahead. He found the sentinel at his station, sitting on a stone, either asleep or in deep meditation. Having assured himself that the sen- tinel was alone, he returned and guided the colonel and his companions to the spot. One of the troopers crept stealthily up, and dropped the unsuspecting brigand by a blow on the head, immediately after which he was securely bound and gagged. The second sentinel was surprised and secured in the very same manner, he also having been found reclining at his ease, though not asleep. The third guard Percival found walking his beat. He took a critical survey, and then returned with his information. The three hussars crept noise- lessly up to within a few yards of the lower end of the beat, where they haltel and consulted. Pre- sently, as the brigand came to the nearest point, and turned, two of them sprang upon him, knock- ing him senseless, and then securing him. Beyond this is but a short distance to the plateau before the cavern. Our hero crept to the edge of the table, and could clearly distinguish that the way to the cavern entrance was clear. The rendezvous could be reached in no earthly way but by the one path up the mountain's side, and surely no intruder could come upon them without challenge by the trusty sentinels. So thought the brigands, and in that faith they rested in peace and comfort, without futher precaution. Upon receiving Percival's last report St. Vincent mustered his force, and having tethered the horses and looked to the priming of their pistols they were ready for the advance. Their chief explained to them the character of the entrance, as he had received it from their guide, and cautioned them against noise. Then he formed them in two ranks, and moved forward by the flank, each and every man knowing exactly what was expected of him. St. Vincent had based his chief movement upon the proposition that the brigands were to be taken entirely by surprise. He believed there was no barrier at the entrance to the cavern, and even should there be a sentinel there' which was of course, probable, it could make little difference. In fact, the presence of a sentinel might be favour- able to the attacking party, for the alarm, given as he would be likely to give it upon being so unexpectedly surprised, would serve to bring the whole brigand force forth to view, and they could be speedily overcome. Of course, they would be most of them bewildered, perhaps not half armed, and, at best, ignorant of the nature and extent of the danger that threatened. The oavern's mouth was approached by a curv- ing movement around the inner edge of the plateau, and upon reaching that point the colonel saw that the cave was well lighted, and such being the case, surely there would be kept a watch. So, with a moment's halt, he passed the order back in a whis- per that the men should push rapidly forward, with a quick, steady locked step, ready to open to the right or left upon entering, should the order be given. The aperture was amply wide for the passage of two men abreast, and, for that matter, three might have gone in without difficulty. However, it was best as it was, and in a brief space of time the head of the double line was within the cave. St. Vincent himself was the first to enter, with his drawn sword in his hand. In an iron sconce, fixed in the wall to the right, burned a large torch, and another at the far side. Directly beneath the first light, upon a wooden box, sat a sentinel— his back against a wall, and his head drooping, evidently napping, but the incoming of the intruders aroused him.

The startled man sprang to his feet and swept his hand across his eyes, and, upon the impulse of the moment, the colonel knocked him down; but the blow, given with the pommel of a heavy sabre, did not entirely stun him, and he yelled murder with all his might. St. Vincent's first thought was of regret that he had not silenced the fellow; but a moment later he was glad that the alarm had been given, for more than half his force had entered before another of the brigands appeared, and the whole of them were in as soon as they were needed. While two of the hussars were engaged in bind- ing the arms of the sentinel the brigand chief appeared on the scene, followed by a dozen or more of his fellows. Though the spectacle that met his gaze greatly surprised him, he did not lose his presence of mind. A single instant he stood to take m the situa.tioa, and then he shouted in tones that sounded through the vaulted cavern like thunder: "To arms 1 To arms Salvio and Antonio, look to the prisoners There was a terrible meaning hidden in these words. Percival heard them, and he saw the two men who answered to the names their chief had pronounced—saw them turn away, cocking their pistols as they went. His movements were quick and decisive. A lieutenant of his own company he caught by the sleeves. "Bring ten men with me to save our colonel !" was his order, spoken so that the lieutenant alone heard. At the very outset—on the moment of Don Lopez de Miranda's appearance—our hero had whis- pered to SE. Vincent that he was the noted robber chief, whereupon the colonel had said to a few of his men who stood near that the brigand leader must be taken alive, if possible; but he had little time for consultation. Don Lopez had recognised him as the commander of the attacking party, and quickly sprang towards him, with sword up- lifted.

The colonel parried two furious strokes of the herculean chieftain, and turned aside an ugly thrust, showing plainly that he was the better swordsman of the two, when he was relieved by three of his troopers, who came up and seized Don Lopez from behind, securely pinioning his arms, and holding him fast. Meantime there had been effective work in another quarter. Percival had kept his eye upon the two brigands who had turned to obey the com- mand of their chief concerning the prisoners, and he had seen two others join them. The four had disappeared beyond a heavy curtain, but they were not suffered to go far. Before they had crossed the empty apartment to which they had gained entrance the hussars were upon them, and three of their number were quickly sprawling upon the floor, utterly powerless. The fourth man, however—a tall, muscular, savage mountaineer, of Gitano lineage—had managed to slip away beyond another curtain, and in a moment more a sharp cry broke upon the air, like the scream of a frightened child. Percival heard that cry, and towards the point whence it came he sped like a flash. He slipped under the hanging arras, and was just in season to see the swarth-visaged Gitano with a beautiful little girl in his grasp, which he was in the act of handing to a woman who looked a perfect fury. She was the gipsy woman of the brigands, and, in fact, wife of the man who offered her the child. Behind the Gitano was another woman— certainly an English woman—upon her knees, begging, in terror tones, that thk. little one might be srared. With a hand as steady and as firm as a hand of steel—the boy levelled his pistol at the ruffian's head and fired; and as the brigand staggered backward, shot through the brain, Percival took the little girl, and passed her to the nurse, who was already on her feet. The gipsy woman seeing her husband fall, and backed by two other women of the cavern force, sprang upon the boy like a tigress, and what the result might have been. with the three furies

against the little fellow, cannot he toll; but at that moment three men appeared upon the scene— Col. Maxwell, Sir Richard Archer, and Tom Craw- ford; and they had no more than entered when, by another way, came in the lieutenant of hussara and four of his men.

For a brief space there was a commotion indes- cribable. The three furies were quickly secured; and while this was being done, Sir Richard caught his child to his bosom to assure himself that she had not been harmed. Then the glad hussars gathered around their beloved chief; and in that moment he knew, if never before, how deep was the place he held in the hearts of his brave and Loyal soldiers. "0, papa! papa! HE did it. HE killed the wicked man. Won't he go with us? " So cried the cherub, as she lifted her head from her father's bosom, and saw the boy in the hands of Col. Max- well.

"Ah, Sir Richard," said the latter, "what think you now of my faith in my hero? And I tell you, but for him, and his true heart and steady nerve, you would have been childless." The baronet realised it fully, and he blessed the boy from his heart; and he had started to speak of fitting recompense, when Maxwell stopped him Instanter. "Don't insult him," he whispered. "Do not take from him the reward that is already his." The baronet understood, and held his peace, leaving his child to offer further thanks as she felt inclined. Harry Maxwell, deeply read in the mysteries of the human heart, watched that childish pair as they stood hand in hand by themselves, and the thought came to him that never, while life should endure, would they forget this momentous hour; and he believed that a. current of deep and fervent feeling—perhaps affection—had started upon its flood, which could only be lost in the boundless ocean of eternity... _ _ _

Having seen all safe in that part of the cavern, with his companions in captivity around him, Col. Maxwell followed the lieutenant out into the prin- cipal cave, where the last of the brigands had been captured and secured. There had been but little blood spilled. Only one of the hussars had been killed, and only three of the brigands; but there had been a few ugly wounds, and many cuts and bruises. The meeting between the chief and his lieutenant-colonel was one of joy unspeakable; and both officers and men manifested their gladness and their love in a manner not to be mistaken.

When everything was quiet, the prisoners secured, and numbered ~nd placed under guard, and the vast cavern had been overhauled for stragglers, it lacked little more than an hour of daybreak; and after a brief consultation it was decided that the hussars should find beds—such as were not on guard-duty—and give a couple of hours to rest ; and and they would breakfast from the brigands' larder, and ihen set forth upon their course upon the track of the English army. During the last hour given to the work of making victory secure, in which work Sir Richard had been called to assist, Percival Gordon and Caroline Archer sat together in one of the most comfortably furnished apartments, with only the nurse, Nancy Winters, to keep them company. Nancy was a loyal, true-hearted woman—a childless widow, who had buried a husband, a son and a daughter—fifty years of age, devoted to little Caroline, as she had been devoted to the feeble mother. She had fallen in love with the brave, bright-eyed boy at sight. Her own son had been of his age when he was taken from her, and she thought, as she gazed upon the frank and handsome face, that she could ask no greater happiness on earth than to have such a boy throw his loving arms around her neck, and call her—MoTnEß !

And there was something in the woman that was truly loveable—a something that never failed to appeal to the love and trust of children. She was good and gentle, and intensely motherly; and, very greatly in her favour, she was really good- looking. She must have been, in her younger days, pretty, and the only change had been in the putting on the looks of the matron in place of the maiden.

Percival had unwittingly captured her in the outset. In the first place, his bravery had excited admiring respect; and then, when she had poured out to him her heart in gratitude for having come so gallantly to the rescue of her sweet charge and herself, he had thrown his arms around her neck and kissed her pale cheek, and feelingly told her that she was the only woman that had loved him since his dear mamma died.

So the good nurse looked upon the children as they sat hand in band, and found happiness in their hearty enjoyment of each other's society. Caroline told Percival the story of her mamma's death; of the travels with her papa, and of the capture by the brigands. And then the boy began his own story. The first event of interest was the death of his mother; then he went on to the voyage by sea, and the adventure with the maniac gunner. This story he had to repeat, and beyond that he was plied with questions, not only by the girl, but also by Nancy, until he had unwittingly spun out a really thrilling romance. He told of the battle of Tala.vera, and of the midnight search after his father; then of his father's death; and then of the death of his grandfather. At this point the nurse discovered, what she had not before learned, that the boy's grandmother had been Mary Patten, and that his grandfather on his father's side had been Captain Archibald Gordon. She had known them both. She had been a waiting-girl in the family of Sir William Patten when Capt. Gordon was courting Mary.

" 0 I bless your dear heart !" she cried, drawing the boy to her bosom, and kissing his fair brow, "I don't wonder you are good and brave. Your grandfather was one of the handsomest and bravest and one of the noblest hearted men I ever knew. Alas! that he was unfortunate, 'God grant that you may have all his virtues, and not one of his faults 1"
And Percival, with deep feeling, uttered a fervent Amen

"And now," said Nancy, with marked eagerness, "you must tell us how you found us here in this dismal cavern; for I know it was every bit of it your doing. Mercy on us I it doesn't seem possible. I can't see into it." But the boy could see nothing wonderful in it. His father and mother had both seen service, and both his grandfathers had been life-long soldiers. As for himself, he could only say it was in him; and he supposed it was born in him. "And now for the story, "said the eager nurse, when she had heard the boy's simple explanation of his seeming precocity. "Oh, yes," cried Caroline, regaining her hero by her side, with her dimpled hand. in his stout grasp. "How did you ever find us, away up in this dreadful place, and with these dreadful, robbers ?"

But they were not to hear the story at that time, for before Percival had commenced it the arras was lifted and Sir Richard and Col. Maxwell appeared, and shortly thereafter the colonel with- drew, taking the lirtle hero with him. And even he would not ask for the boy's story at that time, though he was exceedingly anxious to hear it. He was himself in need of rest, and he knew that Per- cival must be in far greater need; so he offered the lad a good bed, and bade him go to sleep as quickly as possible; but, unwittingly, his healthful resolu- tion was rendered of no avail. As a mere matter of curiosity, before bidding the little fellow good- night,.he said to him: ._ _

"Of course, Percival, you must have hung upon the flank of the enemy, and followed us up the mountain, on the occasion of our capture ?" "Certainly I did," the boy replied, with brightly beaming eyes, and a flush of joyous pride. "I hope you didn't think that I left you because I was afraid ?"

"Never I—never !" answered the colonel, with solemn earnestness. "As you heard me say to Sir Bichard, I had faith in you." "Thank you, my lord. Before I slipped out from the carriage I had thought just what I would do if you should be carried away; and I had heard so much of the doings of the brigands that I was sure they would hold you for ransom." And thence he went on, with simple earnest- ness, to tell how he had hidden away in the thicket, and how he had afterwards discovered the bidden path, and followed the robber troop up the mountain. He grew more earnest when he came to describe the way and manner in which he had avoided the three sentinels; and, as an ending, the boy sat and talked, and the colonel sat and listened, until the whole story had been told, up to the moment of the entrance of St. Vincent into the cavern, with himself close by his side. A season of dead silence followdd the closing of the narrative, which was broken by the colonel. Wiping the moisture from his eyes and cheeks, he laid his hands upon the boy's head, saying, as he did so:

"Percival, you are a brave and noble lad. For reward, none can be richer than the iove and esteem you have won from us all. Yet, in the time to come, I mean that a more substantial return shall be yours."
"-Your love, dear Colonel, is enough, and the love of our brave soldiers. I have done the best knew."

ELEMENTARY EDUCATION.
LAW AND PRACTICE AT WARRINGTON.

"The School Board Chronicle "has the following pertinent comment upon a school case recently re- ferred to in our columns, and upon the law and practice generally at Warrington in matters of Edu- cation :

We are not much surprised to learn that a good deal of newspaper and social controversy has been running at Warrington for some three or four weeks over the merits and the rights of a strabge decision of the Magistrates sitting in the Police Court on a Bye-laws' prosecution case. Warrington, like Pres- ton, is one of those phenomenal boroughs where strange things in public Elementary Education law and practice may happen, and make not much mark on history, by reason of the fact that they have the semblance of School Board law nut no School Board. This notable Police Court case failed to attract our attention, but a little later, looking down a report of a meeting of the Warrington Town Council, we found this passage : From the report of the Inspector to the School attend- ance Committee it appeared that 53 cases had been en- quired into by the Board of Guardians, and school fees allowed in 48 cases for 108 children. That 41 cases had been taken before the magistrates,and fines inflicted in 38 cases, two boys sent to the Industrial School, and one boy ordered to be whipped. Thirty-eight cases were brought before the Committee and dealt with.

The item which we have put in italics was very plain and unqualified. There could not be much chance of a mistake. The innocent School Attend- ance Committee—the Sub-Committee of the Town Council which is the Warrington make-shift for a School Board—proudly laying its trophies before its masters the Alderman and Councillors of the Borough Corporation, put in without note or com- ment the case of the by who had been whipped at the Police Station or in the borough prison; and the Town Council passed on the record. Turning to another page of the Warrington Branziner in which this report appeared, we found a letter from a correspondent, signed "Manlius," calling in ques- tion the law of the whipping case. The writer pointed out that a man named Dunbobbin had been summoned for neglecting to cause his child to at- tend school; that no penalty was inflicted on the parent, but the boy was ordered to be "chastised. with the birch rod." "Manlius " submitted, with some show of reason and good sense, that, " con- sidering that it was not the boy but his father who was summoned before the Bench, this sentence was lan undue and an unlawful exercise of authority." And" Manlius" proceeded to say that he had looked carefully through the Education Act,and that he de- fied anybody to find therein any authority whatever for the imposition of this punishment upon the boy. He develops that line of argument with consistency and point., and makes out a strong case against the magistrates. Since then we have seen a report of the case in the Police Court. It is set down very briefly. Nobody at the time seems to have thought the order of the Court was unusual. It is a brief summary of school case fines,and the last-mentioned runs thus: The son of Thomas Dunbobbin, ship canal labourer, was ordered tl have six strokes with the birch rod. That is the whole story. It is a sample of Elementary Education law and practice at War- rington. We know nothing and do not want to know anything of the evidence in thc case. It is enough that boys cannot be sentenced by the mag- istrates to be flogged under the law of compulsory attendance at school, and it would be an extraord- inary thing in most places that neither Magistrates, Attendance Officer, School Attendance Committee, nor Town Council appear to have been struck for a moment by the curious incident of a boy being ordered six strokes of the birch rod as the outcome of the prosecution of a parent for neglecting to cause his child to attend school. We would like to see some further instances of the administration of education law at Warrington. It was,if we remember aright, the Warrington Town Council which, some years ago, made loud complaint because no warrant was found in the Acts of Parliament for vesting in the Attendance Committee certain functions of a School Board in the matter of the prevision of school accommodation without committing the town to School Board jurisdiction. The Aldermen and Cor- poration were indignant—but they let the accom- modation question go by default rather than bring the institution of the School Board within the gates of Warrington. We need hardly say that Warring- ton, like Preston, is a place where voluntary sub- scriptions rule very low and where the children's fees run high.

div.head: UTOPIA DISASTER.
div.p: THE UTOPIA DISASTER.

Only two bodies of the victims of the Utopia disaster have been recovered since last Sunday. The total num- ber buried either ashore or at sea is now 451 Thirty- four more were recovered along the Spanish coast, thus leaving 66 persons still uuaccounted for. The whole of the personal effects, money, and jewellery found on the bodies of the victims has been handed over to the Italian consul by Mr. Seed, chief of the police.

A WARRINGTON MAN SAVES LIFE AT MONTE CARLO.

Sir,—The following particulars will doubtless be interesting to your readers. I give them to you simply translating as they have appeared in the local journal" Litteral."—Yours, &c., (MARQUIS) EUGENE DE LORIS. Grand Hotel, du Prince de Galles, Monte Carlo, April Bth, 1891. Sunday, April sth, witnessed one of the most ex- citing. scenes of the season. The Jette promenade was crowded with visitors, who were interested in the yacht races. Amongst others of the "Haut monde" were the Prince Michael Orloff and his family. The crush was so great that Mademoiselle Olga, eldest daughter of the Prince, was literally pushed from the " jette " into the surf, and must have lost her life had it not been for the coolness and courage of our fellow townsman, Mr. William Lelliott (late of Bewsev Works). Without waiting to divest himself of his clothing, he plunged into the sea, and by sheer force, succeeded in supporting the lady, and bringing her to land, after a terrible struggle which lasted thirty-five minutes. It is pleasing to learn that in addition to accepting a very valuable diamond ring from his Royal High- ness the Prince Orloff, Mr. Lelliott has been accorded the ribbon of " Merite de Sauvetage " by the Presi- dent of the Republic of France, and the Order of St. Sergius by the Emperor of Russia.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MoNney. DELIVERY OF TELEGRAMS.—Mr. RAISES promised to inquire again with a view to ascertaining if any reduc- tion could be made in the charge for the delivery ol tele- grams in the country. Tart BUDGET.—The Budget, Mr. GOSCHEN announced, would be introduced on Thursday week. RAILWAY RATES CommissioN.—Mr. SEXTON drew atten- tion to a letter from Lord Stalbridge on the subject of the Committee on Railway Rates. Sir Join? MOWBRAY, the Chairman of the Committee of Selection, thought Lord Stalbridge had taken a strong step, and having ex- plained what had been done, said he hoped the Comniit- tee of Selection discharged their duties to the satisfaction of the House. Mr.SmiTH, replying to a suggestion made by Mr. Gladstone, said he thought it would be super- fluous for him to add anything to Sir John's state- ment. THE LABOUR Commtssiow.—Mr. SMITH could hold out no hope that the number of the members of the Labour Commission would be increased; nor would the Govern- ment interfere on the subject of whether the sittings of the Commission should be open to the public or not, that ' being a matter entirely for the discretion of the Commis- sion.

THE OPIUM BESOLITTION.—The SPEAKER having been appealed to as to the position in which Sir Jos. Pease's opium resolution stood, said it would be competent for the Government to make it one of the orders of the day, and Mr. SMITH, in answer to Sir Joseph Pease, said he could not promise to adopt the motion as an order of the day; the question required further consideration. THE Cam-rms.—Mr. Smini detailed the intentions of the Government with regard to public works fcr the bene- St of the crofters in the West of Scotland. LAND BILL.—The House afterwards resumed the con- sideration in Committee of the Irish Land Bill, and ad- journed at 12 25. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY.
Their lordships held their first sitting after the Easter recess. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a

quarter-past four O'clock. Amongst the peers present Were Earl Spencer, the Earl of Kimberley, the Earl of Selborne, the Marquis of Fluntly. the Earl of Bessborough, the Earl of Lathom, the Earl of Derby, Lord Cranbrook, Lord Knutsford, Earl Cowper, Lord Coleridge, Lord Han- non, Lord Bramwell, Lord Norton, Lord Cross, Lord De Ross, Lord Sandburst, Lord Thring,the Earl cf Dunraven, Lord Stanley of Alderley, Lord Stratheden, Lord Teyn- ham, and Lord Colville of Culross. Lord CARLINGFORD‘ on his first appearance in the pre- sent Parliament, took the oath, and subscribed the roll.

BILLS READ A FIRST TimE.—The Army Schools Bill. the Charities Recovery Bill, the Electoral Disabilities Re- moval Bill, the Merchandise Marks Bill, and the Savings Bank Bill were brought from the Commons and read a first time.

THE LATE LORD GBANVILLE.—Lord CRANBROOK re- ferred to the great loss that had fallen upon the House during the recess by the death of Lord Granville. He Paid a warm tribute to the abilities and disposition of the deceased peer, and Lord Kimberley, Lord Derby, and Lord Selborne followed in the same eulogistic strain. NEWFOUNDLAND FISHERIES.—Lord KNUTSFORD reply- ing to Lord Kimberley, said their was no intention of bringing the Newfoundland Fisheries Bill on for second reading in the absence of Lord Salisbury. In rebly to further questions Lord KINTUTSFORD said no one would be Pledged by the second reading to support the Bill in its ‘nbtequent stages. The House adjourned at ten minutes past five o'clock.

div.head: BOUgE OF COMMONS.--7C-Esray:
div.p: BOUgE OF COMMONS.--7C-Esray:

The Speaker took the chair shortly-arteTt;o o'clock. QUESTIONS, &c.—Sir James Fergusson informed Dr. Cameron that it had not yet been decided to take steps for the annexation of Bechuanaland to Cape Coloay, though this course had been contemplated in the estab- lishment of British authority. On the motion of Mr. Ackers Dott;',las a new writ was ordered for the city of London in place of the late Mr. T. C. Baring. Mr. Hun- ter braught in a Bill to amend the law of divorce in togland, and Mr. T. W. Russell a Bill to enable women to act as poor law guardians in Ireland. The !House resumed committee on the Mail Ships Bill but progress Was reported before all the clauses had been agreed to. lama LAND BILL.—The Rouse resumed committee on ,To Purchase of Land and Congested Districts (Ireland) 13111, and after some discussion, in which Mr. Gladstone joined, an amendment, moved by Mr. H. H. Fowler,that the stock should bear 21 per cent. interest to June Ist, 1903, and only 21 per cent. afterwards, was defeated , a majority of sixty-five. Progress was reported and the sitting suspended at five minutes to seven. At the evening sitting a discussion tock place on a resolution by- Mr. Aciand on the subject of local government in rural districts and calling for reform of vestries and the establishment of parish councils, so as to secure to the inhabitants of country villages a reasonable share in the Management of their own affairs. An amendment was Moved by Mr. Hobhouse, urging instead, the grouping of rural parishes under properly elected district councils, and the effective control of local affairs by similar bodies in urban and populous places. On Mr. Hobhouse's amend- ment being put as the substantive motion, Mr. Ritchie moved to insert the words so as to include" The reform of parochial government." It was now five minutes to one, and Mr. John Ellis moved the adjournment of the debate. This course was adopted, and at one o'clock the Houst adjourned, Mr. Webster having occupied the in- !.ervening five minutes amid, uproarious ironical cheers, in an attempt to make a speech on a motion which stood next on the paper in his name. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNEsner. The Speaker took the chair at twenty minutes past twelve o'clock.

NEW Witri.--J-On the motion of Mr. Akers-Douglas a new writ was ordered to be issued for Whitehaven for the election of a member in the place of Mr. Cavendish Bentinck, deceased. INTOXICATING LIQUORS (IRELAND) BILL. Mr. LEA,in moving the second reading of this Bill, said that a Bill for Sunday closing in Ireland was passed in 1878, but it was limitei to four years. The Bill embodied the recommendations of the Committee appointed in 1888. Th. ese were that the existing Act, now annually included In the Expiring Laws Continuance Bill, should be made Pe_ rmanent, and that it should be extended so as to in- vulde the five large cities which have hitherto stood out- side its range. Out of 102 Irish members little over a dozen last year voted against a similar Bill. The Bill was 'cl)Posed Mr. Flynn and Mr. J. Nolan. Sir George Trevel- Zau supported it. Mr. Balfour also announced his inten- "au to support the second reading, on the Understanding, that the Bill should be referred to the Grand Commiteo on Law. Sir William Har- court heard this statement with great satisfaction. After some further conversation, Mr. SEXTON urged that the settlement of the question should be left to a Home Yarliament. Mr. Parnell agreed in this view, managing lu the course of a brief speech to intimate his undying apparently uncontrollable, hatred of "Liberals." then he sat down, Mr. MAURICE HEALY rising from the ~711011 below, quietly declared that neither on this ques- 'Lou nor on any other public question did the hon. mem- ber represent the people of Cork. When the general ..cheering elicited by this declaration had subsided, Mr. •t_teaty went on to observe that if Mr. Parnell had any uoubt on the subject he should keep to the terms of his , challenge with respect to his seat. This incident, which lasted only a couple of minutes, created a profound sen- sation. The amendment for the rejection of the Bill was ,Ilegatived by 248 votes against 94, the large majority of -trish members voting against it. An attempt to raise I,T,Msh debate on the proposal that the Bill be read a second mule was met by the closure, which was carried by 276 'votes against 31. The Bill was then read a second time, aud Mr. Lea moved to refer it to the Grand Committee °D Law. To this Mr. PARNELL objected, and the con- -tersation was interrupted by the arrival of six o'clock. ..,cm which both the debate and the House stood ad Journed.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—THURSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at quarter-past four o'clock. TRH LAW OF MARRIAGR.—The EARL of WISCHILSRA %liked whether the attention of the Government had been called to a statement by certain magistrates with refer- ence to the decision in what was known as the Clitheroe Abduction Case that they would no longer make separa- lion orders, or otherwise interfere in the protection of blarried women, and whether it was intended, in con- .tequence, to propose any legislation on the subject. -1•0, rd ESHER said all that the Court of Appeal decided was that a husband could net, by the law of England, beat wife, or imprison her until she satisfied him that she *ould restore him conjugal rights. The Court of Appeal 'believe that the judge of the Divorce Court might grant .4 decrees and magistrates might make orders for judicial separation, and that they need not attribute to the Court Of Appeal a decision which, if they had read it, they Would probably have seen the court did not azrive a.t.

• ELLS READ A SECOND TIME.—The Evidence Bill and the ,glzrustee Bill, both of which were stated by the Lord i:trANcELLon to be consolidation bills, were read a second „Litle• The Middlesex Registry Bill also passed the second ‘ading. The ir Lordships rose at five minutes past five o'clock.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.--THunsDAY:
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.--THunsDAY:

„,The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past three. "lER CHARGES AGAINST MEMBERS Or THE HOHSE.—Mr. „OHTON.—i desire to ask the Secretary of State, for the •":_ome Department whether it is true that warrants have issued against two members of this House for t'lnlnaal offences, and whether it is also true that both rs have left this country and are now out of the o,t,:trisniction of our law courts.—The HOME SECRETARY BY: •,he answer to the first paragraph is in the affirmative. far as my information goes both members are now "ut of the jurisdiction. THE RIGHTS :OF INDIAN SIIBJECTS.—Mr. CONYBEARE obtained leave to move the adjournment of the House in order to call attention to the arrest Of Abdul Rasoul, an Indian subject, at Bombay, his imprisonment for nine months, and his subsequent deportation to London, without any accusation being made against him.—Sir J. GORST said the reason Rasourwas arrested was because the Indian Government had reason to believe that he was an emissary of Duleep Singh. The arrest was perfectly legal, and at present there were no means of knowing whether the Government had exercised their dis- cretionary powers rightly or wrongly. As to the deportation, the man begged to be either sent back to Cashmere or sent to London, where, he declared, Duleep Singh would support him. He was sent to Loa- don, but instead of going to Duleep Singh he went to the hon. member for Camborno (Mr. Conybeare), who had trotted him out ever since as an Indian grievance. The motion was negatived without a division. limn LAND BILL.—The House again went into Com- mittee on the Irish Land Bill. Mr. J. div.head: MURDER OF A LONDON CABMAN.
div.p: MURDER OF A LONDON CABMAN.

A shocking murder was committed on Monday evening outside the Green Gate public-house, City-road, London, the victim being a cabman, named James Dowlincr.living at Hoxton, and his assassin, Arthur John Hasler, des- cribed as a scientific instrument maker, working in Combe- street. City-road. Dowling was sheCthrough the heart, and died almost immediately. It would appear that about six o'clock in the evening Dowling was standing on the pavement facing the tavern, when Hasler came out from the bar, drew a revolver, and fired two shots. Dowling shouted for aid and fell. Hasler was immedi- ately seized and handed ever to the police. The re- volver, on,being examined,was found to have five cham- bers, three of which were still loaded. On Thursday the inquest on the body of James Dowl- ing, cabman, who was shot through the heart by a man named Arthur Hasler, in City-road, was held at St. Bar- tholomew's Hospital. The description given by witnesses agreed with that already published. Deceased was quite sober, and as far as was seen gave Hasler no provoca- tion. Hasler has stated that he was attacked in a public- house, and let go with the revolver. The jury returned a verdict of" Wilful murder" against Hasler.

div.head: BARBA.RITIES IN MANIPUR.
div.p: BARBA.RITIES IN MANIPUR.
MUTILATION OF THE VICTIMS. OFFICIAL REPORT.

SIMLA, MONDAY. Captain Boileau, who with Mrs. Grimwood, Lieutenant Gurdon, Captain Butcher, and other officers made good his escape from Manipur and reached Lakhipur on March 31st, has made his report to the Indian Government on the subject of the recent events at Manipur. His description of the occurrences before and after the abortive Durbar summoned by Mr. Quinton only confirms the previous narratives. When the seige on the British Residency began, the Manipuris manned the loop-holed walls of the Palace, which were about sixty yards from the Residency and separated from it by an unfordable moat. At eight o'clock in the evening of March 24 Mr. Quinton sent a letter to the Regent proposing terms. A reply was soon afterwards received in which the Regent said that the only terms which he would grant were the unconditional surrender of the whole British force. Colonel Skene advised against any capitulation. Mr. Quinton, however, observed tkat ' the Residency would not be tenable if the guns opened fire upon it, and he discussed the question of the aban- donment of the place with Mr. Grimwood, the Resident. Lieutenant Simpson, after a time, went out and spoke with the enemy. He came back and reported that the Jubraj would meet Mr. Quinton if the latter would come to the gateway of the Palace. The Commissioner ac- cordingly went after some time, accompanied by Colonel Skene, Mr. Grimwood, Lieut Simpson, and Mr. Cossins. With them went also a bugler, who carried the chairs required for the conference, which it was supposed, was to be held at the Palace gateway. This bugler, however, was speedily ordered back by the Manipuris as he was armed with a rifle. At half-past ten the Manipuris shouted out to the people in the Residency that Mr. Quinton would not return, and they then opened fire again. Our men, writes Captain Boileau, replied freely. At midnight Lieutenant Gurdon, Lieutenant Woods, Captain Butcher, and Mrs. Grimwood were standing upon the Residency steps arsong the Sepoys, and &Jells wore bursting in the compound. Captain Boileau con- sulted his brother officers as to what should be done. He said that he would go with the majority. Ultimately .it was resolved to evacuate the Residency, and the retreat was effected in good order. The fugitives made their way across the hills, and finally met Captain Cowley's detachment, with which they proceeded to Laklitpur. Captain Boileau thinks that the Jubraj is alone respon- sible for all that happened. The British officers state that no cruelty whatever was practised by our men, nor indeed was such a thing possible. One of the telegraph officers reports having seen the headless corpses of Mr. Melville and Mr. O'Brien lying on the road 24 miles from Manipur.
The following despatches from the Viceroy have been received by the India Office : .. _

" SIIND&Y. " Grapt retired from Thobal 9th. Reached Pallell safely IDth, meeting relieving force. He held out splen- didly against overwhelming odds ever since 31st. Lost: one killed, four wounded. "Manipur.—Report of Captain Boileau, senior officer surviving, shows Regent's allegations regarding ill-treat- ment of Manipuris by our troops quite unfounded. Manipuris fired first on them. I infer from report that force divided in attempting to arrest Senapati ; that fighting took place in large walled and moated enclosure, containing his house and Rajah's palace, also in Resi- dency, which was commanded from palace enclosure walls. Our troops evidently fought at great dis- advantage." CALCUTTA, TUESDAY. —The latest accounts of the Mani- pur disaster tend to prove that the Jubraj and Senaputty intended to mist from the first, and began hostilities; also that the story of the Goorkhas having desecrated the temples is false. The failure of ammunition was due to the reserve at the Residency being for Martinis, whilst Mr. Quint,on's escort were armed with Sniders. Mrs. Grimwood displayed the greatest heroism, attending the wounded under a heavy fire, and afterwards acting as guide to the refugees. ADVANCE OF A PUNITIVE COLUMN. OUTBREAK OF CHOLERA.
CALCUTTA, WZONESUAY.—A despatch of to-day's date from Kohmia reports that a general advance of the column of 1,100 men which has collected there will be made on Friday. _

It is reported that the Manipuris are fortifying Kait- ambi, and several places on the road between Kohitna and Manipur which the British force will have to pass. A reward of one thousand rupees has been offered for the capture of the Rajah, or the Senaputty. The Mahrajah of Ka purthala has made an offer of 1,000 troops' for service on the frontier. Cholera has broken out in the 3rd Bengal Regiment, which will be placed for a time in quarantine before being permitted to move forward.
