div.head: Ti E EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 18, 1891.
div.p: Ti E EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 18, 1891.
NEW LOCAL RAILWAY.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE SELECT COMMITTEE. The bill for the construction of the Lancashire, Derbyshire, and East Coast Railway was, on Wednesday,under the consideration of a Select Com- mittee of thc House of Commons, consisting of Mr. Walter James (chairman), Sir Thomas Grove, Mr. Kimber and Admiral Mayne. In ppening the case for the promoters, Mr. Pope, Q.C., said this was the largest under- taking which for many years had been before Parlia- ment, and one which reminded him of the early days of railway enterprise in this country. The bill sought the authorisation of Parliament for a line 160 mites long, and involving a capital of £7,000,000, with the ordinary borrowing powers. It had met with the support of every landowner from end to end of the line, with one exception; and the real opponents were the railway companies who would be affected by the scheme. It was to be expected of course, that the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincoln- shire Company would oppose, because the proposed line must of necessity be to some extent be com- petitive with theirs. The Midland Railway Com- pany opposed because the promoters sought running powers over a line in the neighbourhood of Manchester for the purpose of gaining access to the Central Station; and the London and North-Western Company opposed mainly because the promoters proposed to run from Maccles- field to Stockport, and then by joining the Cheshire Lines; to gain access to Manshester,thus giving a competitive route between Macclesfield and Manches- ter. No fewer than 114 petitions had been presented in favour of the bill ; these petitions coming from the Cor- porations of Sheffield, Chesterfield, and Macclesfield, Chambers of Commerce, and in fact all the principal landowners, coalowners, and other influential persons along the route. Among the promoters of the bill were the Duke of Newcastle, who was largely interested as a landowner and coalowner ; Lord Manvers, the Hon. Sydney Holland (son of Lord Knutsford), Mr. Arkwright, who was in fact the originator of the scheme ; Major Dalrymple (Buxton), Mr. Bromley Davenport, M.P., Mr. A. Barnes, M.P., Mr. Nisholson, president of the Macclesfield Chamber of Commerce; Mr. Brocklehurst, Mr. Haslatn, president of the Derbyshire Miners' Associa- tion ; and Mr. Morrison, who was a large shareholder in the Manchester Ship Canal and was well-known in finan- cial circles in London. The whole of these were interested in the district through which the line passed,and in fact, this was one of the most bone fide and influentially pro- moted schemes he had ever known. It originated in the necessity which the promoters had found for a general combination among themselves to procure an adequate railway service for the district. Schemes covering the greater part of the distance had been authorised in pre- vious sessions; and the object of this bill was to knit up into one continuous line a number of these schemes. The terminus of the line at Warrington was at the docks of the Ship Canal tCompany, aad the project had the sympathy of those interested in that great undertaking. The line proceeded from Warrington to Knutsford, and would open to the inhabitants of Warrington a large area for suburban residences. The next places touched were Alderley and Macclesfield,and from the latter town the promoters proposed a connection northward with the Manchester South District line with running powers over the Midland line to Throstle Nest junction and over the Cheshire Lines into the Central Station. From Maccles- field the line was to be carried to Buxton, and the princi- pal engineering difficulties of the scheme would un- doubtedly be met with in the construction of the railway between those points. It had to penetrate the ridge of the "backbone of England "in order to get to Buxton; and this was in fart the great obstacle which had hitherto kept the two sides of the country apart in the matter of railway facilities. The first tunnel between Macclesfield and Buxton would be 543 yards long; and there would is* another, 41, miles east of Macclesfield, some 4,210 yards long. The line reached its summit at Edge Moor, being there some 1,175 feet above the level of the sea. He might mention here that the promoters had been able to arrange their plans to meet the views of the Duke of Devonshire, and that he did not appear in any opposition to the bill. From Buxton the line passed by Baslow—through a dis- trict where there was lead mining and other industries— to Chesterfield ; and from Nether Langwith the promo- ters proposed to construct a branch of the line north- wards to Kilamarsh, with running powers thence to Sheffield over the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincoln- shire Company's system. On the south they had entered into an agreement with the 011erton and New- ark Railway Company to absorb their proposed line, thus obtaining a direct connection with the Great Northern Company's system at Newark. That the proposed line was capable of being made a through route in the bands of the Great Northern Com- pany was obvious. From Chesterfield the line passed through Lincoln to Sutton-on-Sea, the site of the autho- rised North Sea Harbour and Docks, the special feature of which was that they presented possibilities of the con- struction of a deep water harbour that would ultimately become a very formidable competitor with Grimsby. Mr. A. W. Byron,agent for Mr. W. Arkwright, was the first witness called in support of the bill. He informed the Committee that the Directors held 100,000 acres of land along the route, and that the proposed line was in- dependent of every existing railway company. Mr. W. Taylor: Is it the intention, if the Sheffield Company's Extension to London Bill passes, that this line shall pass into the hands of the Great Northern ?—Wit- ness: Certainly not

_ Mr. William Arkwright, of Sutton Scarsdale, the chief promoter of the bill, said he had contributed several thousand pounds towards the bill, and if the line were sanctioned he was prepared to subscribe very largel, to the capital. Cross-examined by Mr. Taylor. he said he wished the line to remain an independent one. Coal would be the principal source of trade. Lord Francis Hone Pelham-Clinton said that he and his

brother the Duke of Newcastle were Strongly in favour of the scheme, and were prepared to subscribe largely towards the capital. Cross-examided by Mr. Taylor: The promoters were satisfied that they would get sufficient traffic to make the line pay. _

Cress-examined by Mr. Philbrick, Q.C. : He believed that apart from the coal the line would pay as a railway. He was acting for his brother in the promotion of the bill, but apart from that he thought the line would be a grand thing for the public. The Committee adjourned. THURSDAY.

The consideration of this Bill was resumed on Thurs- day morning by the Select Committee of the House of Commons, presided over by Mr. Walter James. Mr. William Bromley Davenport, M.P.. was called,and , examined by Mr. Batten. He said that he had a large estate in Cheshire of between 10,000 and 15,000 acres, and also one at Woodford on that part of the proposed line from Macclesfield to Manchester. He was invited to become one of the promoters of the undertaking, and after considering it very carefully he was convinced of its value, and decided to join the board. He represented a consideraikle district about the town of Macclesfield, which wasa very large and important place. The pro- posal to construct a line from Macclesfield to Warrington was not a new oae. It had been projected for a long time past, and curiously enough one of the chief promo- tors in the past had been Sir Edward Watkin on behalf of the Manchester, Sheffield. and Lincolnshire Railway. —Cross-examined by Mr. Worsley Taylor, Q.C., the witness said that he anticipated there would be a con- siderable amount of traffic between Macclesfield and Warringtoa. There would also be traffic between Mac- clesfield and Knutsford. At the latter place there was a
jail. Other witnesses having been called
The Chairman asked s4hat about financial evidence?

Mr. Pembroke Stephens said that if the Chairman meant did the promoters intend to call capitalists from the city they did not. The Committee had heard evid- ence from the promoters, and a number of substantial landowners along the line. Mr. Bidder, Q.C., said he might state that he should challenge most strongly the ability of the promoters to find the capital if the line were sanctioned. Of course they had heard abolit landowners taking the money for their lands in shares, but that was different to putting their lands into their Dockets to find the money. Mr. Pembroke Stephens said he thought it would be admitted that this was a most substantial and bona-fide promotion. The room was then cleared whilst the committee de- liberated in private. Upon the public being re-admitted, The Chairman said the committee thought that the evi- dence which they had heard from landowners was strongly in support of a preamble, and they thought it might be taken for granted that a railway passing through an estate was an advantage to the landowner. However, the committee would like further evidence of that character, compressed as much as convenient, and for a selection to be made of the witnesses.
Mr. Batten undertook that this should be done, and the committee adjourned until next day.

In the Appeal Court, on Wednesday, the appeal was heard in the suit of Mrs. O'Shea v. Wood and another from the orders of Justice Jeune, refusing production of certain 'documents. The court held that Mrs. O'Shea could not be ordered to produce documents not in her custody, but regarding those in respect of which " privi- lege " was pleaded, the plea had not been sufficiently made out. She must make further affidavit.

The Bradford police having given notice that an over- flow meeting in connection with the Manningham strike would not be permitted on the open space adjoining the Bradford Town Hall on Sunday, it was determined to test the right of public meeting. Mr. Ben Turner, Mr. W. P. Byles, of Bradford, and Councillor Saunders, of Nottingham, attempted to organize a meeting, and 500 men assembled. A hundred and fifty police were kept in readiness at the Town Hall, and dispersed the meet-1

ing by using their batons. in the evening another attempt was made to hold a meeting. Enormous crowds of people gathered. Councillor Saunders, Mr. Drew, president of the Strike Committee, and others attempted to hold the meeting. Councillor Saunders was inimedi- lately taken into custody. The police again dispersed the crowd. The Mayor and Town Clerk were at the Town Hall, and it was resolved to allow Councillor Saunders to go free, with the intimation that if he again addressed the people he would be re-arrested. After nightfall a crowd estimated at 10,000, gathered at the Town Hall and indulged in stone-throwing at the police, who, to the number of about one hundred, guarded the site of the prohibited meeting. Repeated charges were made by the police, both foot and mounted, but little impression was made on the crowd. The Riot Act was then read by the Mayor, and a combined charge of police and soldier, under the command of Major Woodland, was made, the former using their batons freely, whilst the solidiers acted as supporters. The rioters were slowly driven up the various streets near the square, contesting the ground inch by inch.

div.head: Sole Proprietors— FRAZER & CO., 11, Ludgate Sq.,
div.p: Sole Proprietors— FRAZER & CO., 11, Ludgate Sq.,
LONDON, E.C.
THE RIOT ACT HELD A SECOND TIME,

At the Police Court, on Tuesday morning, prosecutions were conducted by the Town clerk against about nine persons for stone throwing and assaulting the police. As night came on the numbers of the crowds increased, and the ordinary police, 80 special constables, and four com- panies of the Durham Regiment, who did service on the previous night, were gathered at the Town Hall, outside which enormous crowds assembled, and occasionally stones were thrown at the door. Just about half-past eight it occurred to some evil genius to pull down a hpard- ing adjoining the open space, and soon an immense pile of building materials, whichlad been frequently noticed by people during the past few days, was partially distri- buted amongst the crowd. Instantly there commenced an attack upon the windows of the Town Hall, large num- bers of which were broken. The Mayor then read the Riot Act by the light of a lantern, the streets being in pitch darkness. The forces again charged the crowd up the streets, and in less than ten minutes from the charge no fewer than four persons were brought in. There were three doctors at the Town Hall, and as cases of injury continued to come in they were 'kept going for awhile. At ten o'clock it seemed as if all the trouble was practi- callyended, though the police were still making occasional rushes. The people were eventually dispersed, but not before they had thrown a large number of stones at the police. At 11 o'clock the Durham Light Infantry were marched off to the barracks, and the members of the fire brigade, who had also taken their share of the night's trouble, were withdrawn from the streets.

On Wednesday the magistrates at Bradford heard two charges of assault, brought by Mr. Elaydon Saunders, of Rotherham, against the police constables in connection with Sunday's prohibited meeting. Great interest was taken in the proceedings, as it was expected that it would decide the right of public meeting in "Dockers' Square." The magistrates, however, carefully avoided this issue in their judgment. They dismissed the charges against the police, holding that as Saunders had obstructed them in the execution of their duty they were justified in arresting him, but they intimated that they did not consider the right of public meeting involved in the case, and did not think it necessary to decide whether "Docker? Square" was a public highway or not. There was no serious renewal of the disturbances on Wednesday night last, but stones were thrown at a small force of police sent to disperse a crowd of roughs.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
AN ALARMING BUT UNFOUNDED RUMOUR

Under the heading " Rumoured disaster to the Man- chester Ship Canal," the " Liverpool Daily Post" Yes- terday published the following :—" During the past .few days a rumour (originating with the "Liverpool Star 'p has gained currency in Liverpool—and we publish it under all reserve—that serious engineering difficulties have arisen in making the necessary entrance to the Man- chester Ship Canal at Eastham. It is said that unex- pected obstacles, in the shape of 400,000 cubic yards of solid rock in the bed of the river, and that sand shoals

, have been encountered, which may render it absolutely ,I necessary to continue the canal to Tranmere Pool. Of course the success of the great enterprise depends upon .I a good deepwater approach to the present locks that have been built at so much expenditure of time and money, and if it be true that the cost of removing the rocks will involve an expenditure of something like £1,000,000, the report as to a contemplated extension of the canal , to a spot four miles nearer Liverpool would gain cre- i dence. In the event of the Eastham fairway proving too costly an undertaking the company would have to seek I Parliamentary powers to enable them to carry the canal 1 to Trantnere. The startling rumour has created a verit- able sensation in this city." Mr. Leader Williams. engineer to the company, who was engaged in the canal works was telephoned to on Monday morning from the head offices of the company in reference to the paragraph, and he at once replied: "You can absolutely contradict the truth of the report in to-day's' Post.' All the necessary rock and sand dredg- ing has been provided for. Mr. Leader Williams in an interview at Eastham on Monday denied that there was any truth in the state- ment made by the " Liverpool Daily Post." Mr. Williams added that the channel at Eastham has turned out more favourable than anticipated. At the present time they had water at Eastham for a deeper dock than any in Liverpool. He, however, proposed to go deeper still.and it was possible they might find a (rood deal of rock at the bottom ; but if they did it was of comparatively small moment, and had been provided for in the estimates. The Eastham works had made such progress that the canal would be open at that point next June. The docks were finished, gates erected, and machinery in its piace. All the excavation, in fact, up to the Weaver will be finished in a couple of months at the present rate of I progress.
THE SHIP CANAL FATALITY AT RUNCORN. INQUEST AT THELIVALL.

On Monday Mr: H. C. Yates. county coroner, held an inquiry at the Thelwall Hospital, into the circumstances associated with the death of Harry Ankers, aged 26, of Church View, Runcorn, which took place while he was engaged in pile-driving operations at Runcorn Locks on the Friday previous. Mr. Wynne Humphreys, solicitor, of Runcorn, represented the relatives of the deceased, and Mr. Percy Davies the Ship Canal Company. Thomas Ankers, father of the deceased, gave evidence of identification. His son, he said, had been engaged en the canal for three years, and had been pile-driving nine months.

Robert Clarke, of 6, Hope-st., Runcorn, said he was engaged in pile-driving operations in connection with the diversion of the river Mersey. Deceased was work- ing on the top of the hammer, and had to stand on the second stage of the machine. It was his duty to rule the hammer, by the nipper dogs, and he had to put the dog into the leader to enable the hammer to drop. The accident occurred at 10.30 on the morning of Friday. Witness was on a raft at the time, but could see deceased working. When the ram came down en the pile the top shaft broke, and a piece of the broken shaft struck him on the held, knocking him into the river. He fell a distance of about 301 t. into the water. The water carried the body across, but when it was recovered deceased was insensible. He was conveyed on an engine to the hospital. On arrival there the injured man was found to be dead. The piece of iron (produced) was about five inches long, and before striking deceased fell about 301 t. It wasthe duty of the deceased to examine the top part of the machinery, and to oil it. If anything was wrong he ought to report it to the foreman. If any defect had been discovered, the machine would not have been allowed to work until it had been remedied—By Mr. Davies: At the time the accident occurred the engine driver was in the act of lowering the hammer. As far as he could see, the hammer was being lowered carefully. The hammer was about four feet from the . pile, the length of chain being 20ft. The deceased had been working at the engine, to witness's knowledge, for six months.—By Mr..lltimphreys : It was possible for a flaw to be in the metal without it being visible. Witness was about 40ft. from deceased at the time of the acci- dent. There was no special strain to cause the breakage at that moment. There was no sudden movement or jerk. There were about seven or eight men working round the machine. The piece of iron that broke was new five week ago. They had had similar breakages before.

Thomas Cann, ganger and foreman pile-engine driver, said that at about 10.15 he ttood at the pile end of the engine. One pile had been driven, and witness gave orders to raise the hammer or "monkey." Deceased was standing ready to take the pin out. When it was taken out, he stepped back and said "All right for lowering." ' Witness then told the engine driver to " lower out." Deceased did so in the usual way. Witnesc then saw no more until he helped to get the body out of the water.— By Mr. Davies: Witness saw deceased oil the broken part of the shaft on the morning of the accident. It was his duty to do so, and also to examine the machinery.— Resuming, witness said he heard the shaft break, and shouted as hard as he could for the men to get out Of the way. Witness examined the machine cm Wednesday last. It was then all right.—By Mr. Humphreys: It was impossible for the chain attached to the hammer to become slack.

Peter Coyne, chief mechanic on the Runcorn section, was next called. He said he had examined the broken shaft, and could not account for the breakage unless it was wear arid tear. It had only been in use five weeks. He had known a similar shaft to the one produced to last as long as twelve months without breaking. Others had lasted no longer than two months. There was no flawin the iron. . _
After Elliott Walker had given evidence, The Coroner said the whole question hinged upon the production of the engine driver. In his opinion he was the most important witness. -
The inquiry was accordingly adjourned until Wednes- day, the 22nd inst.
FIRE ON THE CANAL AT ACTON GRANGE. DAMAGE £1,500.

A conflagration of a rather alarming character broke out on the Ship Canal Wooks at Acton Grange on Sun- day night. The scene of the fire was the engine shed erected there, and before the flames were extinguished this erection was partially destroyed. and much damage done to three lo&anotive engines and other material which was stored in the shed. Other engines were saved by being drawn from the building by horses. What made the fire at this particular spot all the more seriou s is the fact that there are other wooden structures on both sides of the engine shed, and not far away from it, one Of these having stored in it a very large amount of valu- able plant. Fortunately, however, there was no wind prevalent at the time,and the flames were prevented from spreading. The outbreak was noticed by employes on the canal before it had spread to any extent, and the Warrington Fire Brigade was sent for at once. Consider- ing the distance that had to be covered, and the nature of some of the roads that had to be traversed, the bri- gade was quickly on the spot, and, aided by those al- ready at the scene, they set to work with a will to subdue the flames. In this they were successful not- withstanding that there was soma difficulty in obtaining an adequate supply of water. tlad the old Runcorn and Latchford canal been a little nearer the scene of operations there would, of course, have been an ample supply, but the places are separated by a wide stretch of wood and field. As it was the hoses had to be con- nected with a small brook a short distance away. It is but fair to say that the brigade were energetically as- sisted by Mr. Griffiths, sub-agent of that section of the Canal, and a considerable number of other employes of the Company. The damage to shed and plant is esti- mated at something like £1,500. The larger portion of 1 the damage is to be debited to the injury done to the ' locomotives, one or two of which had a very sorry appearance after the flames were extinguished. It is not known how the fire originated. FINAN.CIAL. ASSISTANCE By SALFORD.

At a special meeting, on Wednesday, of the Salford County Borough Council, the following resolution, proposed by the Mayor and seconded by Mr. Mandley, was carried by a large majority, only three or four members voting against it :—"-That, as recommended by the General Purposes Committee, one-third of the £3,000,000 required to complete the Manchester Ship Canatbe subscribed by this county-borough, subject to Salford having a proportionate representation with Man- chester on the board of directors, and that the Parlia- mentary Committee take such steps as may be advised to carry the proposal into effect."

IMPENDING ELECTIONS. DEATH Or MR. E. GREENE, M.P. Mr. Edward Greene, the Conservative M.P. for the Stowmarket Division of Suffolk, died on Wednesday morning. The deceased member was the son of Mr. Benjamin Greene, of Bloomsbury, and was born in 1815. He was married twice, for the second time in 1870. He ownad a brewery at Bury St. Edmunds. At the last election in the Stowmarket Division the figures of the polling were as follows E. Greene (C). Edward North Buxton (GL) 3,363
Majority
WHITEHAVEN.

The contest at Whitehaven commenced on Wednesday. The addresses of the candidates have been issued. Sir James Bain, the Unionist, promises nothing but that he will support the Government, and he approves of the policy of the Government inregard to Ireland. Mr. Shee has pledged himself to support the eight hours for miners, and has adopted the Liberal party's programme, inelud- ing the direct veto. THE CITY OF LONDON.
To-day (Saturday) has been fixed for the nomination of candidates for the City of London, and the polling,. if any, on the 23rd inst.

At a largely-attended meeting of the election commit- tee of the City of London Liberal Association,on Wednes- day afternoon, the following resolution was unanimously adopted :—" That, in view of the near approach of the general election.it is not deemed advisable to contest the present by-election."

• MID-OXFORDSHIRE. The nominations for the vacancy in the representa- tion of Mid-Oxfordshire Division, caused by the appoint- ment of Mr. F. W. Maclean to the Master in Lunacy, took place on Wednesday, the gentlemen nominated being Mr. G. H. Morrell (C) and Mr. G. R Benson (G.L.) Mr. Benson, Liberal candidate, reached Oxford on Wednesday night, and made a speech near the martyr's memorial, animadverting on the was' in which the vacancy had been caused. Both parties held meet- ings in villages.

THE HARBOROUGH DIVISION. A Leicester correspondent states that a meeting of the Conservative party in the Harborough Division will be held to-day (Saturday) to sPlect a candidate in the room of the late Mr. Tapling. Mr. Logan, the Liberal candi- date, will open his campaign on Monday.

THE VACANCY IN SOUTH DORSET. At a largely attended meeetine of the Conservative party, held at Dorchester on Tuesday it was stated that Mr. W. Brymer, who is on his way from the Continent. has consented to contest the vacancy in South Dorset, caused by the death of Colonel Hambro The funeral of the late member, Colonel Hambro, will take place cin Monday, the body not having arrived in England. Both i parties are actively engaged n preparing for the con- test. It is now fully understood that Mr. Brymer will Ice the Conservative, and Mr. Pearce Edgcumbe the Liberal, candidate.
EXTRAORDINARY CHARGES AGAINST MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT.

The "Central News" says a warrant has been issued for thearrest of Captain Edmund Rope Verney, M.P. for North Bucks,for offences under the Criminal Law Amend- ment Act. The alleged offence was committed in the autumn of last year, when, it was charged, the hon. and gallant member in the name of Wilson, counselled and procured, and conspired to procure, a female for immoral purposes contrary to the Act. Information was laid in the ordinary manner against Mr. Wilson, and a warrant was issued for his arrest at the end of October last year. Mr. Wilson had disappeared, but the detectives to whom the warrant had been entrusted for execution continued their inquiries, in the course of which it is alleged they discovered that the culprit's real name was Captain Ver- ney, M.P. Further evidence of identity haying been obtained, a fresh warrant was recently issued for the ar- rest of "Captain Edmund Hope Verney, M.P., deputy lieutenant and justice of the peace for Anglesey, and a member of the London County Council for the Brixton Division, of 9, Bridge-st., Westminster, and Rhianva, Anglesey." The warrant has not yet been executed, as Captain Verney's whereabouts at present are unknown. Captain Verney's case arose out of a recent prosecution, in which a foreign woman was sent to prison for attempt- ' ing to procure a young Englishwoman. The latter was enticed to Paris, and was there introduced to a Mr. Wil- son, who, it is now alleged, was Captain Verney. The man did not effect his purpose, however, and the young lady got safe back to her friends in England. THE CHARGE AGAINST MR. DE COBAIN. The other member of Parliament against whom a war- rant has been issued is, the Central News says, Mr, Edward S. W. De Cobain, member for East Belfast, and he is charged with the commission of unnatural offences in Belfast. The offences,or some of them, are alleged to have been committed as far back as two years ago,and they have been the subject of inquiry by the Irish police for several months past. On Easter Monday three in- formations were sworn against the hon. member, and a warrant for his arrest was issued on Thursday, the 2nd inst. Its execution was entrusted to Head Constable Hussey who, with several Belfast detectives, started for London, where they kept a close watch on the hon. gen- tleman's lodgings. It soon became evident, however, ' that Mr. de Cobain had left the conntry, and on Saturday last the detectivesreturned to Belfast. It is stated that Mr. de Cobain had timely warning of the steps which were being taken against him, and sailed from Goole for a continental port on the very day that the warrant was issued at Belfast.

Some uncertainty prevails in Mr. De Cobain's consti- tuency as to the political effect of the secious position in which he is placed. Some weeks ago a form of applica- tion for the Chiltern Hundreds was sent to Mr. De Cobain to sign and return, but the hon. gentleman declined to do anything of the kind. For the present Mr. De Cobain'a election committee will take no active steps in the mat- ter. It may be added that Mr. De Cobain was for five years Grand Master of the Belfast Orangemen, and for many years past he has taken a leading part in evange- listic and temperance movements in the town. Among ether services in which he took a deep interest was a weekly prayer meeting which has been held almost un- interruptedly at his residence in Ormean-road, Belfast. since the visit of the American evangelists, Moody and Sankey.

The THE decision in the JACKSON case, Marriage that a woman need not live with Question. her husband unless she likes, is fraught with momentous consequences, and it is already having no small influence over domestic relations, as the police court records week by week testify. The other day there was a case in point at Warrington—the parties to it being, by a singular coincidence,also named JACKSON. It seems there had been a judicial separation, in the first instance, coupled with a maintenance order of 10s. per week. The husband, to get rid of this payment, took a house under the impression that he could require his wife to live with him ; but he was • told by the Bench that he would have to go on paying, as, under the decision in the Clitheroe case, no woman was obliged to live with her husband. It does not of course follow from this that a wife may leave her home, and still be maintained by her husband. It cannot be too clearly understood that the woman who thus walks off at her own sweet will has no claim upon her deposed lord, unless she can come into court and make out a case ' not only for judicial separation but for a maintenance order. There are cases in which a husband would be glad to be rid of a wife by her going away and troubling him no more, and the reverse of course holds good. But apart from this minor issue, the decision in the Clith9,roe case is one which ought to be further tested; and we are

per week for all persons over sixty-five years of age, irrespective of their rank in life. His esti- mate is that, after deducting the present cost of maintaining paupers over sixty-five, the thud of the 'insurance money to be provided out of taxation would be £2,575,000. Nobody can say this would be a heavy burden; and it could be taken odt of the swollen army and navy estimates and the country would be the better for it. He would have the provision of the other two-thirds divided between the work- man and the employer; while, with regard to those who desired a larger pension, he would have them ;supply all the extra money for it out of their own pockets. The plan would, it hardly need be said, re- quire tobe compulsory to be effective ; and if it were likely to be successful there could be no valid oh= jection upon-that ground, seeing that the principle of compulsion is already in operation in the pay- ment of rates and taxes. There is a growing feel- ing that, while immense fortunes are being made by capitalists and large employers of labour, the labourer himself is not receiving his fair share of the fruits of industry. An insurance scheme such as is now proposed would be one way.of adjusting the balance in some degree. Itis easy to say that the workers should themselves make provision for old age, but it is very hard to do, as most of the critics would find, if they were put to the task of bringing up a family decently on thirty shillings per week. Parents indeed, and those not the worst, sometimes neglect their own interests in providing for their children by equipping them with a good education. The most industrious, too, are often the most kindly, and they are induced to help others until the time comes when, either from misfortune, or failing health, they find there is nothing before them but the Workhouse. Who can say that this is a fitting termination of an honest and laborious life? Such people are the salt of the earth; they deserve something better when old age overtakes them; and we cannot but think that "the way out" for them is through some such door as would be opened by a system of National Pensions. What do the workers them- selves think of the proposal? It is for them,in the end, to pronounce on the subject rather than for anybody on their behalf.

The Russian Government are in arms in the old bad style against freedom of the press. Several papers have been impended, and others have been warned against discussing military preparations. This sitting on the safety valve is a poor sort of policy ; it will most likely end in explosion before long. The Government are muddling along, and attaining a certain sort of success in the policy of "How not to do it." We are apparently as far as ever off the local self-government for Ireland,which Was promised as soon as they came into office in 1886. And as for "Assisted education," who hears Of it now? There was some tall talk abottt a big surplus, but even that seems to have reached thp vanishing point.

_ -- Mr. Brunner,M.P., keeps his band to the plough in the matter of promoting education. He Is moving to get a-return of the number of institu- tions founded under the provisions of the Literary and Scientific InstitAtions Act of 1854. It seems that the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster is / empowered under the act to grant lands for the sites of institutions. It may happen that this will prove to be good ground, in a double sense, for Technical Education Committees to work upon. ,

Mr. Rigby's dream of a College of Agriculture for Cheshire is likely to be realised. The County Council is being applied to by the Chamber of Agriculture ; and; as the Council has money in hand for the promotion of technical education, there is every reason to hope that the application will be successful. The farmer is slow to learn,but he will find in due time that knowledge is power in raising crops as in threshing by steam.

'Lieut. Simpson, who was amongst the massa- cred at Manipur, lathe nephew of Mr. John Simp- son, of Runcorn. He acted as 'intermediary be- tween the British Commissioner and the rebels; and met his sad fate through forming one of the party that went to the gateway of the Palace to discuss terms of surrender. The Jubraj broke faith, and the party were murdered. An avenging force, it is some satisfaction toknow, is now on the track of the traitors.

Mr. B. G. Jenkens, F.R.A.S., issues a penny Weather Almanac and Chart" which has secured aim some reputation as a weather prophet. He Predicts that May will be a dry warm month, and that June, July, and August will be on the whole Wet and stormy. As to April he says" snow about he Ist and 30th." A pleasant proposal truly nut we take heart in the fact that we have not yet found the man who can with certainty tell what the weather will be the day aftcr to-morrow.

The licensing Case disposed of, on Tuesday, by the Court of Appeal, although in favour of the ap- Pellant, cannot be said to affect the Sharps v. ,Walcefield decision. The appellant was a beer- neuse-keeper, not the holder of a full license; and there is a special provision for dealing with beer- houses under the Act of 1869, which does not ,Pply to full-licensed houses. Still, the case is, as lax as it goes, of importance, andit may be thought Aecessary to carry it to the House of Lords.

-- The cottage which Wordsworth lived in at qrasroere—not the house which he afterwards Occupied at Rydal Mount—has been purchased by •llational subscription, as was the case with Shakes- Peare's house, and will become a sort of shrine to the ever-widening circle of his admirers. It was here that he pursued his plain living and high thinking which gave such dignity to his character; and it Was here that he wrote his "Intimations of Im- zoortality "—a poem unsurpassed in the literature ..;)! any country, and described by Emerson as the sigh-water mark of thought upon that great subject.

But that? If Englishmen thought fit to say tiv e Will he directed bytthe clergy" who should Llbm nay? Mr. W. H. Smith showedsign,in answering a ques- tion in the House of Commons,on Monday,of back- ing out in the matter of the motion on the opium traffic adopted by the House on Friday night. That motion affirmed that" the system by which the Indian opium revenue is raised is morally inde- fensible," and urged upon the Indian Government "that they should refuse to grant licenses for the cultivation of the poppy and sale of opium in British India, except to supply the legitimate de- mand for medical purposes, and that they should at the same time take measures to arrest the tran- sit of Malwa opium through British territory." Mr. Smith voted for the. motion, and if he doesnot not support his vote as leader of the House, he will bring discredit on the Government and make a mockery of the opinion of Parliament.

The "Chester Courant" has been taking Mr. and Mrs. Tomkinson to task for their speeches, and charging them with saying what is not true. Indeed, the Tory organ went so far as to put the issue in this rude and crude form—" When, more- over Mr. Tomkinson says that the Tory landlords ruin their tenants and dictate to them politically he knows he is saying what is net true." This was to arm that Mr. Tomkinson was deliberately lying; but it transpires from the published reports that he has been grossly and stupidly misrepre- sented. What he did say was that "he was afraid there was more than a tendency on many estates to use all the political power and pressure the Tory landlords could bring to bear in order to keep their estates as free as possiblc from those terrible Radical farmers, who were such a nuisance in matters political." Keeping Radical farmers.off an estate is surely not the saint, as taking them on and ruining them! - -

The same incapacity or ineudacity is displayed in dealing with Mrs. Tomkinson. Her statment was that " wa,res could not ho fixed by A.et of Parliament, but what it was possible to do was to make those wages go further by cheapening the necessaries of life; and that was one of the reasons why the Liberals had systematically gone on the ground that taxation of the necessaries of life should be brought as low as possible or done away with altogether.' The "Courant's" way of putting this is to say :—"Mrs. Tomkinson knows very well that when she says the Tories are standing between a fair day's wage for a fair day's work and the worker she is saying what is not true." Now, there is not a word about the Tories in Mrs. Tom- kinson's statement. That is the" weak invention of the enemy" who is " saying what is • not true." It used to be said there was a lying spirit abroad. Can it be that it has taken up its abode at the office of the "Chester Courant ? "

. . The second reading of the Irish Sunday Closing Bill was passed with a large majority, on Wednes- day, and it may now be said to be assured of a place on the statute book. Mr. Parnell,;by opposing it, shows that he stands for the Shebeen and the Shillaly. And yet he does not abide by his chal- lenge to contest Cork with his co-representative. Mr. M. Healy created a sensation in the House, and was loudly cheered, when he rose after Mr. Parnell, told him that he did not represent the views of the people of Cork, and asked him to keep to the terms of his challenge. But the de- posed chief made no sign. As to this Cork episode, he is like the soldier of whom the ballad says:— He was a gallant captain, in battle much delighting, But he ran away In the middle of the fray— And bade the rest keep fighting.

A MONTH'S ACCOUNTS AT WIDNES. The accounts presented to and passed by Widnes Local Board, at their monthly meeting, on Tuesday, amounted to £5,031 us. lid. BUILDING OPERATIONS IN WIDNES. The Widnes Local Board at the monthly meeting on Tuesday passed the following building plans :—J. E. Johnson, 5 houses off Albert-road; E. Wood, 1 house, Albert-read; W. Smith, house and outbuildings, Salis- bury-street ; John Gerrard, 10 houses, Millfield-road and Knowles-street; John Taylor, 4 houses, Salisbury-street; Wm. Farrant, 3 houses (amended plan) ; Wm. Lowe, 1 house. Albert-road. SPRING Fasuioxs now Showing at J. A. W. Durrox's Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. WIDNES FIRB BRIGADE. Mr. I. Carr, the superintendent of the Fire Brigade, presented his report to the Local Government Board, on Tuesday, upon the operations of the FiKe Brigade during the past twelve months. The total number of fires that had occurred during the year, within the rateable dis- trict (exclusive of chimney fires) was 8 ; outside the rate- able district, 1. Of this number two had been destruc- tive. The estimated total less from fires was £2,076. The estimated value of property at risk was £221,700. The present strength of the brigade was three officers and seven men. One member had been dismissed during the year The condition of the brigade,as regarded efficiency and discipline, was fairly good, but when the new Fire Station and firemen's houses were completed; it would. he felt sure have the effect of improving the brigade in this respect'. The police, as in previous years, had ren- dered the brigade excellent assistance. The total num- ber of street hydrants is 190.

ROBBERIES AT WIDNES. Before Mr. Gossage and. Mr. H. Ga,skell junior, at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Alice Hannah Beech, New-road, Ditton, nine years of age, was charged with stealing two shawls valued at ss. 6d., the property of J. Kilbride and Frank McGovan ; and her mother, Sarah Frances Beech, was also charged with receiving the stolen goods, knowing them to have been stolen. The children of toth the prosecutors attended Ditton Hall School, and the shawls produced, which they wore when going to school, were missed from the school.—Mr W. Houghton, pawnbroker, deposed to receiving the shawls in pledge from the mother, to whom he advanced 4s.—The girl, who pleaded guilty to stealing the shawls, was bound over in her father's recognizances for six mouths, to come up for judgment when called upon. The mother, who pleaded not guilty, said when the girl brought the shawls home she said a woman had told her to hold them for her, which was some two or three weeks previous, and thy had not since been owned.—The charge against the mother was dismissed.—Catherine Agnes Mulloy, 15, New-st., was charged with stealing a gold keeper ring, a purse, and three sheets, valued at 155., the property of John Maguire, her brother-in-law. About midnight on Saturday night the prosecutor's wife was taken ill, and was placed on the sofa by the prisoner. Early the fol- lowing morning she missed her purse, and charged the prisoner with having taken it, whereupon the prisoner threw the purse at her. She alsc saw the sheets, produced, under her arm.—ln answer to the charge, prisoner pleaded not guilty, but the Chairman said there was no doubt that she took the articles.—A tine of 20s. was its- posed, or ill default of payment 14 days. HALTON BURIAL,BoARD. The annual meeting was held on Tuesday when the following officers were appointed :—Rev. G. D. Wray, chairman; Mr. James Looker, vice-chairman ; Mr. Hugh Rowe, treasurer; and Mr. W. H. Bradbury, secretary. liassuigrrEs.—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge-St., Warringten.--Advt. THE COOPER'S STRUM AT RUNCORN AND WIDNES. The strike of coopers at Widnes and Runcorn still continues, and the Coopers Union have increased the strike pay to Li per week, per man, which will be con- tinued for a month, when the position will be reconsidered. Both masters and meu seem very determined not to

yield. Sr. Joires CHILDREN'S GUILD. RUNCORN. •In connection with this Society the cantata "The }lower Queen and her court" was performed before a good audience en Wednesday evening. The decorations had been executed with great taste, and the various characters were well represented by the,children. Songs and recitations were also given. I.lr. James Pritchard

presided. ST. JOHN AMBULANCE ASSOCIATION, Rtmconx. On Thursday afternoon, a most successful start was made with the recently-formed Ladies' Class in connec- tion with the above. Nearly 80 ladies were present to hear the introductory lecture by Dr. McDougall. This consisted of a short history of the Ambulance Association, the objects it had in view, and a resume of the work and successes of the class in the past. The work of the class will commence in earnest next week. Any lady still de- sirous of joining is requested to forward her name at once to the Secretary, Mr. W. Epps, residing at 28, Lord- st.,land not as stated last week. THE USE OF THE KNIFE AT WIDNES. At Widnes Police Court on Monday, Hugh Hyland, 20, Wareing-St., was brought up on remand charged with causing grievous bodily harm to Timothy Burns, by stabbing him on the left thigh with a sharp instrument, on Saturday night, the 28th ult.—lt appeared that the prosecutor Burns and another man named Patrick Green, were in the Market Hotel, Widnes, and com- menced to argue about sea-voyaging, and a quarrel en 7 sued, which resulted in their both being ejected from the hotel. Immediately after being put out of the hotel, Burns alleged that the prisoner stabbed him on the left thigh with a knife.—Dr. Hutchinson deposed that en the morning of the 29th ult. he was called to see the prose- cutor, who was suffering from a clean-cut wound, 211 Inches in length and half an inch deep, which must ha* been caused by a sharp instrument. The prosecutor would be unable to work for a fortnight yet.—The Bench considered that there was a prima fame case against the prisoner, and committed him for trial at the next Liver- pool Assizes. GIFTS TO THE WIDNES HOSPITALS. At a meeting of the Widnes Local Board on Tuesday, the thanks of the members were tendered to the d onors of articles to the Ancient Hospital and tithe Infectious Diseases Hospital. The gifts to the Accident Hospital were made by Messrs. H.W. Deacon, J. P.,T.S.Swale. The proprietors of the Guardian, A.Walker,D. Wright,Davies, Hartland, J.Treacy, Hall, Ra,wlinson,Wilbralism Wood, Bray, Hough; Neil, Rev. J. Chapman, Rev. R. ASSAULT ON A CONSTABLII A/ WIDNES. James Duffy, 4, Mary-st. was charged with having assaulted P.C. Simpson whilst in the execution of his duty, on Saturday night. The constable, whose face was much bruised, stated that about five minutes to nine on Saturday night, lie was in Moss Bank- road, when he was called into the Rose and Crown Inn to eject the prisoner. Prisoner was put out by an assis- tant, and when he got into the read, he commenced making a disturbance. Witne=s told him he would be locked up if be did not go home, and mile did not go, witness took hold of him to take him to the Police Sta- tion,whereupon prisoner struck him several violent blows on the face, and kicked him on the knee. Prisoner ad- mitted the assault, but said the officer aggravated him by striking him. Prisoner's sister, Mrs. Burns, said that when she came up they both had hold of one another and Simpson struck the first blow. They were both drunk. Inspector Keighley said he saw Simpson at 8 10 and 11 0 the same night, and he was not drunk. When he saw him at eleven o'clock, he had been badly used. Superin- tendent Noblett stated that the prisoner, who got away ,on Saturday, gave himself up that morning. The pri- soner was ordered to pay 20s. and Bs. 6d. costs, or go to

goal for 14 days THE BANKRUPTCY OF DYFRIG DAVIES. At the Wrexham Bankruptcy Court, on Tuesday, Dyfrig Davies, a joiner, living at Wrexham, again cane up for public examination. The debtor filed his own petition after having a verdict given against him 'at the Chester Assizes of £l5O and costs, in an action brought against him by a Miss Flardcastle, of Runcorn, for breach of promise of marriage and seduction. His assets were nil, and his only liability the £l5O and costs duo to Miss Hardcastle. Prior to the action brought by Miss Hard- castle, the debtor was in partnership with a Mr Brad- shaw, at Gwersyllt, as a joiner and builder, but gave up the partnership about that time, and drew as his share of the profits, when he left £l5O. Of this £l5O he paid RlOO 16s. to hie mother. Examined as to his money, the debtor said it was due to his mother for board and lodgings and clothing, his mother having advanced him money during the first Year of his partnership, when he drew no money from 'the firm except for lodging when working in the country. His mother paid for his beard as well as his clothing. He kept:an account of the money his mother paid for him on little bits of paper. He had destroyed those bits of paper. He could not say when he destroyed them. The receipts produced signed by his mother, for £25 and £75 165., were prepared and signed after he filed his petition and some time after he paid his mother the mot ey.—The examination was declared closed. SPRING FASHIONS now Showing at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st.. Warrington.—Advt. WIDNES FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE. The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday. Mr. ll. Wade Deacon presided, and there was a good attendance of members.—The Chairman referred to the great loss the Committee had sustained by the death of Mr. Allen. He mentioned the great work Mr. Allen carried out on the formation of the Library, and the great services he had constantly rendered since. He paid a high tribute to Mr. Allen's personal character and proposed That the Library Committee desires t o re- cord its deep sense of the loss suffered by the death of Mr. J. T. Allen and begs to offer its sincere sympathy with Mrs. Allen and her tamily."—Mr.W.Sadler see,onded the motion.—Mr. Lee. Mr. Pankhurst, Mr. Brown, and Mr. Moaison supported the motion, which was carried unanimously. Miss Proctor, The librarian, reported that ' during the past month the total attendance at the library was 11,527 ; days open 23 ; daily average attendance 501 ; last year 557. 4,302 books had been issued, being a daily average of 187. The sum of £1 4s. sd. has been received for fines.—On the proposition of Mr. Pankhurst, seconded by Dr.O'Keeffe and supported by Mr. Robinson, a cordial vote of thanks was passed to the chairman for his ser- vices during the past year; and much satisfaction was expressed at his recovery from illness.—The Chairman acknowledged the vote, and said it was pleasant to come back that day and be welcomed as warmly as he had been. He trusted the Library Committee would be as successful in the future as it had been in the past. A RUNCORN CHIMNEY SWEEP'S BANKRUPTCY. At the Crewe Bankruptcy Court, on Wednesday, before the Registrar, Mr. C. E. Speakman, John Dyson Sum- merfield, described as of Barton, Cheshire, chimney sweep, latb of Runcorn, came up for his public examina- tion. The debtor's statement of affairs showed liabilities £lO4 19s. Bd. and preferential claims £1 10s. The assets consisted of '£l4 cash deposited with solicitor for the costs of the petition, and book debts £3 25., leaving a deficiency of £B9 7s. Bd. The bankrupt stated that the causes of his failure were family sickness, being unable to dispose of his business at Runcorn to advantage,ow- ing to his landlady refusing to accept an intending pur- chaser as tenant, loss of horses and bad trade. The bank- rupt was formerly a waterman, and commenced business as a chimaey sweep at High-st., Runcorn, twelve years ago. In April last he went into business as a coal dealer at Barton. There were 31 creditors, four only being for amounts of £lO. With the exception of £22 money bor- rowed by the bankrupt in October, 1889, the whole of the liabilities were for goods supplied and work done. The bankrupt stated that he had been compelled to dis- pose of the whole of hia effects during the last two months to provide necessaries for his Wife and children and to raise money, to enable him to file his petition. The only book he had kept was one showing coal. &c., sold by him on credit. In reply to the Official Receiver, the debtor said that the debt for £2B to Potter, of Runcorn, was for coal. Re had tried to sell his business at Runcorn, and had agreed to sell it for £6O, but just as he was about to have the agreement signed, Mrs. Blythe, his landlady, gave him a moniles notice to leave the premises. The business was worth £250. Since he left the business he and his family had lived on the pro- ceeds of his furniture, and had a lodger. He filed a peti- tion in consequence of his creditors suing him. He had given a dog cart to Mr. Walker, to whom he owed £2 18s. He knew that he owed Potter more, but he gave the dog cart to Mr. Walker ignorantly. He kept a pony just be- fore he left Runcorn Helost about £7 by it, a.nd lie had bought another in Chester, and this he had to destroy because it had slipped on the ice. He had walked from Barnton to Crewe that morning, and had left his family without a morsel of meat in the house. He had not been able to work, as he had been under the doctor for three months. In reply to the Registrar, the debtor said he was going to walk back to Barnton that day. It waft 14?; miles to where he lived. He had disclosed the whole of his property, and had not handed any over to anyone, except what he left at Runcorn in Hughes' hands. The examination was then closed. DROWNING MYSTERY AT RUNCOUN. Mary Ann Williams. wife of;a flatman named Walter Williams, was found drowned in the tidal basin at half- past ten on Wednesday night. Her husband had left her in the flats' cabin an hour or two :previously, and how she got into the water is a mystery. An inquest will be held to-day.

TRIAL BY JURY AT RUNCORN. With the object of aiding the funds of the University Extension Commiaee, a representation of the comic opera "Trial by Jury" will be given in Runcorn on Tuesday and Wednesday evenings next. The principals will be Miss Florence Dick, Mr. Thomas Barlow, and Mr. John Allen, and thc! chorus of local amateurs is a very capable one. Mr. E. W. Humphreys is the conductor.

THE BISHOP OP CHESTER. The Bishop of Chester becomes entitled to take his seat in the House of Lords, owing to the resig- nation of the Bishop of Truro. It is a singular fact that all the Bishops of the Northern Province, are spiritual peers. THE SHROPSHIRE MYSTERY. A woman named Margaret Evans, housemaid at the Ship Canal Hospital. Barton, Manchester, was arrested on Wednesday morning on the charge of murdering her child, four years old, four years ago last July. The infant's remains were found in a wood near the prisoner's home at Clurn, Shropshire, on the 7th of this month, and the body was identi- fied through its clothes. Prisoner was handed over to the Shropshire police for removal to Bishop- castle. • . " On, YEs!' Cough Mixture, Chiretta Bllsarn. Relief in three minutes. Cures Bronchitis. Hope. late Methuen, Deansgate, Manchester. and [di Dealers.—Advt.

TECHNICAL EDUCATION. The St. Helens Trades Council have had under consideration the question of technical education, and it is probable that next week a deputation re- presentative of the various trades in the borough will wait upon the Technical Education Committee of the Town Council and state their views. The idea is that a school in which mining and art and Science in all its bearings upon the various trades of the tOwn should be established, and that it should be open to the working classes and their children. NEWTON IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION. in response to the application of the Commis- sioners to the Town Council for a grant in aid of technical education for the district, Mr. Lloyd Evans. of Grange-over-Sands, attended at the Town Hall, Newton, on Tuesday morning for the purpose of making inquiries into the, requirements of the township. Ile was met by Mr. Brierley, Dr. Watkins, and Mr. Harrison. secretary to the Viaduct Inltitute, Earlestown. These gentlemen fully explained to the Inspector what was needed, and pointed out what was being done at Earlestown to further the education of the inhabitants. The inspector then paid a visit to the Viaduct Institute and inspected the accommodation there provided foi educational purposts, and expressed himself as perfectly sitislied with the arrangements. Bram FASHIONS now Showing at J. &. W. DUTTON'S Sankey-St.. Warrington.—Advt. THE SUBSIDENCE COMPENSATION BILL. On Monday, a Select Committee of the House of Commons began the inquiry into the brine pumping compensation for subsidence bill. Mr. Gathorne Hardy presided. There are ten petitioners against the bill, including the Salt Uniton, Brunner, Mond and Co.. and the Railway Company. Mr. Balfour Browne explained the provisions of the bill, which provides for the creation of compensation districts, and the laying of a rate of 3d. per 1,000 gallons in those districts, to compensate owners whose pro- perty is injured by subsidence arising from brine pumping. In his opening statement, Mr. Balfour Browne suggested that the committee might do worse than visit the districts affected. He had done so, and had been shown a house which was formerly on the level of the street, but which: had now so sunk, that letters had to be delivered through the chimney. PREMIER SAFETIES, Cash or Hire. —Gnu, AND. Warrington. —Advt.

PROPERTY SALE AT EARLESTOWN. At the New Market Inn, Earlestown, on Monday evening, Mr. Thomas Eutton, auctioneer, Warring- ton, brought under the hammer, two lots of shop property, situate in Eallestown, by order of the mortgagees of Mr. Joseph Birchall. There was a good company present, and the bidding was fairly spirited. The first lot offered consisted of two shops and a dwelling-house,Nos. 6, and 8, Bridge-st., Earlestown, in the occupation of Mr. Jos. Birchall, and this was bought by Mr. Peter McMahon for .EBOO. The second lot consisted of two shops and dwelling-houses, Nos. 10, 12, and 14, 'Bridge-3t., Earlestown, which were purchased by Mr. W. Mills for £705. At the same place on the same evening, Mr. W. Mills offered for sale three shops, dwelling- houses and premises,situate -in Oxford-st., and num- bered 3,5, and 7, in the occupation of Messrs. M. Winstanlev, Jno. Clarke, and Jonathan Rothwell, respectively. The bidding for these started at £BOO, and ad vancd to £1,036, at which price they were sold to Mr. S. Hazleton, Earlestown. LAWN MovrEns.—Garland, 51, Bridge-St., Warrington, and at Earlestown.—Advt. _

LABOUR DISPUTES AT ST. HELENS. The strike of builders' labourers, has been going OR for over a fortnight at St. Helens, and seems no nearer termination. The men asked for 6d. an hour, in lieu of the 50. they have received, and the masters informed them they could not grant it,tts the price they already paid was higher than in the large majority of towns in the kingdom. A deputa- tion from the St. Helens Trades Council has waited upon the representatives of the employers, but without being able to alter the position.—The painters of the town are also agitating for an ad- vance of wages,and a struggle for it may commence at the end of the present month.—At a meeting of the Trades Council, on Wednescay night, it was decided to continue to support the bricklayers labourers who are on strike for one halfpenny per hour. An appeal issued by the council says : " Their application for an advance, when we take into consideration their hours and averages earnings for a period of twelve months. which doe not exceed a£l a week, may be considered a just and reasonable one.

ACCIDENT TO A BICYCLIST AT NEWTON. An accident of a peculiar nature, but fortunately unattended with any serious effects, happened to Mr. James Liptrott, of High-st., Newton, on Thurs- day evening week. It appears Mr. Liptrott and a friend were riding their bicycles at a good speed i along Crow-lane, n the direction of Newton. At the same time, a horse and trap, belonging to Mr. W. Thompson, was being driven by Mr. Thompson's son to Earlestown, and when opposite the Congre- gational Church, the occupants of the trap noticed the two bicyclists coming towards them, Mr. Lip- trott having his head bent down. When he got within a few yards of the trap, they shonted, but Mr. Liptrott evidently did not hear the warning, but kept on his course, and before he discovered his danger, dashed full speed at the horse's head. The impact must have been very great, as, after the collision, nothing was seen of the bicyclist or his machine, for some few minutes, until the horse began to plunge, when the occupants of .the trap could hear the bicycle being dragged along, and, on alighting, they found it entangled in the step of the carriage. By the time it was released, Mr. Liptrott had gathered himself together, and came forward to claim his machine, which, strange to say, was only slightly damaged. Neither Mr. Liptrott, Mr. Thompson, nor his friend,Can say how he escaped so singularly, but it is thought that the force of the collision had thrown him clear from the wheels of the trap. SPRING FASHIONS now Showing at 7. 8G W. Br moles Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. FAILURE OF A CHESHIRE CONTRAUTOIL—THE

CENSUS OF THE WESLEYAN METHODISTS. The following completed returns of the r.:ensus of Wesleyan Methodists were made public on Thurs- day :—Membership in Great Britian, 424,303; on trial for membership, 28,095; young persons in junior classes, 62,416. Nineteen of the districts show an increase, and 16 a decrease. Cardiff and Swansea districts head the former, and Lincoln the latter. Methodism in London shows substantial progress. The net connexional increase is 688.

MAKtIAGE OF LORD HARTINGTON'S OPPONENT. On Wednesday morning, at the Mornington-road Wesleyan Chapel, Southport, the marriage. of Mr. John Henry Maden (Messrs. Maden and Son, cotton spinners and manufacturers, Bacup), and Liberal candidate for Rossentjale Division, and Miss Alice Maden Meller, second daughter of Mr, and Mrs. Joshua Meller, Lytham, was.solemnized in the pre- sence of a very large gathering of Mends, including many from the Rossendale Division.. The service was fully choral, and the ceremony was conducted by the Rev. G. Barlow (Kendal) and the Rev. T. H. Mawson (Southport).

div.head: NORTON WATER TOWER CONTRACT.
div.p: NORTON WATER TOWER CONTRACT.

At Crewe Court on Wednesday, Mr. Fletcher applied to His I.lonour Judge Hughes for the dis- charge of George Rethborie, residing at 35, Victoria- road, Northwich, and Robert Rathbone, of 9, Had- field-st., in ale same town, who for some years were in business as builders and contractors,carrying out very large contracts in Cheshire. Mr. Fletcher stated that they commenced business at Northwich, in 1872, under the title of nathbone and Co., and after ten years' business commenced to take large contracts, including an agreement with the Liver- pool Corporation te build a water tower at Norton in connection with the Vyrnwy scheme. At that time a quarry containing 20,009 cubit feet of rock was purchased, but this speculation proved dis- astrous, as most of the stone was condemned by the engineers of these works. The petition was filed in 1886 with estimated liabilities at £4,525 12s. 11d. A trustee, however, declared them to be £5,669 13s. id. and £3,593 13s. 4d. assets. A first and final dividend of 2s. 13-d. in the pound was paid. His Honour thought that the cirdunistanc6 of the books was not b.s bad as in some eases, though lie commented on other points, and characterised the taking 5f such large contracts on small capital as a very risky pro- ceeding. He would not make an immediate order unless ss. more in the pound was paid, and as he could see no possible chance of that being done, he would suspend the discharge for one month.
