div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday under the presidency of Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P. Present, Dr. O'Keeffe,,Messrs. S. Sadler, J. Houghton, J. Tay- lor, F. Reyes, F. Liddell, (1: I. Neil, H. Timmis, J. Midwood, B. Brown, D. Wright; Oppenheim (acting clerk), Hoyle (accountant), Sinclair (surveyor;, Carr (engineer.)

ME BOROUGH WARDS. Mr. T. W. H. Pelham, the Commissioner who held the Inquiry on the incorporation petition, wrote to Mr. Ges- sage that he was very much grieved to hear of the sudden death ot Mr. Allen. Almost thelast words he (Mr. Gos- sage) said to him on the Bridge last week were to the effect that the Board were fortunate in having so excel- lent a clerk. Ile felt sure trom what he saw of Mr. Allen that Widnes had sustained a great loss. Ile ventured to address to him some observations with respect to the proposed division of the borough into wards. He had received a copy from the Local Government Board of their acts as to electoral divisions. They had departed from the original proposals made by the Local Board, and had transferred a large. area situate between the Sheffield and Midland Railway, and the St. Helens canal to the southern division. Consequently this part must be annexed to the Waterloo Ward. It would he thought make the Waterloo Ward so large that he thought part of the Waterloo Ward should be transferred to the West Bank Ward. It would be better not to dis- turb the Victoria Ward, which is very compact. West Bank Ward is smaller, and cannot grow, so could bear some additions. Perhaps the Surveyor would let them have particulars of any alteration which the Board re- comrnend.—ln reply Mr. Gossage sent a letter enclosing the following amended schedule of ward areas, popula- tion, &c.

No. of houses Ward. Population. Acraage. and Hateable Value. Burgesses. £. s. d. Parnworth 3,303 1.150 551 11,042 15 0 Halton . 4,704 600 784 17,705 15 0 Simm's C-ross 5.742 247 957 11,417 10 0 Victoria ... 5.948 255 941 19,489 10 0 Waterloo.. 6.053 491 1,010 49,017 15 0 West Bank 4.854 296 809 30,666 10 0

- 30,612 3,039 5,102 139,339 15 0 Mr. Pelham in acknowledging the receipt said he was much obliged for the informetion, but he had sent in his report to the Privy Council before the letter arrived. If his description was not quite accurate it could be easily amended when (if the applicatioa be granted) they had to prepare the draft charter. THE WORK OF THE LATE MR. ALLEN. A TEMPORARY SUCCESSOR APPOINTED. The Finance Committee reportel as follows :—/acor- poration.—The Committee being of opinion that the late Mr. Allen was entitled to be remunerated for the arduous work performed by him outside his ordinary duties as Clerk and Accountant in connection with the enquiry recently held with regard to the proposed incorporation of ,the district, recommend that the sum of £l.OO be allowed for such services, and that the same be charged as part of the cost of Incorporation, and the Committee further recommend that the said sum of £lOO be paid to Mr. Allen's widow.—ClerA:ship.—The Committee then discussed the arrangements to be made in consequence of the death of Mr. Allen, the late Clerk and Accountant to the Board, and after full and careful consideration, recommend that Mr. H. S. Oppenheim be appointed interim clerk to the Board, and that the duties of interim elerk shall comprise :—All the duties performed by, Mr. Allen as clerk at the date of his death, but not any 'ser- vices as accountant or in connection with the Science and Art Schools. He shall be required to attend person- ally at the Board's offices as occasion shall require, and shall be responsible for the due performance of the duties of the Clerk's office. He shall at his own cost provide an efficient representative who shall be in atteridance at the Town Hall during business hours; and on the other hand shall be entitled to such use of the clerical staff as may be required for the due performance of the Board's business. The remuneration of the iuterim clerk shall be at the rate of £350 per annum, payable monthly, tagether with his reasonable travelling and other out of pocket ' expenses. and in addition proper legal charges for work he may have to do similar • in character to that accas- tomed to be done by the solicitor to the Board in the past. In case of any doubt arising as to whether any particular work falls within the one category or the other, the same shall be referred to the present Chairman of the Board, whose decision shall be final. The first election of councillors not to be taken to be included in the above remuneration. Accountant—Recommended that Mr. S. Hoyle be appointed • accountant at a salary at the rate of £250 per annum. Recommended that a general clerk be adver- tised for at a salary at the rate of £7O per annum. Mr. Mid wood moved the adoption of the minutes with the exception of those relating to the interim clerk, be- cause he did not think they were getting value for their money. In order that the matter might be straightfor-. ward, Mr. Hayes moved the adoption of the whole of the minutes. and said he was under the impressipn the Com- mittee were unanimous and was surprised to find it was not so. He thought the arrangement the best possible under the circumstances.—Mr. Houghton seconded.—Mr. Midwood said seeing that Mr. Hoyle was to be given an advance of £BO a'year. and that a clerk was to be ob- tained at £7O a year, he thought those two would do nearly the whole of the work Mr. Allen might have done and what was there left for Mr. Oppeuheim ? The resolu- tions were so nicely worded that scarcely any work was left for Mr. Oppenheim to do. To pay him £7 a week as salary and to pay law charges in addition was in his opinion a bad and dear way of doing businees.—Mr. Sad- ler said it seemed about the most one-sided engagement ever submitted to that Board for approval during his term of office. As Mr. Oppenhelin did not intend to ren- der any service in connection with the accountant's de- partment, and no service in connection with the Science and Art School, and that he was to use the Board's cleri- cal staff and in addition be paid for all legal advice,Mr. Oppenheim might be fairly asked to define the precise individual duties he proposed to render for his salary.— The Chairman said he understood Mr. Oppenheim to say thathe would undertake to do all the legal business that Mr. Allen, the late clerk,- was able to do, and which he would net charge for. And they knew perfectly well thas they saved a good deal by Mr. Allen not being a legal gentleman, because he did that work. Any business on which it would have been necessary to consult a solici- tor was the only business for which Mr. Oppenheim would charge during the term for width lie was appointed. ,—Mr. Hayes explained that Mr. Oppenheitn was going to do nearly the whole of the work Mr. Allen did. He would attend all Committee meetings, take the minutes, get out the a)geada, and he would have to keep a man in the office constantly to attend to extra work that might crop up. This could not he done for nothing—it would cost two or three pounds a week, and he could not see that the Committee were recommending anything extravagant: What had previously cost the Board £450 a year would now cost them at the rate of £5OO per annum.—Mr. Sadler said if those duties could be done by a subordinate, whom Mr. Oppenheim would place there, he considered there were men in the town better able to do the work than any man Mr. Oppenheim could send.—Mr. Reyes said the Committee were instructed by the Board to appoint Mr. Oppenheiin and not to search for a better man, and they had no' right to complain now. —TheChairman pointed out that Mr. Allen performed the duties of clerk and accountant, and Mr. Hoyle said if he had to do the duty Mr. Allen did as accountant he would have more work, and that he could not undertake more work than the department in which he was ap- pointed ,and for that he would require an increase of salary. It appeared to the Committee that an advance should be given him and that it was necessary that a clerk should be advertised for to help in his department.—Mr. Oppen- heim would perform all the ordinary duties of the clerk distinct from the accountant's office and would only charge for those legal matters when it was necessary to consult a solicitor.—Mr. Brown said they had always to pay more for temporary efficient service than for perma- nent. There was no doubt Mr. Allen was exceedingly overworked, and they could not expect a man to do the work for the same money that he did. Mr. Hoyle's in- crease was quite justilied,and he did not think they would be able to do much better than carry out the recommenda- tion in regard to M:. Oppenheim,who had got ability and experience, and the business of the Board would be safe in his hands.—After further discussion,the minutes were adopted by eight votes to three.—For: Messrs. Wright, Brown Titnnuns, Liddle, Reyes, Taylor, Houghton, and Dr. O'keeffe. Against: Messrs. Midwood, Neil, and Sadler.

GAS AND WATER. COMIIITTSII. 'The Engineer rtTorted as follows : lllll.—The work. of planting trees and shrubs and trimming hedges, m the avenue approach to l'ex Hill is now complete, and instructions are requested relative to the making of footpaths and c!earing a pnition of land on the hill. 'Boring No. 1 Well, .s:tock's Tfl.—Boring was suspended and the Contractor's men withdrawn on the 14th ult. The depth sunk by the Contractor 192021 t. 10n. making thetotal depth from the engine house floor line 5541 t. 6in. The nature of the strata for the last 22ft. was

coarse and had all the appearance of water bearing, but the level of the water has not been raised. It is evident, however, that tkere is an increase of water from the fact that the level remains at 98ft. 6in., as mentioned in my last report, notwithstanding the continued heavy pump- ing and the unusually long spell of dry weather. It would new appear unlikely that the water can be made to rise to the level of the pumps in this well, and if the Virginia and Mary engine; are to be utilized it will still be necessary for the pumps to be lowered to the water,and a scheme for doing this ifi now in course of preparation. Burst Main in .3famh-st.—On the 24th ult., a 3-inch water main was found to be broken and running full bore into an old sewer with/et showing on the surface. The estimated quantity of water lost is six million gal- lons. The (iefekeive length of pipe was found to be very much decomposed as also a number of others in the im- mediate vicinity which were taken out and replaced. Considerable saving might be effected by placing this district under the waste water meter system. The mean rainfa,ll for the month had been .935 inches. The illumi- nating, power of the gas during the month bad averaged 17.32 candles. The wages required during the next four weeks was for gas and water works £lO5 per week. The Committee recomthended that the tender (£1,336 103.) of Charles Chapman, of Salford, be accepted, subject to the inquiries to be made by the gas and water engineer proving satisfactory—Mr. Brown moved the adoption of t:-,e minutes, and said there had been an increase of 150 million gallons of water delivered during the past month as compared with last year.—The minutes were ap- proved.

HEALTH COMMITTEE. The Medical Officer reported that during March there had been 107 births and 43 deaths, being at the respec- tive rates of 41.41 per 1,000 and 18.58 per 1,000. There were 14. deaths amongst children under one year, and 10 amongst children between one and five years. Whoop- count], caused 4 deaths and measles 2, total 6. Notifi- cations of infectious diseases had been received as follows :—Enteric or typhoid fever 4, scarlatina 7. erysipelas 9, measles 3, total 23. There were 4- patients in the Accident Hospital and 5 in the Fever Hospital.— Recommended that the tender of Mr. W. G. Bucknall to Supply internal telephonic communication at the Fever and Accident Hospitals for the sum of £2l 155., be accepted, subject to the work being done to the satisfac- tion of the Surveyor, and the communications kept in working order for six months after completion.—The Surveyor reported that the apparatus for the extinction of fire was in an unsatisfactory state.—Resommended that the Surveyor take charge of the appliances, and have them tested at least once a month. MR. \MIDWGOD HIS A GRIEVANCE. Mr. Midwood said he saw he was included in the re- commendation ordering legal proceedings to be taken against a number of property owners for insanitary pro- perty. In his case it was an alleged foul ditch. The late inspector, if any nuisance existed on premises in which he (Mr. Midwood) was interestei in, would see him and point it out, and he had always had the matter remedied as soon as possible. The present inspector, he supposed, was too large to trouble himself with that sort of thing. He was not aware that there was any ditch of his which was a nuisance to the Board. The ditch was at the bat- tom of Timperley-st.,the Board had cleaned it out for the past twenty years, and if the inspector referred to that it was a waste of time and trouble and expense to place the subject in the agenda.—Mr. Wright replied that the medical officer had reported that the ditch was injurious to the health of the people residing in the locality. and Mr. Midwood was informed of the matter, and nothing hadnbeen done. The officials of the Board had not time to run about after anybody and everybody.
CORDIAL THANKS TO THE CHAIRMAN.

Dr. O'Keeffe proposed a vote of thanks t) the Chair- man for his services during the past year. The members had had an agreeable time under Mr. Gossage's chair- manship. He hoped he would be long spared to preside over their deliberations.—Mr. Wright seconded the motion, and remarked that the good temper and patience and forbearance displayed by Mr. Gossage was something extraordinary, and the members all felt and hoped that he would occupy a higher position and become the first mayor of Widnes. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Brown supported the motion. Widnes, he said, was exceedingly fortunate in having men of position and good judgment, and who had taken such a deep interest in the welfare of the place. Mr. Gossage and his family had been mixed up with Widnes since its inception, and what he had seen lately did not show any degree or lack of Interest that he (Mr. Gossage) had taken in Widnes. —Mr. Sadler endorsed the re-narks of the previous speakers,and expressed the hope that Mr. Gossage would long be spared to cheat the doctor of his fees.—The motion was carried by acclamation.—The Chairman thanked the members most heartily for thdway in which they-had passed this vote of thanks. He felt very often that his conduct at the Board was not as clear as it might be. and he should in future feel the loss of a strong sup- porter who was better informed en many occasions than he had been and had mentioned points which had oc3urred to him (the chairmAn)—and that was their late friend Mr. Allen. As for himself, he was alwlys at the service of %Widnes and willing to do anything he possibly could for the inhabitants. (Appla,usszo

div.head: lUNCORN SAILORS' INSTITUTE SND MISSION ROOM. SPEECH BY LORD EGERTON.
div.p: lUNCORN SAILORS' INSTITUTE SND MISSION ROOM. SPEECH BY LORD EGERTON.

The Runcorn branch of the Mersey Mission to Seamen have for the past twenty years carried on a good work amongst the floating population of the town; but, for some time past it has been felt that the mission room at Bolton Leeks had become too small for the purpose. It is moreover situated in a locality out of the customary track of those whom it was intended to benefit, and inconvenient of access, and the local Committee determined to erect a new building. By means of a bazaar and subscrip- tions, sufficient money was obtained to warrant a start, and a capital site was obtained in Station- road from Major Orred. The new building as shown on the plans prepared by Mr. John Wilson, die architect, will be a plain gothic structure of brick. On the ground floor there will be a large room and two ante rooms, where there will be provided newspapers and books, various games for the amusement of the visitors and a smoke room. The first floor will consist of one large room 29 feet by 63 feet and capable of accommo- dating c, about 350 persons. This room will be utilised for holdin religious services on week days and Sundays.* 'lt is expected this Institute will have a much wider field of usefulness than the present mission room. The contract for erecting tho building has been let to Mr. Henry Coward, and the total cost will amount to about £1,560, of which £627 has been raised. The ceremony of laying the foundation stone was per- formed on Thursday afternoon, by the Right Hon. Lord Egertion, of Tatton, in the presence of a very large assembly. Amongst those present were the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood (vicar), the Rev. C. M. Woosnam (chap- lain), Rev. J. Fell (chaplain). Major Jolliffe, Messrs. C. J. Bushell (chairman, Mersey Mission), W. Hayes, S. Taylor R. Abel, W, Copper, J. K. Digges, J. Horseeld, G. Moss, J. Meadoweroft, J. J. 'Hewitt, J. J. W. Potter, J. Wil- liams, J. B. Holland, W. Garnett (sec.), 11. Coward, F. Wilson W. Hankinson, T. Handley, I. Speakman. F. A. Lake. ,A. Lightburn, J. Pritchard, W. Mellor, NV. Whittaker, N. Large (superintendent of police), John Howard (missionary Ellesmere Port), Thomas Wil- liams (missionary Liverpool). Eurickson (colporteur Liverpool), W. Shaw (missionary Runcorn), Isc. Mr. Bushell, in introducing Lord Egertoa to the Com- pany, said no one more fit could have been selected to perform the ceremony of laying the foundation stone, not only because his warm interest in all philanthropic effort throughout the country was known to them all, but els° because they believed that the Manchester Ship Canal, one of the greatest commercial and eagineering enterprises of modern times, must of necessity add to the dignity of Runcorn as a port, and therefore to the necessity for increasing their efforts to ameliorate the spiritual and temporal condition'of the canal and seafar- ing population which were sure Lobe largely increased in the course of time. As to the building of that institute it was well known that there was a large floating popu- lation which could not be reached by the ordinary paroch- ial machinery of the Church of England, and the mission to seamen had taken under its fostering care this popu- lation, and worked amongst them with the consent and in harmony with the local clergy, who had always been exceedingly glad to weleome the efforts the mission were making. In 1875 the Bridgewater Trustees placed at their 'disposal a building near the locks and the work there had since • that time been carried out with considerable success. Large numbers of boatmen and their families and sea- men had been gathered into that building until it had ' become too small for the purpose, and it it was, besides, • not conveniently situated at the present time. Hence the deterinination oh the committee to build this new insti- tute, and with the cordial co-operation of the Runcorn Committee—a most valuable one—a consinerable sum had been collected. They all recognised the importance of doing everything possible to bridge the gulf that some- times existed between the upper and the lower classes. If this country was to continue to prosper,and if the Church of England was to hold the position which they believed it ought to do, it could only be by bringing all classes of the population under the influence of the Gospel, which was the one thing which could lead them all to do their duty to God p.nd man. Under God's blessing he believed that building would be the means of accomplishing that most important object. (Applause.) His Lordship who had a most cordial reception, then placed in the cavity of the foundation stone, a bottle containing coins of the realm, the last report of the Mer- sey Missions, and the lacal papers of the day. He then using his trowel and mallet in a workmanlike style, laid the stone, which was inscribed " ro the glory of God this stone was laid by the Rt. Hon. Lerd Egerton of Tattoo, April 16th, 1891." His Lordship said he had great pleasure in laying the foundation stone of the new Institute of Runcorn, which he believed would be for a lasting benefit both sp ritual and -temporal of the sea- faring men of that locality. He was not, as they might know, a stranger to that town, as he had been there on various public occasions for the last 30 years or more. But that day.he had come in the new capac its' of director of the ImipCanal, and he felt that owing to his connec- tion with that body he had still some sloseconnection and

responsibility with the town of Runcorn. (Applause.) It seemed that it was fated to those who bore his name to ' have a connection with Runcorn. In the last century his ancestor and kinsman came there to build the Brigewater Canal (hear, hear) —and j that he believed was one of the foundations of IRuncorn as a seaport. They believed that the greater I work of this century—the Ship Canal—would lead to a still la.roer development of Runcorn as a port, and although it was said that Corporations like the Ship Canal Company had no conscience he believed the indi-• viduals who composed them had conscience like other people and therefure it was of great interest to him to be present that day, because such an institute was much wanted. The sea-faring population was necessarily a transitory one, and could not be provided for by the ordinary parochial machinery of the Church of England. The Church of England he was glad to say was repro. seated on that occasion by the excellent Vicar of the town, Canon Wood, who would no doubt give the same fos- tering care to that institute as he had done by the prayer and religious services which he had given them in con- secrating that building for pious uses. (Hear,hear.) He was told that at least 1857,coasting vessels visited the port of Runcorn last year, and he was certain that before tea years had passed the number would not be merely doubled but increased manifold. The work of the Mersey Mission had teen most valuable to the seafaring and the canal population, and its usefulness would be increased by that new institute where these men would find a kindly welcome, and various provisions made for their intellectual education and for their spiritual welfare. He feltcertain that the sum of money wanted to com- plete the building would be cordially supplied by those who took a deep and lasting interest in the welfare of the seafaring population of Runcorn. (Applause.) Mr. W. Hayes proposed a hearty vote of thanks to Lord Egerton for coming amongst them that afternoon. It was no exceptional case; he had spent his whole life do- ing good. He was the hereditary Duke of Bridgewater —the likeness of his ancestor was in the Big House—and by law he would have had all that fine property. He had control of that very large undertaking the Ship Canal, which he hoped was for the success of everyone, but whether it was a success or not, there would hare been no Ship Canal but for Lord Egerton. (Hear, hear.) To show what a beneficieot man he was he had contri- buted £25 to the collection that afternoon. (Applause.) 1 At the all of Mr. Hayes three cheers were g,iven for his lordship.

Mr. S. Taylor seconded the motion, and said they had a very large floating population in Runcorn. There were several thousand sailors came there annually and they had a very large canal population more boats and flats being registered at Runcorn, he believed, than any other place in the United Kingdom. Boat people were a class who had no homes only their cabins, and that institute would provide accommodation figr them and amuse- ment and instruction for which thdy would bless all who had been connected with it. (Applause.) The motion was carried by acclamation, and Lord Egerton having replied. Mr. Shaw called for three cheers for Mr. Taylor and Mr. Heyes, stating that but for those gentlemen there would never have been a seaman's institute in Runcorn. The cheers were heartily glven and the com- pany dispersed. In the evening the band of the training ship Indefati- gable gave a concert in aid of the institute. Mr. C. J. Bushell occupied the chair, and he was supported by the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, the Rev. Canon Atcheson (St. Paul's, Chester), Rev. C. M. Woo snain (chaplain), Messrs. S. Taylor, J. J. Howitt, J. Meadowcroft, and R. Abel. During an interval in the programme, the Chair- man delivered an address. A very important and useful work, he said, had been carried on amongst the canal ' population, and the seafaring population in Runcorn, by ' the Mersey Missions'and its indefatigable agent Mr. Win. Shaw. (Applause.) To Mr. Shaw thc work was a labour of love, and like all who were in earnest he had sue- ceeded. They would join with him in fervent hope that the new building would be opened free of debt. The land and building would cost about £1,500 and as only £7OO had been collected, there was a large sum yet to be found. Liverpool would do something, but there would be something left for the people of Runcorn to do; and by helping this good work they were opening out their sympathies and conferring a great deal of happinesa on themselves. (Applause.) The Rev. C. M. Woosnam congratulated Mr. Shaw and his willing helpers, upon the accomplishment that after- noon of their long looked for desire, and went on to des- cribe how useful and what a tremendous boon the institute would be to the sailors of the port. They would there find every accommodation for writing home to their wives and sweethearts; they could sit and have a chat and a smoke with their friends, on personal matters or the affairs of the country ; there would be newspapers and books, and also various games provided. The institute he believed would be a great counter attraction to the public-house which was at present the only place where the sailors and boatmen could spend a social evening.—Mr. J. Meadowcroft confirmed Mr. Woos- nam's remarks, and said he was weekly receiving most - touching letters of inquiry about husbands and sons, and if they had only provided sailors means and opportunity to communicate with their friends, they had accomplished one excellent step. As to the boating population there were 50,000 to 60,000 boats passing through the town annually, and that represented a very large number of people, and it was pitiable at times to see how the poor fellows were hang- ing about in the rain with nowhere to go unless it was the public-house, and unfortunately they had experi- enced many sad calamities through men under the influ- ence of drink falling into the locks and docks. If by that Institute they could save one or two lives they would ' have accomplished a great deal. He hoped the mission would receive sympathy and support, and encourage- ment in the work, which was for the benefit of those who benefited the town, for what would Runcorn be without the port and without the floating population. (Hear, hear.) He proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman.— Mr. J. J. Howitt seconded the proposition, and said being connected with the Mersey Mission Committee he had striven to do his duty in trying to get the Institute commenced, and he was clad to see they had got the foundations down. The Chairman had said that the Mersey Mission was connected with the church. ' The mission was connected with the church but it was with the Church of Christ. That was the church that they all believed in and that they had all determined that the poor sailors should be interested in. They would try to give them amusement, for if they did not supply it, they would find it elsewhere. (Elear, hear.) There had been a good work done in the old mission-room which would be now handed over to the Ship Canal people and he hoped they would give £5OO towards the new mission. (Applause.) Let his friend Mr. Meadowcroft carry the message that _ _ _ _ _ . _

_ they wanted £5OO from the Ship Canal. (Applause.)—The motion was carried by acclamation.—The entertainment consisted of instrumental selections, choruses, songs, re- citations, &c., the boys acquitting themselves in a manner which reflected the highest credit upon themselves, and upon their conductor and instructor, Mr. A. B. Smith. Encores were frequent. Mr. W. G. Mitchell accom- panied.

div.head: RUNCORN FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY.
div.p: RUNCORN FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY.

The monthly meeting of the members of the above named Committee was held at the Town Hall, Run- corn, on Wednesday, when there were present the Rev. Canon Wood, 'Messrs. W. Handley, 11. J. Grice, T. Riley, and J. D. Jones (secretary and librarian.) The Librarian reported that the issue for the past month had been as follows :—Theology, 46; philosophy, 6; science. 90 ; history, &c., 179; poetry, 19 ; fiction, 1,644; miscellaneous, 155 ; total, 2,139, or a decrease of 213 as compared with the corresponding month of last year.—The Secretary presented the annual financial statement, which showed that £l9l 3s. 6d. had been re- ceived from the free library rate, the total receipts being £219 ss. Bd.' which, on being added to the balace of £6 13s. 6d., at the commencement of the year, made a total of £226 4s. 91. After meeting all expenses there was a balance of £lO 16s. ld., to carry forward. In answer to the Chairman Mr. Handley said that the amount re- ceived from die library rate ten years ago was about £lBO, but elurin,„a that period there had been an increase of about £lO. A short discussion took place with refer- ence to the manner in which the outside districts took advantage of the library, Mr. Handley pointing out that the rateable value of Weston was about one- fourth of that of Runcorn.—Mr. Grice thought if West- on would take the matter up it would be a great addi- tion to the Library.—Mr. Handley observed that the poeple of Wes'on would get the same advantage of four times their rateable value.. He thought the statement was a very satisfactory one, and he moved that it be approved.—Mr. Grice seconded the motion.—On the proposition of Mr. Handley, seconded by Mr. Riley, it was decided to ask for the rate to be paid in instalments on the same principle as last year. This was the whole of the business.

The strike of Glasgow joiners ended on Thursday, the masters having decided to concede the men's demands for an advance of a half-penny per hour, pending further arrangements. BISMARCK'S ELECTIONEERING CAMPAIGN. As Prince Bismarck has no an absolute majority of votes, a second election will be necesslry between him and the Socialist candidate.

div.head: GWILYM EVANS' QUININE BITTERS
div.p: GWILYM EVANS' QUININE BITTERS
BEFORE TLIE MAGISTRATE 6.
SUPPOSED THEFT OF CLOTHING.

James Towey- , a convicted thief, was charged at the Borough Court, on Wednesday morning, with being found in possession of a lady's singlet, a pair of gentleman's drawers, and _a lady's jacket and nightdress, supposed to have been stolen. Detective-Sergeant Monaghaa deposed to seeing the prisoner in Mersey-street, on Tuesday after- noon with a bag ,coming from Leslie's the clothes dealer's. Witness stepped him, and discovered that the bag con- tained the articles mentioned. He said he had bought them from a woman in Manchester-road; but he had told Mrs. Leslie they belonged to his sister-in-law. He was remanded until Saturday. ON PREMISES von UNLAWFUL PURPOSES. _ _

Bodelia Knockton, a young woman, and a convicted thief, was charged at the Borough Police Court, on Wed- nesday with being found at half-past three o'clock that morning at the lodging-house of Ann Farrell, Cloth Hall Yard, for an unlawful purpose. Inspector Spinks deposed that at the time in question he was with P.C. Turner at the lodging-house and saw some one leave the premises. They subsequently found the prisoner crouched down hi the ash-pit. Someone who had been with her went upstairs while they were on the premises. The landlady said the woman had not been in the house that night. She had been found in the cellar of the house on a previous occasion. Complaints had been made of people in the house being robbed by tho prisoner and the landlady's son, Wm. Farrell, with whom she was intim- ate. About a fortnight ago the police had complaints of the theft of a Cardigan jacket there, and after searching the house they found the prisoner and Wm. Farrell just outside, the latter with his boots off.—The Chief Con- stable said they met in the house when the people in it were sound asleep. She was forbidden to come there.— Inspector Spinks said Mrs. Farrell harboured the woman.—The Chief-Constable said there was a very formidable report by Inspector Spinks against Ann Farrell's house to the Sanitary Committee, and no doubt she would be brought up next Monday. The Bench expressed the opinion that she was disqualified for keep- ing a lodging house if she harboured bad characters, but said they could not convict the prisoner without the evi- dence of Mrs. Farrell, and dismissed her.
THEFTS FROM CLOTHES DEALERS.

At the Borough Police Court on Wednesday, Catherine Cunningham, wife of William Cunningham,forgeman,3B, St. James's-st., was charged with stealing from the shop of John Gibbons, old clothes dealer, 75 Mersey-st., on Sun- day night a child's coat and cape, value 25., and the same night from the shop of William Leslie, old clothes dealer, 65 Mersey-st, two children's frocks value 3s: Chief Constable Hunt said on Sunday night the prisoner went to Gibbons's shop and asked Mrs. Gibbons for is. on a man's coat,but she would have nothing to do with her, it being Sunday night. She missed the child's coat and cape next day. The prisoner after being at Gibbons's went to Leslie's, and Mrs. Leslie was induced to give her a is. on the man's coat, and on Monday morning missed two children's frocks from the counter. Sergeant Monaghan was informed, with the result that the pri- soner was apprehended by him on suspicion. She said the child's coat and cape must have stuck to one of the buttons of the man's coat on her leaving Gibbons's, and as she durst not bring them home because the "old fel- low" was in,she had put them into the ashpit. This was -searched and nothing discovered, and she said the ashpit man must have taken them. She denied knowledge of the other articles, and none of the things had been traced. Corroborative evidence having been given, the prisoner was sent to jail for a month's hard labour.—The Bench and the Chief Constable pointed out to Mrs. Leslie that by advancing the Is. on the coat she had acted as a pawnbroker which she had no license to do, and she might be called to account by the inland revenue authorities.
ANOTHER WOMEN'S ROW.-DISGRACEFUL SIINDIY ROWYDISM.

At the Borough Police Court, on Monday, Harriet Warburton, Ann Denmade, Margaret Mannion, and Mary Jane Dagnall were charged with lighting' on Siinday afternoon week in Buckley-st. Police -Sergeant Jones deposed that about five minutes past three o'clock on the afternoon of the sth inst. be and P.C. Robinson received information at Town's End that a row was going on in Buckley-st. They proceeded there,and saw Warburton and Denmade, who were with Mannion, making use of very bad language. He went into Mrs. Dagnall's and asked er what the bother was about, and she said she had been assaulted by Warburton and-Mannion. There was a large crowd of people about.—P.C. Robinson corroborated.— Mary Weaver deposed that Mrs. Dagnall called Mannion nothing but a street-walker and a bastard, and then the row commenced. This witness also stated that Mrs. Dagnall made an indecent exposure of herself in sight of the people coming out of church at the time. Another female witness said she heard screams and cries of "murder" and " police," and went out and saw a crowd about Mrs. Dagnall's door. She went into the house and saw Mrs. Dagnall on the floor, with her mouth bleeding. Warburton and Mannion were in, and witness said "You ought to be ashamed to go into a woman's house and ill- use her so." Warburton with an oath said "give her another thump." Witness shouted for the police, and Sergeant Jones came. Witness also deposed to Warbur- ton provoking Denmade and to their having a fight.— Mrs.. Dagnall was the only one of the defendants who pleaded not guilty,and was most noisily voluble through- -out the proceedings in court, the other women joining in the result being a clamour which the magistrates had some difficulty in silencing.—P.C. Robinson said the very wornan that had pleaded not guilty had made the greatea row, and was the worst of the lot.—The Mayor: There is no doubt about it. She has done it here.—Mrs. Dag- called a female witness who stated that Mannion and Warburton gave Dagnall provocation by calling her all sorts of names.—The Mayor: They are a very happy lot in Buckley-st.—. Mrs. Dagnall: I will leave it.— rhe Mayor: I should be sorry for the street you go into, You had better step where you are. (Laughter.)—War- burton stated that she was standing at Mrs. Mannion's doar when Dagnall came and called her a foul name, and struck her three or four times. Then she struck back. —P.C. Robinson said the defendants were not drunk,but Dagnall had had a drop.—The Chief Constable: It was three o'clock; the bottles were empty.—The defendants were fined the costs 10s. each and bound over in the sum .of £5 each to keep the peace for six months.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
SA.TUrt. Alderm-an. Burgess (chaiiman) and

.. • Council* Voisey. NON-MAINTENANCE.—John Locker was biought charged by Mr. B. Shearer, on behalf of the Guardians, with leaving his two children chargeable to the Union. Be had deserted them, by leaving the town in August, 1889. Their support had cost the Guardians £l4 Bs. A warrant had been issued for his apprehension but he had given himslp up the previous night. He was sent to prison for six weeks. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman R. W. Fran- comb), and Aldermen Harrison and Suttoyi.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY. - John Collins and Ann Welsh. drunk and disorderly at one o'clock the previous morning in Litton's Road, were fined ss. and costs each. —James Cook, drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket- . at., the urevious night fined ss. DRUNK.—John Potter, file cutter, 15, Priestley-st.,who .3,ppeartid with his head bandaged, and had to be

accommodated with a chair, was charged with being drunk in Golden Grove-st.. on the Bth inst. The officer who proved the case said the defendant fell on the back of his head and split it, and was conveyed unconscious to the Infirmary. The defendant pleaded that it was neuralgic giddiness not drink he had had that made him fall, for he only took a glass, thinking it would make him better, and then had another with a friend.— Chief-Constable Hunt said he had reason to believe that the defendant's statement was true, and it had not been intended to bring him there that morning but to apply for an adjournment; but ttfe defendant had come there of his own accord. The defendant was discharged, and had to be helped out of court on account of his weak condition. ANOTHER NEGLECTED ORDER. Patrick McDonald, forgeman, was charged under a warrant by Mr. B. Shearer, on behalf of the Board of Guardians, with non- compliance with an order to pay 3s. a week for the maintenance of his illegitimate child in the Union. An order was now made for 6s. a week to cover the arrears.

•Prren AND Toss.—Martin McGuire and James Rowe, youths, for playing at pitch and toss in a passage off Buckley-st., on Sunday afternoon week, were ordered to nay the costs, 3s. ed. each. FURIOUS DDIVING.—Thomas Outram, was charged with furiously driving a horse and cart in Battersby-lane, on the 6th inst. The defendant said the horse shied at some cinders in the road, and was frightened at an engine on the bridge. He was fined ss. CHIMNEYS ON FlaE.—Samuel Dodd, Water-st., Latch- ford, and Henry Heald, 7, Church-st., for having their chimneys on fire on the 4th and 3rd inst. respectively, were fined is. each. _ _ . _
TIIE-SDAY.—Betore Messrs. W. Owen (chairman), E. M.
Crosfield, and E. J. Guest.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—John Ward, charged with not appearing to a summons for being drunk and dis- orderly in Bridge-st., on the 14th of February, was fined ss. and costs.—John Farley, drunk and disorderly in Dial-st., on the previous night, was fined ss. and costs. —Bridget Murphy, drunk and disorderly in Stockton-rd. the previous night, was fined ss. and costs.—John Whit- taker, drunk and disorderly in Horsemarket-st., the pre- vious night, was fined ss. and costs.—Jane Griffiths, drunk and disorderly in Church-street, the previous night was fined ss. including costs.—Sarah Jane Dinney, drunk and disorderly in Scotland-road, on Monday night was fined ss. and costs. _ _ _ _ _

Dnuxx.—John Highfield, drunk in Wilderspool-road, on Monday night, was fined ss. and costs. VAGRANCY.—Bridget Dooney, a married woman, John Dooney, Edward Dooney, a boy, and Mary Ann Smith were charged with sleeping in an empty house, 36 IJames-st. Evidence was given as to damage being done to the premises by the breaking of the door off the hinges, also breaking the window. The Dooneys had formerly lived in the house': and Bridget denied that the damage was done by the defendants. Edward Dooney was dis- missed, and the others were committed to prison for seven days' hard labour. The police were instructed to place Edward Dooney in the Workhouse, his father hav- ing deserted him. ASSAULTING A CONSTABLE.—John Nicholls was charged with assaulting P.C. RylPtt, in Fennell-st., on the pre- vious night, and fined 103. and costs. BREACHES OF SANITARY REGULATIONS.—John Collins, Thos. Hart, and Michael Roach, for not keeping their lodging-houses in Stanley-st., clean, were each fined ss. including costs.—Thos. Berry and John Dutton, Silver- st..and Silver-square,were charged with having outbuild- ings in an offensive condition. Berry very voceferously pleaded that he did not live in the house and it was not taken in his name. Mr. Norman the prosecutor, stated that the woman the defendant lived with occupied the house. She r.iw stated, much to the indignation of the defendant, that if he was out one five minutes he was in the next. (Laughter.)—Berry was fined 10s. and Dutton ss.—John Wright and John Neons, Turners-yard, and Hannah Smith, Turner-st., were charged with a similar offence. Smith was dismissed,and Wright and Noons were fined 2s. ed. including costs each. ScHoor, ATTENDANCE Cum. George Dunbobbin's case was adjourned, the mother producing a medical certificate; George Battams, navvy, 247, Mersey-st., was fined 2s. ed. including costs; Sarah Cook, laundress, Rose-yard, 24. ed. and costs; Edward Coulter, labourer, 12, Ship-yard, ss. including costs; Michael Flynn, 85, Catherine-st., ss. including costs; Thomas Leigh, plate- layer, Florence-st., had to pay costs and had an atten- dance order made against him.—ln the case of John McDonald, dl Back Ship-yard, employed at the White- cross Works, Mrs. McDonald said the boy's father had thrashed him most scandalously, but he would not go to school, and he was caned at the Roman Catholhf School for not going to chapel. The case was dismissed, the lad as to whom the defendant was charged being threatened with the birch if his case was brought up again.—John Plunkett, labourer, Old-road, was fined ss. including costs. WEDNESDAY.—Before Aldermen Holmes (chairman) and Chandley and Mr. J. Fairclough. . .

DRUNK. Thomas Brown was charged with being (hunk in Buttermarket-st., also with peddling without a license. The defendant appeared with his arm in a sling, but Detective-Sergeant Monaghan said he could throw his arms about freely when he liked. He was sent to pri- son for 14 days' hard labour. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—John Duffy, drunk and dis- orderly in Winwick-st., on Tuesday night, was fined 55., including costs. Ping AND Toss.—Martin Joseph Watson was charged under a warrant, with playing at pitch and toss, on the 28th of June, 1885. A police-constable said on the day in question he was on duty at Bridge Foot when a lady and gentleman from Arpley Meadows complained to him that a lot'of young fellows were playing at pitch and toss. He could not get at them because they had pickets out, but he got permission to go into a house down River-road, and he watched them through a field glass and took down their names. As the result, all were convicted, except Watson, who left the town. He had been back occa- sionally, and that morning surrendered himself. He was fined the costs.

FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison and Dr. Gornall. DRUNK AND DISODDERLY.—John Turner, Michael Coffey, and Frank Greenough, militiamen, were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-st.,the previous night. Greenough was also charged with assaulting John Turner.—P.C. Turner, deposed that he found the defendants drunk and fighting in the street mentioned. Turner was on the ground, and Greenough was kicking him. Witness got him up. Then Coffey Came and tried his best to take Turner out of custody, and said to witness "I've a good mind to pull my belt off and give you a bit:" He was in company with a WOMRII of bad character,and used very bad language. He said " I have served one six months, and will serve another for you yet."—P.C. Marsh corroborated and said the defend- ant Turner pulled off his belt to strike the constable Turner.—The defendant Turner declined to give evidence against Greenough as to the assault.—The defendants were fined 55. and costs each.

_ FIGHTING.—Ann Platt was charged on a warrant with fighting on the night of August 26th, in Morris's-yard, off Church-st., and was bound over in her own recogniz- ances to keep the peace for six months. •NON-MAINTENANCE. —Joseph Phillips, Kendrick-st., Michael Loughlin, Stamford-st., and Wm. Nicholson, Akin-st., for not contributing to the support of their mothers were dealt with. Phillips had a warrant against him suspended for a month to allow him the opportunity of paying: Loughlin was sent to goal for seven days. and Nicholson was ordered to pay is. a week .towards arrears or go to prison for a month.

WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. At this court on Monday, before Major Pickmere, James Walsh was charged with being drunk at Golborne on the previous Saturday, and fined 55., including costs. At the same court; on Tuesday morning, before Messrs. E. Greenall and J. C. Parr, Thomas Pilling was charged with being drunk and disorderly whilst in charge of a horse and cart, at Stretton, on the 13th inst. He was fined 2s. 6d. and costs. The fine was paid.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY _ SESSIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY _ SESSIONS.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. G. Comber (chairman) Major Pickmere and _Mr. J. J. Bleckley._

DAMAGING TELEGRATII INSULATORS.—Johii Thos. Will- ing and Albert Fisher, boys, were charged with damag- ing on March 22nd, two insulators in connection with the electric telegraph wire belonging to the Cheshire Lines Committeep—Mr. P. Davies appeared for the pro- secution and said he was instructed to press the case,as a considerable amount of damage had been done through the breaking of these insulators. There was a great danger of stopping the current of electricity by breaking these, and it was most difficult to discover where the, stoppage was caused. In this case the insulators had not been so completely broken as to stop the current.—P.C. Devlin deposed to seeing the defendants throw about a dozen stones at the insulators,which fell to the ground in pieces.—P.C. Dugdale corroborated.—T. Young, detec- tive, in the employ of the Cheshire Lines Committer, said he called on the defendants with P.C. Devlin on the 28th ult., and asked them why they had been throwing stones at the insulaters,and they replied that they did so because they were a good mark, but they blamed each other for throwing the stones. He had had a great many com- plaints about stones being thrown into carriages from the railway arches and breaking the windows and striking passengers.—The defendants who pleaded guilty were fined ss. each, including costs. Box AND DlCE.—Joseph Richards and Robert Farnworth were charged with playing at box and dice on Good Fri- day, near the general Elliott at Croft.—A police-sergeant deposed that RiFharcls was'down on his knees with money before him playing at the game, with a crowd round him, and Farnworth was keeping watch for the police.—A constable corroborated and said Farnworth had been play- ing at the game before Richards.—Farnworth said he had given up the game three years since, but it was shown i that he had been fined for tin 1890. Richards was fined ss. and costs, and Farnworth 10s. and costs.

div.p: RUNCORN_PETTy_ SESSIONS.

MONDAY.—Befo-re Mr. C. Reyriolds and Mr. A. Thomas. ZiIISCELLANEOUS.—Thos Kelly, James Cappon,Michael Lowey, John Johnson and Richard Brannon, were each fined ss. and costs for drunkenness.—James Kershaw, was fined ss. and costs for being drunk at the Grap9s Inn, lialton-road.—Patrick Moran was ordered to pay costs 4s. ed. for allowing the chimney of his dwelling. house to be on fire.

div.head: RUGBY.
div.p: RUGBY.

WARRINGTON RANGERS V. LEIGH SHAMROCKS.—PIayed at Warrington, before a fair attendance. The visitors winning the toss, played with the wind, and Savage on behalf of the home team kicked off. The opening stages found the Leighites defending, but getting warm to their work, they rushed the ball b3.ck to neutral ground. The game was evenly contested, both sides showing splendid form, and was without doubt the finest played on the Rangers' ground this season. Potts assisted his old club. but was too well watched to do much damage. The game eventually resulted in a draw—Rangers, 3 minors; Leigh, 2 minors. RuscoßN v. WIDNES.—These neiethbouring rivals met on the Runcorn ground, on Wednesday evening, in the presence of about 6,000 spectators. During the first half Widnes played with the wind in their favour, and imme- diately pressed thehome team. Their passing and drib- bling was very fine, but the defensive tactics of the Run- cornians proved fully equal to the occasion. For nearly twenty minutes they held Runcorn in their own quarters, and then Widnes in turn were pressed. The game at half time stood—Widnes 3 minors, Runcorn 2 minors. On changing ends Runcorn asserted their superiority, the visitors' forwards falling off considerably in their efforts. From a line out Owen Hughes got hold and dashed over the line in fine style, Houghton failing to kick the goal. A few minutes before the close,Crompton received a pass and made a capital dodgy run,argl placed the ball behind the posts. Houghton added the goal. The game was throughout fought in a friendly spirit, and was of a very fast description ; Runcorn were the winners by 1 goal, 1 try, 6 minors, to 3 minors. RUNCORN V. SALFORD.—A large body of spectators was drawn together on the Irwell-lane ground, Runcorn, on Saturday, the attraction being thereturn match between the above named clubs. The weather was beautifully fine. The teams were as follows :—Runcorn: Houghton back ; T. Davies, J. H. Crompton, and H. Hughes, three- quarter backs; Antrobus and S. Abrams, half backs; W. Hughes, A. Hampson, W. Faulkner, 0. Hughei, J. Gayton, R. Dolan, W . Shaw, and H. Williams, forwards. Salford: Mainwaring, back ; Myles, Barrett, and Barrett three-quarter backs ; Green and Walsh, half backs ; Kent Knowles, Roberts, Birch, King, Makin. A. Knowles, and Lough (forwards). The ball was put in motion by the visitors. Faulkner returned, and a scrimmage was formed, and then followed a series of passes between Antrobus, Abrams, Hughes, and Crompton. Play was then forced on to the visitors' lines, and from a kick by Crompton, Mainwaring was compelled to touch down. A vigorous attack was made on the visitors' citadel. A second edition of passing was given, the prime actors being W. Hughes, 0. Hughes, and T. Davies who scored a try. A capital though unsuccessful attempt was made at goal by Houghton. Myles then put in a splendid run; but Gayter, who was en the alert, brought him down. Gayter made a capital attempt to secure a try ; and was only brought up near the line. The register at half time was Runcorn 1 try, 5 minors ; Salford nil. In the second half the play was of a similar character, and Runcorn only succeeded in scoring one minor,although they pressed throughout.

WARRINGTON 2ND V. CLAUGHTON'.—This match was played at Warrington. Warrington kicked off against the wind, and an attack, headed by Russell, Buckley, and Ho'croft, was at once made. The home half backs early demonstrated their superiority, but a strong run by Mitchell found the leather dodging about the centre. After Phillips, Bailey, and Isherwood had put in some good work, Warburton, from Lawless's pass, got off into his opponerifs' 25, and the visitors were hard pressed for sometime, Rowe ultimately scoring, from which Heesom placed the goal. After this Russell ran finely to the lines, but Claughton retaliated by rushirfg into the home 25, and a capital run by Williams endangered the Warrington lines, and a minor was conceded. The drop-out found Claughton in the ascendant, until Warburton and Plinston transferred the game to midfield, and soon afterwards Rowe, passing to Warburton, enabled the latter to drop a capital goal. The kick off Was of no advantage, for some strong play by Buckley and Rowlands carried the oval to the visiting quarters, and Barnes soon scored, Buckley converting. A grand bit of play then ensued between Lawless. Rowe, and Russell, and had the latter's good pass been taken, a further score would have resulted. Half-time arrived with Warrington 3-0-0 to 0-0-I. The second half was a fac-simile of the early portion of the contest, a bit of play by Plinston early forcing a minor, and a similar point was conceded after a very near thing for a dropped goal by Lawless. The rest of the game was all in Warrington's favour, Rowe, Bailey, and War- burton scoring, the final result reading—Warrington 4-2-5 to Claughton 0-0-1. WIDNES v. Cnourrow.—The return match between these two clubs was played at Widnes on Saturday after- noon. Smith for Widnes kicked off against the wind, but Crompton returned well, and by excellent passing, the home line was placed in great danger. Hartles and Drummond relieved, and the ball was carried to centre. Crompton now had to defend his line, Brennan making a good bid for a try. Drummond next made a splendid run from quarter to quarter, and the ball being subse- quently carried over the ling, Brennan scored for Widnes. The kick at goal, however, failed. Widnes kept up the attack, Barber forcing a minor. Howarth then scored a try, placing the ball behind the posts. Notwithstanding the easy position for goal, the kick by Tweedale failed. From the drop out Peters failed to return, and a scrim- mage ensued on the home line, from which Mills scored the second try Crompton. Whitehead also failed a goal. At half-time the score was—Crompton, two tries and two minors ; Widnes, one try and one minor. On chang- ing ends, the visitors again attacked, but Hartles, Bar- ber, and Peters relieved, and carried play into the visit- ors' quarter, but only for a time. Butterworth next scored an unimproved try for Crompton. After splendid passing between Barber, Peters, and Johnson, Barber scored a try. Smith took the place kick, and a goal re- sulted. Widnes, now leading by a try, maintained the advantage, and sorely pressed the visitors. From a throw in in the visitors' quarter Gordon got possession, and, running through, placed the hall again in an easy position for goal. Smith again was successful. The game was a very fast one, and Widnes gained a very creditable victory by two goals, one try, and two minors, to Crompton's three tries and two minors. WARRINGTON (FAIR TURNER'S TEAM) v. swlN- s TON (VALENTINE'S TEAM.)

Teams under the above heading met at Swinton on Monday evening, the object being to give a helping hand to a junior cricket club in connection with the Swinton Football Club. Turner relied upon members of the Warrington first team, his contingent being composed of the same players, with one exception, that of Povey for Nevins, which defeated Barrow on Saturday. Val- entine, on the other hand, had a strong lot up, the team comprising two internationals and seven county men. Soon after six o'clock Valentine started before nearly three thousand. The ex changes between Evans and Wiaterbottom settled play at half way, but on the first scrimmage breaking up Jolley dribbled finely down the touch, Paul judiciously saving. • Aided by smart play on the part of Bumby and Brockhank, the Warrington quarter-flag was reached, and an over anxiety on the part of Hallam and Hotchkiss penalized the homesters. Fair Turner's kick forcing Swinton to defend. Paul got the oval away, but Warrington, combining well in the forward division, again aggressed, Berry being conspicu- ous. Passing by the Bates all but ended in a score, Val- entine and Martinscroft, by accurate tackling, !staving off disaster. Fine passing between Bumby, Valentine, and Myleq saw Daniels tackling well, and Fair Turner brought the Salford three-quarter down a moment later, a yard from the line. Slowly the oval was worked out of danger, and although Martinscroft got in a huge kick, Boscow awaited its coming with commendable coolness, and Swinton were kept at Bay. Free kicks were at this point very frequent, Ra9dles, Evans, and Barnes Valen- tine, and Myles, for their respective sides, all showirig up ito advantage. From a mark by Valentine, Paul had a shot at goal, and Barnes conceded a minor. Sharp passing by the visitors' half gave Warrington a footing in Swinton territory,. and Evans with a power- ful kick and quick follow up prevented a reply. Some fine passing by Randles, Ashton, Povey, and Evans was applauded to the echo, and although this effort was the cause of Warrington reaching the line, Valentine, Martinscroft, Bumby, and Myles, by excellent combin- ation, took the play to neutral ground. From some huge kicking by Evans and Baynes the oval was rushed over, and Miles conceded a minor. On the drop-out another spell of exchange kicking was loudly applauded,and then a determined raid was made on the Swinton citadel. Another display of passing by the Warrington forwards found Evans dropping at goal, and a second minor was recorded. James Bate metthe drop-out in fine style,and although Warrington attacked slightly, Walker, Hallam, and Rothwell dribbled to beyond the half-way flag,where Bumby passed to Martinscroft, and Valentine and Myles joining in the movement, the latter put the finishing

MISS COBDEN'S APPEAL

The Court of Appeal on Thursday dismissed the appeal of Jane Cobden from the judgment of Mr. Justice Day, casting her in penalties for voting at the London County Council. The Court held that Mis3Cobden could attend the Counc:l meetings, but not vote. Considering the circumstance, her penalties were reduced to 50s. and costs.

The football match on Wednesday between Dterton and'QUeen's Park, played on the EVerton ground before 10;000kpectators, resulted in a draw of one goal each. Aston Villa. beat Notts County by 2 goals to none, Hyde beat Preston North Bnd by 3 goals to 1, and Sheffield Wednesday and Glasgow Rangers played a drawn game of three goals each.
RAILWAY DISASTER IN AMERICA.
A, TRAIN ON FIRE.-DISTRESSING SCENES.

Mgr YORK, TUESDAY.—A fast freight train on the Delaware and Hudson Railroad came into collision yester- day with a gravel train near Cableshill, New- York State, and a number of cars were wrecked. One of these, which, was attached to the gravel train, and which con- tained five Italian workmen, was thrown into the centre of the wreck, and the whole mass caught fire. Two of the men were killed outright, and the remaining three were injured. Pinioned in the wreckage, as the flames reaohed them their cries and groans were heartrending. Owing to the position of the car and the intense heat, the rescuers Were unable to reach them, and were compelled to *atoll them slowly burn. to death J All ' the victims leave families.

div.head: TM', EXAMINER,. SATURDAY, APRIL 1, 1891. NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. FOOTBALL.-RUGBY.
div.p: TM', EXAMINER,. SATURDAY, APRIL 1, 1891. NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. FOOTBALL.-RUGBY.

touch on a brilliant effort. Paul made a good bid for ,zoal. Another minor fell to Warrington before the call of half-time, the score then reading—Swinton-0-1—l; Warrington, 0-0-3. On resuming, Holmes nearly scored from the kick-off, Paul luckily saving. However, a minute later a grand run by Povey forced the Swin- tonians on their line, and after James Bate had tricked Bumby, Randles scored from a line-out. Frank Turner took the place, which was on the touch line, the ball fall- ing short by about a foot. Encouraged by this success the visitors still pressed, and J. T. Bate with a zigzag run harassed the home defence. Relief came when Kent, Rothwell, and Martinscroft got clear away, the pluaky saving tactics of Boscow preventing the trio from pass- ing the quarter flag. A spurt by Valentine failed to make any impression. Free kicks were frequent, and about ten minutes from tho call of lime Brockbank got clear of his field, and running to Boscow handed over the charge to Bumby, who completed the try, Paul landing an easy goal. This was the last item of an interesting game, and the final score read—Swinton, I—/—I; War- ington. —O--I-3. The following comprised Valentine's team :—Paul, back; Valentine,Winterbottom, Martins- croft (Walken),and Myles (Salford), three-quarter backs ; Bumby and Brockbank, half backs • Hotchkiss Rothwell, A. Sharples, G. Sharpies, W. Walker, T. Hallam' . R Powell, and T. Kent (Salford), forwards. Referee, Mr. E. Seddon, Broughton Rangers.

In dealing with the season's perfoimances of clubs oat- the Manchester district, a writer in the "Manchester Guardian" says "perhaps the only club that has per- formed with consistency is that of Walkden. Here we find a team that includes several players who deserve to be better known, and the record of the club certainly warrants a better list of fixtures. A team that can twice beat Wigan, besides other notable victories, is entitled in every respect. Their colours have only been lowered twice. Wigan are still powerful, but they have not equalled their doings of twelve months ago' when they were undefeated in the West Lancashire Leakue tourna- ment. Oldham have exhibited in and out form, and yet they have a capitarreserve of players. Rochdale Hornets have sadly deteriorated, some of their reverses having been terribly heavy.. St. Helens Recreation have had a goodly time of it on the whole, and both Runcorn and Warrington have held their own as a general thing. None of the Liverpool' clubs are as formidable as in nest years, and as a rule they are very poorly supported by the public, Rugby football being now RCA) patronised in the city."

On Saturday the South-east Lancashire trophy passed out of the possession of the late holders, Ratcliffe,into the keeping of their neighbours from Tottington, who were the smarter team. A goal and a try fairly represented tho superiority of the winners, whose backs were too strong for the Ratcliffe men. The tie attracted some 6,000 spectators to the Whalley Range enclosure. This , was fairly satisfactory. but it pales before the assemblage of 15,000 which was seen at the final for the Yorkshire cup at Leeds. Here was a great struggle between Ponte- fract and Wakefield Trinity, when the latter,." the heroes ef a hundred fights," were vanquished after looking like winners until well into the second half. Pontefract laboured hard after the Trinity obtained the lead, and in the end they came out triumphant by a goal and a try to a goal. Pontefract had never reached tho final previously,but their antagonist are seasoned cup fighters. They kayo figured in the last round nine times; and carried off the honours on four occasions:. Twelve months ago they opposed Huddersfield in the final game.

div.head: WARRINGTON v. BARROW.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. BARROW.

The return match between these clubs was played at Wilderspool on Saturday. Barrow have now appeared on the Warrington list for the past six seasons, but it 19, questionable if during the whole of that time they have been participators in such a grand game as that of Satur- day. The Warringtonians were seen at their best, and although Barrow claimed to have a weak team on hand, we doubt whether the presence of the "two absentees"' would have materially altered the final result of the game. The start was delayed until nearly five o'clock, and at that time- there would be four thousand pre- sent.

Frank Turner kicked off, and some exchange kicking between A. Harley, Barnes, and Evans found the game at Barrow quarters. Ashton was prominent with &short dribble, and although the Barrow goal was in jeopardy,. the defence of Dickinson and Bowker was excellent. A• long pass from Barnes to Daniels led up to the Northeners trespassing on Warrington ground, a combined dribble by Frank' Turner. Holmes. and Jolley relieving terns porarily. Bowker put in some telling kicks on thepopu- lar side, and from one of these some loose scrambling play among the visiting backs was witnessed,. and Hainey passing to A. Harley, the latter dropped a smart goal. This point had its effect, and from the kick. off play was taken almost under the Barrow. posts. James Bate was almost in from some tricky work, and although the visitors were allowed a free kick by way of penalty, the Warringtonians would not be denied and put oretho same pressure loubly strong. Boscow with a long kick and Nevins with a strong rush improved tee position I of the local team, but Daniels failed to take advantage of a beautiful pass from J. T. Bate, and Barrow soon re- I gained thelost ground. Barnes and Evans put in some , splendid runs, and although sharp passing between the two Bates gained but little ground. J. T. Bate ran in dodgy style, being pulled up a yard from the line. From the subsequent throw out the oval was crossed by Fair Turner to Barnes, who made the score equal by a clever drop. Fair Turner met the drop out, and a run and quick follow up saw him with the- oval, and matters again looked bad for Barrow. A mull was made of the pass, and a couple of kicks by Bowker caused the game to rest at the home 25. Boscow only partially responded against the strong breeze, and some fine combination amongst the forwards was backed ueoby J. T. Bate, who ran and dodged in grand style,.his effort being slightly I marred by holding the oval a little too long. The visiting forwards combined better, and fair catches by Leaks and Jolley gaited little for either side. lEvans kicked finely, and Barrow were forced to defend once more. A sharp passing bout between Hainey and Dickinson changed the venue, and Randles caused some amusement by a long kick, which considerably aided the visitors. A fine run and pass by Berry to Donohue saw the leather being well held, and although Fair Turnergot clear a momect later, the Barrow backs got the oval working amongst them, and a sharp running movement resulted in Bowker scor- ing, the same player failing, at the place. Jolley was prominent on.the drop out, and from a tall kick by James Bate, Ashton's height served him to advantage, and Marsh having his kick charged, the home skipper promptly equalised. Evans failed at the place. The Warringtonians were now playing splendidly together, and no sooner had the drop out been effected than the Bates passed correctly, and Evans being the final reci- pient, one of the finest runs ever seen at this enclosure landed him a scorer behind the posts. This was a bril- liant effort, and well worth the applause which greeted it. Barnes hit the posts with the place. Near the call of half time Ashton made an effort, being brought down near the line, but amends were made from the scrim- mage which followed, James Bate tricking his oppon- ents, and scoring behind the uosts, Barnes this time putting the finishing touch on it. Score at half-time— Warrington, 2-2-0; Barrow,.l-1-0. On resuming,Barrow opened the game, and although they attacked in the first few minutes, they were in reality never dangerous. after-- wards. Jolley put in a long run along touch, and a passing movement between the two Bates,. Barnes, and Evans found the latter being held on the line. Rainey got the °vat away smartly, and Daniels apparently scored, but the verdict was against him. Short passing by the home backs once more roused enthusiasm, and Fair Turner forced the first minor with a ions. kick. Evans threw to Barnes, but Marsh brought the amester down on the line, and E.vans next essayed a drop at goal with a futile result. A fine run by Donohue from a pass by J. T. Bate was productive of a strong attack, but the task to open the scoring account of this half fell to tee lot of Jolley, who got away from a pass by,Donohue: and ran clean round the Barrow backs, planting the oval I behind the posts, Barnes failing at the easy place. Anotherfinerun by: Evans almost brought disaster on the Barrow goal. Sharp practice between Bate and Berry I neutralised the drop out, Donohue being collared. Bowker again relieved with judicious kicks, but the grand combination of the homesters saw the Barrow backs offering but feeble resistance to the strong attack, and Holmes scored, Randles placing a goal. A fair catch to Warrington was taken by Jolley, but nothing came of it, whilst Fair Turner should certainly have scored on two occasions. Minors fell to the credit of Warrinaton in quick succession, and near the call of time the front rank rushed the oval over, and Nevins was credited with the final point. Fair Turner placed a goal, which was the last point of interest, a grand game eon- ' eluding with the score as—Warrington, 4-3-5; Barrow, 1-1-0.

Teams :Warrington: BO3COW, back ; Daniels, Barnes, and Evans, three-quarters ; James Bate and J. T.. Bate half-backs; Ashton, Fair Turner, Frank Turner, Bandies, Jolley, Berry, Donohue, Holmes, and Nevins, forwards. Barrow: Marsh, back; T. Bowker, Dickinson, and A. Harley, three-quarters; Rainey and Leake, half backs; Todd, Blizard, Garner, Greaves, J. Bowker, Babbs, Fell, Alsall, and Hall, forwards. Mr. S. Williams, referee.

ASSOCIATION. GARSTON V. WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION.—These teams met on the ground of the former to play their return fix- ture. In the former encounter the Garston team were the victors by 3 goals to one. Warrington were without Davies at back while Garston had their full team on. Kicking off about 3.45 p.m., the home team had the best of the opening exchanges, but the visitors, livening up, severely taxed the home defence, being eventually re- warded by Ball scoring the first goal, with a splendid shot, twenty minutes from start. From the re-start, some smart play was the result, Finch scoring for the home team, Brown adding another shortly afterwards. , The visitors played up after this and severely taxed the home defence, Powell heading the ball vary strongly against the upright. They repeatedly had hard lines but failed to equalise the half-time, result being Garston 2 goals, Warrington 1. From the re-start, the visitors played a hard game, Ball, Powell, Mather, and Ayling sending some stinging shot into the home goal, but the custodian was equal to the Gccasion. Eventually trom a pass by Ball. Ouions equalised. The Warrington for- wards and halves were now noticeable for some fine head play, taking the ball almost the length of the field, but nevertheless were unable to increase their score, the whistle sounding with the Warrington men in the home goal. Final result: Garston 2 goals, Warrington 2. Warrington team: Goal, Jones; backs, Phillips and Parry (captain) ; half backs, Ayling, Warburton and Mather; forwards, Clayton, Ball, Onions, Powell, and T. Mather.

Very !few of the leading Association clubs can point to any material advance on previous seasons. EVerton pose as the League champions, but this is due to the Wing off in the play of the Preston North Did rather than to any improvement on the part of their successors. Al/ the same, however, Everton have rilayed better foot- ball;. all things considered, than any of their rivals, and aree entitled to their proud position. No club in the kingdom has a brighter prospect. They have taken far and away more gate looney than any other club ,and have a splendid list of players in their service.

Blhckburn Rovers have again carried off' the much- coveted English Cup, but this is their only comfort, as in every other respect they have done badly. During the last few weeks the victory at the Opal was the only success in a ion.., series of matches. The Mirth End have come down rthe ladder with a rattle. They have not the consolation of a championship or a cup of any description, and have not more than half a dozen players fit fora League team. Their glory has departed, and they are not likely to ever akain approach the excellence they achieved two or threeyears ago.

AN ACTRESS'S ACTION FOR BREACH
OF PROMISE.

In the Queen's Bench Divisioilom Tuesday, the breach of promise action brought by an actress named Miss Gertrude Ellis, or Evelyn, against Mr. W. Hurlbert, to recover £lO,OOO damages was resumed. Plaintiff gave evidence of an extraordinary character relating to her meeting with the defendant, the:galleged promise of marriage, and visits with him to Paris, Brussels, and other places. She told him of her discovery that he was married while in Paris„ and he then proposed to pay her £BOO down, and £1.50, yearly tor life. He had not carried out his promise. In cross-examination by the. Attorney- General, witness admitted she lived in the same house as Mr. Jackson when she made the detendant's acquaint- ance. Mr. Jackson had been known as Mr. Evelyn, and she had passed as Mrs. Evelyn,but not before parting from defendant in May, 1890. Before then she had lived on the Continent as Mrs. Evelyn, and in the same house as Mr. Evelyn at Monte Carlo. Defendant had shown. her many indecent pictures, and written disgusting let- ters. Defendant was then known as Wilfred Murray„ and she was astonished when she learnt that he denied, the whole story. ,Through defendant she was intro- duced to Mr. Wilson Barrett.

On Wednesday various persons were called to identify the defendant 'S person and handwriting. The Attorney- General denounced the case as a gross,and wicked at- tempt to levy black-mail. Mr. Hurlbeet had employed up to 1890. a person named Murray, whose handwriting was 'marvellously Pike his own. Murray asked him to befriend plaintiff, who was anxious to go on the stage. He saw her once with Murray, and subsequently wrote to Mr. Wilson Barrat, on her behalf. It would be proved that on the day when plaintiff alleged that she stayed with Mr..Huribert at the Windsor Hotel he was travelling to Paris with two ladies, whose names he would write down also that he was not at Brighton at the tune alleged, and that Mr. and Mrs. Harlhert were staying with Mr. Beckett, M.P. during Jtuncaster races, when plaintiff alleged she was with him. His contention, counsel said, was that plaintiff,,at the times she speci- fied, was carrying on an intimacy, not with Mr. Hurl- bert, but with Murray. Mr. nurlbert was called, and swore that the letters produced were not 116,' . but Mur- ray's. The case was adjournkalL The hearing of the breach of promise, Evelyn v. Hurl- bert, was resumed on Thursday. Mr. Wilson Barrett, actor, said he had known defendant five years, but did not remember seeing plaintiff before the present proceed- ings. In 1887 he received a letter in which defendant asked him to find a small part for a lady in whom he Was interested. Defendant,reealled, said he could not find W. Murray. It was untrue that lie had been intimate with the plaintiff, or that he, had promised her, marriage. Defendant went to Brussels on May 6th, 1887, and did not return to London tilt the end of the month. He had net been to Ghent for .30 years. When. at Brighton in 1887, he stayed with Mr. Beckett. He had never been at Virginia Water. Defendant, cross-examined, said it was untrue that a ft= of solicitors declined to under- take his case. No rationat being knowing him would believe he wrote the \ letters produced. He had made every effort to !Ind Murray, and last beard of him at Philadelphia. He wrote down for counsel the place where he believed Murray now was. George Bert- ram, hall-porter at the Grosvenor Hotel, stated that he knew defendant only asMr. Hurlbert. A person signing I himself Wilfred Murray was at the hotel in 1887. The case was again adjourned.
