_ STOCKTON 11EA.TII CONyIRUATION.

Sir,—Having been absent in London, I missed your paper of the 4th inst., but was asked,yesterday if I had seen Ur) account, in the letter of a correspondent, of the Bishop's lunch acid champagne at Stockton Heath. I had not done soAut I at once referred to the paper, in which I find the following extraordinary remark "How the reverend father enjoyed his lunch and cham- pagne after the performance (i.e. the eonfirmation) it is not my business to enquire, although it cost the poor agricultural labourers of England some £12." The only foundation for such a statement is that, considering that -some of the clergy and candidates had come several miles to attend the confirmation, a tea was given to them in the schoolroom, which was provided by spon- taneous liberality, and no one was asked to contribute a penny. The Bishop remained with us in the school- room above an hour. and I believe enjoyed his tea, and the opportunity afforded him of seeing the neighbouring clergy, and making the acquaintance of many of our parishioners, in this friendly way. So he expressed himself to me. There were no stimalants of any kind ever thought of. 'The Bishop had no other refreshment during his visit, and was treated no better than the poorest person there. What is meant by its costing Eng- lish agricultural labourers £l2, Ido not ‘understand. Yours &c.,
ROBERT DAVIES, Churchwarden
16th April, 1891.

AN ASSEMBLY HALL FOR WARRINGTON. Sir,—lt has struck me as a most anomalous thing that a place like Warrington, a corporate town, numbering some 50,000 citizens, should be unprovided with a public hall anything like commensurate with the wants of its inhabitants. One would imagine that the necessity for the provision of such a -building would be the all- absorbing subject that would be engaging the attention of its authorities ; but on the contrary it appears to be at present a matter quite remote from their consideration. The Public Hall has answered the purpose very well for the more immature period of Warrington's history,but the town is beginning to expand; and to feel all that arterial energy about it,which demands more advanced conditions than satisfied it in its adolescent state. The Town Hall is a building well adapted for the purposes for which it is at present used, but from Sits situation and its want of accommodation for public meetings its name may be said to be almost an incongruity. The imperative need of thl town is a really commodious and useful building, which both the ratepayers and the community at large can feel is their own; and which may constitute a centre for the discussion of municipal and other public matters. The Public Hall is usually so monopolised with entertain- ments that it would be a difficult matter to secure it for a meeting on any momentous local question; and its accommodation is far from adequate. It is a standing reproach against Warrington that it has no really worthy representative building to which it can point a stranger, or in which the inhabitants can meet to venti- late local grievances. There is no deficiency which seems more to argue the absence of public spirit than the want of such an edifice. Ido trust that a determined effort will be made in the Town Council, and on the part of the inhabitants, to remedy this most palpable, vital, and inexcusable defect in the constitution of things in Warrington .—Yours truly,

div.p: ENTERPRISE.
THE GAS SUPPLY FOR SANKEY AND •PENKETII.

Sir,—ln reading over/the report of last week's Town Council proceedings, I noticed that one of the members "wanted to know why the ratepayers of Warrington should have their profits dealt with for the purpose of providing a capital expenditure for the ratepayers of San- key and Penketh." (Cries of "Hear, hear.) "He hoped the Council would have an opportunity of debat- ing the question." Please allow me to put the case in a nutshell. The old Gas Company, whose powers and privileges are now vested in the Corporation, and have been since 1877, have had power to supply gas to Sankey ever since 1847, and to Penketh ever since 1871, yet neither the company nor the Corporation have hitherto chosen to avail themselves of the powers and privileges vested in them, and have left Penketh and Sankey in darkness. Now certain of the inhabitants want gas (good coal and cannel gas, , and • not Town Council gas), and long-headed people as • they are • (some of them), they foresaw that if they attempted to supply themselves and foithed themselves into a com- pany, and went to Parliament for an Act to clothe them with the necessary powers, the very first and probably the only persons who would oppose them and put them to several hundreds of pounds of expense would be the Corporation ef Warrington, en the ground that the pro- moters were poaching: upon the preserves of the Corpora- tion. So the aforesaid long-headed persons decided on shaping their course in such "a manner as would have the effect of either making the Corporation exercise their own powers or of taking the sting oueof their opposition tail. Applications were made to the Coporation for a supply of gas to Sankey and Penketh. The Corporation may either supply it or not,as they please. If they supply it,well and good. If they decline, they will he precluded from acting the role of "Dog in the manger," and from opposing others who are ready and willing to help them- selves.—Yours &c., WILLIAM DAMPIER JEANS. Great Sankey, 14th April, 1891.

VERITAS.
April, 1891.

A NEW ASSEMBLY HALL FOR WARRINGTON Sir,—l was very much interested in the letter of your able correspondent, Mr. George Woods, advocating some better provision in the town in the way of an Assembly Hall or Concert-room. Mr. Woods's letter is so exhaustive and the arguments are so strongly buttressed with perti- nent facts and figures that little is left to be said as to the feasibility of the scheme. Agreeing, as I do, with the opinion that the need of further accommodation is sorely elt, I shall be curious to note the attitude taken up by our representatives in the Town Council upon the subject Surely there is amongst our men of "light and leading," some enterprising and far-seeing individual with a soul above the Intercepting and Losgford Depots who will see to the ventilation of this question. Granting that the urgent need of a building such as that suggested by your correspondent can be demonstrated—and as to this there can I think be little doubt—then the. s. d.of the matter should be thoroughly gone into. Mr. Woods propounds a scheme which will not aciti materially, if anything, to our burden of local taxation, and of course we are all in- terested in keeping the rates on the down grade course upon which is gratifying to note they have at length en- tered. Let the arguments pro and con. be thoroughly sifted. It seems to me that the Auggestion of combining the long-talked of Baths with a Concert-room is a good one, and money may be ultimately saved to the ratepayers by considering the two projects I simultaneously. The locality is a very important point for a building devoted to one or both purposes. If a combined building were decided upon, there would seem to be room enough on the Legh-st. site, and the position is fairly central. But it has been suggested to me that, if the Assembly Hall idea is taken to by those in authority, the old Market Hall sheltering the butchers is the most desirable site. As this building is understood to have been more or less of a white elephant on our hands ever since it WM erected, its conversion and enlargement into a first-class concert hall with the.frontr• age to Horsemarket-st., would afford relief in more than one direction. Sooner or later the shops in Horsetnarket- st., must come d.)wn. Why not, tßen, Tiring forward the Market Hall with suitable enlargements and adoptions for the special purposes in view? I trust that the scheme for a now Assembly Hall, now that it has been promul- gated, will go forward. If he needs of Warrington in this direction could only be made sufficiently widely-known, I feet sure there are capitalists outside the Borough who would look favour- ably on the scheme as a purely commercial investment. —Yours, &c.,
SPECIAL MEETING OF RUNCORN
COMMISSIONERS.

A special meeting of this Board was held at the Town Hall, on Thursday. Mr. S. Taylor presided, and there were also present—Messrs. El. White, H. J. White, W. Mellor, E. Imison, W. Hankinson, F. Wiswall, E. Marshall, (sec.), and M. Barker (sur- veyor.) TIE MOW RATE AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION. Mr. Imison, chairman of the Finance Committee moved that the seal of the Board be affixed to the general dis- trict rate of Zs. 4d. in the 2.—Mr. Mellor seconded the motion, which was carried, only Mr. White voting against.—Mr. White remarked that the rate was big enough without any extra penny being put on.—The Chairman said he was sorry Mr. White had not the same feeling that he (Mr. Taylor) had. In no possible form could technical education benefit him or his, and he felt too broad on the subject to expect benefit from it. (Mr. Imison: Bear' hear.) The ratepayers could not charge him with selfishness, and he should be glad to pay hie proportion of the rate.—Mr. White : Yes and I shall have to pay my share.—The %meeting then resolved itself into the Legal and Parliamentary Committee.
SPECI ATOB.
A POINT OF CASUISTRY.

Sir,—ln your last impression there appears the report of the sentencing of a boy at Warrington, to seven days' imprisonment with bard labour, for stealing eight shillings and five postage stamps from the pre- mises of his employer, and of his being convict, but not sentenced for the theft of a shilling from the same pre- mises. As to the latter charge, the prosecutrix deposed that she having missed eight shillings and the stamps from her box, marked the shilling and placed it under some scissors, the object being to ascertain whether the boy would steal it or not, and if he did, give him in cus- tody on both charges. I must say that to me this method of procedure in such cases appears to be very objectionable. The end, of course is supposed to justify the means, but this sounds to me rather like Machiavel- lian casuistry. I think, under the circumstances, it would have been more becoming on the part of the prose- cutrix if she had contented herself with merely proceed- ing against the boy for the principal theft, and not charged him with the minor offence. Since reading the report of the case, I have road the account of a similar one heard at the West Ham Police Court, London, on the very same day. In this case a marine store dealer, named Robert Jacques, charged his servant, Ada Baytie, aged 13, with stealing eightpence in bronze coins, whieli he had marked for her detection. The following is the dialogue which took place between- the magistrate (Mr. Baggallayl, and Mr. Jacques in court; and I would commend it to the attention of all local employers and magistrates :—"Mr. Baggallay : If you missed the money, why did you leave it about? Witness: We are used to leaving it. Mr. Ba.ggallay : Don't you think it would have been better to have removed temptation from the girl ? She is not fourteen yet. Do you think it was fair, or just. or kind? Mr. Jacques was then called in, and he said that he put the small bowl containing the money on the sideboard. Mr. Baggallay : What did you put it there for? Witness: To catch her. Mr. Baggallay : Why? Witness: Beciuse I caught her before, on Monday week. Mr. Baggallay : Did you speak to her at the time? Witness :No:. I thoeght I would be certain and have proof. Mr. Baggallay : Don't you think it would have been more kindly for you to have put the money out of her way? I discharge the , girl, and 1 think it a most disgraceful thing to throw temptation in the way." Ido not mean to say,of course, that the deeision at West Ham was strictly according to law, but it is one with which a great many of your readers will have difficulty, like myself, in not 'feeling a certain moral sympathy. Ido not know whether the Warring- ton magistrates were influenced by any such feeling in the case of the boy, but I was glad to see that they did not add to his severe enough penalty, too severe in my estimation, by sentencing him for the theft of the shil- ling.—Yours truly,

OPENING OF THE WESTON MARSH LOCK.I The first lock connected with the Ship Canal, that ' at Weston Marsh, which is to take the traffic be- tween the river Weaver and the Ship Canal, was held on Thursday. There were present Mr. S. Platt (chairman of the Works Committee), Alderman W. H. Bailey, Councillor H. Boddington, Mr. J. K. Bythell, Mr. Leader Williams, Mr. Abernethy, jun. (resident engineer of the section), and Mr. J. Weston contractor's agent), who has executed the work. The party embarked on the con- tractor's steamtrig, and .the gates being opened, steamed into the lock. The lock, which is 315 feet long, 42 feet 6 inches broad, and 16 feet deep, has three pairs of gates, the intermediate ones dividing the basin. The gates are worked by hydraulic power, obtained by using the water of the Weaver Canal. and are put into gear by friction cones. The machinery has been constructed by Messrs. pleghorn and Wilson, IVl.iver Foundry, Northwich. Boats can pass through the lock in from three to lour minute.• . The gates, which are made of the finest greenheurt • wood, have been tested by the Weaver Trustees, and are as tight as a bottle. Eventually they will be handed over to the charge of the Trustees. In the course of the day, the party visited Eastbani section, and were highly gratified at the rate at which progress is being made. In the course of a month, it is expected, the monster lock at Eastham will be in working order. All the gates are now hung. KILLED ON THE CANAL/AT ECCLES..

Yesterday afternoon. Mr. F. Price, held an inquest touching the dea9l of Richard Knight, 26 years of age, late of 15, ThArton Grove, Patricroft. Deceased was em- ployed as a labourer, and on Monday last was at work in the Eccles cutting. He endeavoured to pass between the boiler end of a working steam navvy and the " face " of some rock, when he was caught between the frame work on which the boiler stood and was severely crushed by the moving of the navvy against the rock. He died from his injuries on Wednesday. A verdict of accidental death was returned.
DR. KOCH.
Professor Koch is 47 years of age. In 1843 he saw
le light at Clansthal,wh ere his father was an ogeial
EMIN PASIIA.

dward Schnitzler, who has become famous under the name of Emin Pasha, was born on March 28th, 1840, in Opptln, Silesia. He was educated at the Nehise mnasium, and at the medi- cal schools of Breslau and Berlin, where he graduated in 1864. He subsevently ac- quired the mastery of several European and Asiatic lan- guages. About 18 he set out for Turkey, where he fell in with Hakki Pasha,. whom he accompanied on official

in the employ of the milling company. From the age of nineteen to twenty-three, he studied at Gottingen, where he was brought under the influence of the famous Jacob Henle. Henle wain all-round man of science,who had gained his laurels as an antagonist, but who held enlightened and advanced views on many mect _ Among other things he held very strongly that the influence of plant life in its lower forms would be found to underlie many of the .diseases to which the frame is liable. lt is more than probable that to Henle's suggestions may be traced that line of thought which in the case of Koch heti- led to such great results. After taking his degree, Koch became assistant physician at the hospital of Hamburg, and shortly afterwards he started in private practice in the little town of Lanv.,enhagen, in Hanover. Hence he migrated to Wolistein, where,in a little village, he settled down to the hum-drum life of a country doctor. He was then twenty-nine years of age, strong and vigour- ous, with all his great powers striving for in outlet, even in the unpropitious surroundings in which he found himself. Never, surely, could a man have found himself in a position 'less favourable f6l. scientific research—poor, humble, unknown, isolated from sympathy and from the scientific appliances which are th.....-cwswiry Louis or tee investigator. Yet he was a man of trio strong a eharacter.to allow himself to be warped by the position in which he found himself, or to be diverted from the line of work which was most congenial to his nature. Looking round, he saw that in one respect, at least;. he might claim, an advantage over his scientific brethren. If they had chemicals,* laboratories, instruments, microscopes, he, at least had cattle— nothing but cattle. To cattle, therefore, be turned himself, and soomproved that work of first-class importance might be achieved amongst these humblest of patients. Splenic fever,which has been surmised to have been one of the plagues of Egypt, has long been, a bugbear of Continental farmers,and the important results which followed Koch's re- searches into the causes of the disease gave him a world-wide reputation. In 1880 Koch finally abandoned hi g country practice and, went to the University of: &inn as assistant to Professor Pinkelnburg. In the scientific atmosphere of Bonn, Koch found himself at last in a thoroughly con- genial situation, and was. soon at work again with his miCroseopes and his solutions. In 1882 he an- nounced and demonstrated the bacillus of tubercle, and a year or two later, after pursuing his studies in India, he. discovered :the choleralmcillus. But, above all, so far as present appearances go,_ the greatest of all Dr. Koch's achievements is the dis- covery of a remedy, or partial remedy, for tuber- culosis,the announcement of which towards the end of last yearrerused'so. great a stir all the World over.

In 1875 l+e returned home, only to stay, however, fbr a few months; for in 1876 we find him acting as surgeon PEI the Egyptian army as Dr. Emin Effendi, , and in that capacity he was ordered to Khartoum: In 1878 when General Gordon was governor of the Soudan, Emin was appointed governor of the Equa— torial Province of Egypt., In 1886 he appealed for help. In consequence of this appeal a relief ex- pedition, under Stanley was sent out in January 1887. and succeeded in reaching him. Emin, how- ever, preferred to remain in tne land or nth choice. The patron's medal of the London Geographical , Society was awarded to Itmin in June, 1890,and was 'received on his behalf by Dr. Felkin. Owing to his 'falling from a window in-the latter part of Decem- ber, 1860, Emit suffered from a severe illness. At :one time indeed his recovery was scarcely expected that occasion he received an expression of sym- pathy from the Queen. Emir,, it may be added, Ails a post in Africa 'under. the German Government. Emin Pasha, we are told " is extremely interesting as a finished type of the kind of product which the scientific culture of the modern world turns out. He is the naturalist who, although he has.acted as Gbvernor Pasha and Commander-in-chief is always, first and foremost, a man of all the ologies.' Ento- mology, ornithology, zoology, everything but the- ology, absorbs his attention."

div.head: HAYSTACK FIRE AT MOO,PAL
div.p: HAYSTACK FIRE AT MOO,PAL

About half-past ten o'clock on Sunday night an alarm of fire was raised at Stockton Heath by the ringing of the firebell at the brewery. The Wilders- pool Brewery brigade and eight firemen were soon in attendance, and started for the scene of the con- flagration,which proved to be on the premises of Mr. Jonesthe landlord of the Red Lion Inn, Moore. It appears that a haystack had caught fire, and the brigade succeeded in saving about half of it. The origin of the fire is unknown, hut the damage is not ' very great. The flames were extinguished about midnight.

Parish, J.P., of Chester, presided, and he was supported on the platform by the Hon. Lady Sebright. The first portion of the proceedings consisted of vocal and instrumental music, which proved highly enjoyable. Miss Edith Crosby and Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys con. tributed a pianoforte duet and then Miss Crosby per- formed a s)lo. Miss Clara Taylor gave a song and in conjunction with Miss Simkia rendered a duet. Miss Nina Harrison, who is only 14 years of age, performed a, violin solo in capital style to the accompaniment of her sister Miss Kitty Harrison. The Chairman in introduc- ing Lady Sebright to that meeting said he was delighted to find in Runcorn as in Chester and many other towns,. that they were to have an organisation of ladies for the promotion of temperance work. Up and down the coun- try the ladies connected with the movemen had done an, immense amount of work in opposing the proposal to compensate publicans. In his opinion the temperance party were on the highway to complete triumph as they had gained two great victories, one,in respect tea:the Welsh Veto Bill and the other in the House of Lords upon the Sharpe-Wakefield licensing case. The latter victory had settled for ever the question of compensation to publicans. (Applause.) They . had made two great steps forward, and they might do much more by form- ing associations like the one they- wete inaugurating that evening. (Applause.) Lady Sebright who had a cordial welcome, then delivered a chatty speech, which sparkled with wit and apprppriate anecdote. She de.scrilled'the .gigantic evils attending the liquor traffic, and urged the women of England to band themselves in an organised attempt to put an end to it. She did not believe in moderation but in total abstinence which was the only remedy. (Hear, hear.) The only cure for drunkeness was not to drink. It was from the ranks of the moder- ate drinkers that drunkards were made. She hoped every woman present was prepared to join the Runcorn Women's Temperance Association and sign the pledge. She did not approve of the temperance party attaching themselves to one political party or the other. Ireland, Scotland and Wales had Sunday Closing Acts and shame upon England that they had not thot one; and when they had obtained that piece of legislation, she hoped we should go in for closing altogether. (Applause.) Let them stick to their guns and get Sunday closing, local option, prohibition, and grocers licenses withdrawn. (Applause.) Illustrations of the temperance story "Buy your own cherries" were then shown by limelight, the lantern being manipulated by Mr. Horace W. Handley. The customary votes of thanks concluded the proceed- ings.'

div.head: BOATING; DISASTER AT WESTON POINT.
div.p: BOATING; DISASTER AT WESTON POINT.

On Sunday afternoon a shocking • boating acci- dent occurred on the Mersey, near Weston Point. 1 Five men who were employed on the Ship Canal works obtained a small boat and went on the Mer- sey for a sail. By some means the boat was cap- sized and the wholA of the occupants 'were thrown into the water. At considerable personal risk a flatman named J. Tansey of Widnes and a seaman named Frank Davies re.ieued three of the men and brought them to the shore. The other men were washed away by the tide and drowned. Afterwards the body of David S. Thomas, a stonernason, was recovered, but the body of the other, who is only known by the cognomen of "cockney," could not be found. The accident occurred near Frodsham Marsh, and it is said the men bad no experience in the management of boats. INQUEST. _

On Tuesday an inquest was held by Mr. J. E. Worsley, coroner, on the body of Thomas, at the Weaver Hotel, Weston Point. William: Thomas, Glenallan, Bangor, deposed that the deceased was his son, who was a maso.n and 24 years of age. William Snape, belonging to a. travelling theatre stationed at Runcorn, said he was com- ing down he line at Weston on Sunday and saw the five men in the boat on the river. He then saw the boat among the piles upon the new works. The men were trying to catch hold of •a. niece of wood when the boat heeled over and they were thrown into the water. Itohert Gregson, of Weston Point, one of the five men in the boat said as they were passing one another to have a spell at nullity! the boat upset, and they were all thrown out. He swam to the piles, and got hold of the boat and was saved. Thomas and another man, Blakeman, were drowned. • The others were saved. Witness was picked Up by a boat. There was an ebb on, and the tide was running out. He thought it safe in the boat. John Tansy, cooper, of Widnes, said he witnessed the acci- dent, and called to tome men who threw some planks out to the drowningnum Orle of the former lay upon a plank and swam milt() the drowning men. The tide was running out, and theater was running very heavily frpm the sluice. The drowning men fought very des- perately, but the strain was too great for them to swim against the tide. He saw Thomas go down. Witness could swim, but no one could jump into the stream as it was with five men struggling in it. The jury returned a verdict that the deceased was drowned through the up- setting of a boat in the river.
PENKETH.

div.head: ANNUAL. MEETING OF THE LIBERAL
div.p: ANNUAL. MEETING OF THE LIBERAL
ASSOCIATION

On Monday evening the annoal general meeting of the Penketh Liberal Associatiion was held in the cluh-room. Ameagst those present were—Messrs. C. E. Parker (chairman), J. Mainley, G. Randall, T. Seed, W. Lcrngslravv, R. Routledge, H. Wilkinson, E. Cross, T.. Dram A. J. White (treasurer), and F. Hughes (secretary). Mr. Parker apologised for the absence; through illness, of the President (Mr. J. T. Gumersall). The treasurer's report was read by Mr. A. J. White, which showed that the year was started with a balance-, of £4 4s. lLd. The total income for the year amouthed to .c.e54 3s. Bd., and the total ex penditure was £5l Os. lid.; balance in hand £3 2s. 9d. Some discussion arose amongst those present with reeard.to some of the items in the report.—Mr. Par- ker asked how it was the members' subscriptions had gone down.—Mr. White said that was explained by the fact that the subscription of one member had not come in. It was also mentioned that the recbipts from the billiard table were lower than last year. This was ex- plained. however, by Mr. White saying the receipts last year were abnormal,being rgaly in excess of the amour.t taken in previous years. The receipts this year were up to the average.—On the motion of Mr.Mainley,seconded by Mr. Longshaw. the treasurer's report waa adopted, with one dissentient.—Mr. White said that in, the min- utes.just read by the Secretary, one gentleman had com- plained that the Association did not do much politically. —The Treasurer said he would like to read a statement of the money which was collected to be sent to the execu- tive. This was done, and showed that the total amount collected was £9 is.; the amount sent to the executive was £?; sixpence was paid for a receipt book; balance in hand, sixpence. A vote of thanks te. the retiring 'officers, was proposed by Mr. E. Cross, seconded by Mr. J. Routledge, and carried unanimously,— Mr. Randall proposed, and Mr. Longshaw seconded, that Mr. George Broadhurst be elected president. Caryied unanimously. The following gentlemen were elected vice-presidents, on the motion of Mr. F.... Hughes, seconded by Mr. E. Cross :—Messrs. Parker, Belton, Htiehes,. Gar- nett. Peers, D. Garnett, and J. T. Gumersall.—Mr.. A. J. -White was unanimously re-elected treasurer, and ltr. F; Hughes secretary. saveral of those present bearing testi- many to the excellent service they have rendered in past years.—Mr. F. Hughes proposed ,alui Mr. T. Seed seconded, that Mr. T. Drury be elected a.ssistantsecretary. Carried unanimonsly.—The following were (unanimously elected as the Committee :----Messrs. Longshaw, Seed, R. Rout- ledge, H. Wilkinson, George Bates, J. T. Budden,.G. Ran-. dell, E. Cross. It was decided to have the annual mem- bers' trip on the afternoon of the third Saturday in July, details to be decided at a Cemraittee meeting to be called. —This concluded the business for the evening. The meeting was.then declared open for the discussion of any subject of interest to the members.—Mr. J. T. Budden suggested that something should be done in the way of instruction of the younger members in the tenet; of the Liberal faith.—Mr. Longshaw, Jr. Ra.ndslt, and several others also spoke on the subject, and Mr. Randall said he thought it would be a very good thing if a number of papers and lectures were written by these who were willing, dealing with the opinions of the Liberal party, Src., and read before the members.—The Chairman (Mr. C. E. Parker), in a short speech briefly referred to several of the burning questions which are before the country at the present time, and recommended them to the serious I consideration and study of his hearers. He mentioned the eight hours yestion, the one man one vote bill, free education, technical education, the land question, &c.— Mr. White, Mr. Drury, and others also spoke at some length on these questions.—The. meeting was concluded by Mr. Cross proposing and Mr. Mainley seconding a vote of thanks to Mr. Parker for his services as chairman, the motion being carried unanimously.

THE'CLITFIEROE GAM. STATEMENT BY MRS. TACKSON.

Yesterday Mrs. Jackson published in the "Lancashire Evening Post" her own statement in explanation of the recent abduction of her by her husband. She says that Mr. Jackson was known tb her a few years before their marriage. Meeting him at different places as she did,she thought he wasa man ofieisure,living upon bismeans. He several times proposadto her, and she refused. When she became engaged to him in 18T he said he had enough to keep himselnut not to keep a wife and him- self.. She believed he cared for her, and would make a good husband. Aftcrwards she was advised not to be I married to him unless he consented to remain iq England and sho told him. He said all arrangements were made for him to ao abroad, and she broke off the engagement, much to Mr. Jackson's annoyance. He afterwards wrote saying how miserable he was, and she renewed the engagement. Thoy discussed the plans of what he was going:. to do in New Zealand. She adds:—On the following Saturday, as he was going away on the. Sunday, I allowed the objections I had to the proposal to be overruled, and gave way. I asked him many times over and over again, whilst in the drawingroom, to be always good and kind to me, and he promised this, and it was proposed that I was to go out to him when they shontd be well settled on their land. On the-follbwing Friday,3ovember 4,1 met Mr. Jackson in the ferenoon at the house of a friend, and it was then arranged that I should go on the following day to his sister's heuse at Blackburn to be married. My people knew nothing of these meetings or arrangements. I did not tell them because I I,..nevr they did not like Mr. Jack- son."- The above is believed to be only the first instalment of the story which Mrs. Xackson proposes to make pub-

THE QUEEN AT GRASSE. GRASSE, TUESDAY. Beautiful weather favoured the anniversary of Prin- cess Beatrice's birthday to-day. The town was gaily decorated with flags, and, this evening, was illuminated. The streets were filled with enornyus crowds of sight- seers. Her Majesty held a reception, at which the chief notabilities of the town were present. Princess Beatrice received hundi eds of bouquets from all parts of the coun- try, as well as congratulatory telegrams from the various European Courts.
